Uniform Title: Kriyākramadyotikāvyākhyā Author: Kacchapeśvaraśivācārya Manuscript: IFP Transcript T00109
Description: IFP transcript T00109, copied from a manuscript belonging to Śivaśrī Svāminātha Śivācārya of Tiruvāḍuturai, Tanjore District.
Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.

The *Kriyākramadyotikā* by Aghoraśivācārya, who lived in South India during the twelfth century, is the primary ritual manual that guides the liturgical procedures in most of the major Śaiva temples of South India. This is a major commentary upon it by Kacchepeśvara, who resided in Kāñcī. At its outset, he refers to Aghoraśiva as his teacher, stating that he composed this work impelled by the latter’s grace.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: November 21, 2014.
Country of publication: India.
Salutations to the illustrious Śiva and Śivā.
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by saluting whom at the commencement of all undertakings, Vāgīśa and the other wise ones become fulfilled in their purpose.
Salutations to the venerable Śiva and Śivā.
This [is the property] of Svāminātha Śarman, the worshipper of the illustrious Gomuttīśvara.
Salutations to Śrī Śiva, the Supreme Brahman.
I bow to Mahāgaṇapati, the son of the enemy of Madana,
who stands gracefully upon the beautiful thighs of his consort with his body embraced by her arms—
the elder brother of the Lord of the Vellīs, the bestower of desires upon those who take refuge in him.
O Lord, whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods, including the Lord of Speech (Brahmā).

Whose limbs are gazed upon by the bracelets of his beloved, who is stainless and beyond the limitations of time, who out of compassion is intent on bestowing desired boons upon all men who worship his own feet,
who is the cause of the destruction of the limbs of desire, the destroyer of the Kali age, and whose throat shines like a surging wave;
I am Kāmākṣī, the wife of my lord, who is eternally the leader of Kāñcīpura.
Śambhu himself, who previously descended directly from the abode of Sadāśiva in order to bestow grace upon other devotees, has come here.
I bow to that teacher of ours, renowned here in Kāñcī by the name Sadāśiva, who is possessed of exceedingly gentle qualities.
Having prostrated before the stainless Lord Īśāna and the Śakti who resides in him,
as well as Gaṇeśa, Vāṇī, and the gurus beginning with Sadeśa;
By the grace of my guru, I shall provide an exposition of the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, a manual on the path of the Agamas composed by the supreme teacher Aghora.
Here, indeed, the illustrious Aghora Śivadeśikendra, who is skilled in the knowledge of the entire Śiva-āgama,

[addresses] in the first verse Paraśiva— the root cause of the collection of rites and other matters to be described— and the Śakti inherent within him, for the sake of completing the work he has begun without obstacles.
Having paid homage (p.
by means of the second verse, preceded by a salutation to his own guru, he states the subject matter of the treatise which he is about to compose.
He makes a formal declaration regarding the eternal nature [of the Lord] with the words beginning "I bow to Him who is superior to the universe":
superior to the universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving, peaceful— meaning free from passion, hatred, and the like— and beginningless.

"Nidhana" means end; "janmanidhana" means destruction. "Ādi" means beginning. That which has neither beginning nor end is "ādinidhana. Thus: "He for whom birth and destruction do not exist in any way—He is without beginning or end, and is devoid of the sixfold modifications."

Because it has been stated thus: "Niṣkala" means devoid of parts (*kalā*); "niṣkalaṅka" means devoid of blemish (*kalaṅka*), that is to say, stainless. I bow to—that is, I pay homage to—Śiva who is of such a nature. Immediately following this, [I praise] her whose essential nature consists of knowledge and action (*jñānakriyātmikā*), where *jñāna* (knowledge) and *kriyā* (action) constitute her very self.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "I bow to the power of Śiva as previously described, and to the power [of the aforementioned deities]. (p. 4)

He states the second verse: "Having bowed to the gurus"—those who have come down in succession from the Supreme Lord (Āparameśvara) through an unbroken lineage of sons; those who are *parāpara* such as Sadāśiva and others, and those who are *apara* such as Durvāsas and others, down to one's own personal guru—having thus paid homage to those gurus.

Regarding "of the daily and so forth": the daily [rite] refers to obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) such as ritual bathing and the like; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the occasional (*naimittika*) is meant, by which initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) are included. As it has been said:
"Bathing, worship, recitation, fire-offering, and meditation—this is the pentad."

Thus one should always and constantly perform [these rites]. Initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) should be known as the two types of occasional (*naimittika*) rites. Thus, this [work] is the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, which illuminates the sequence of rituals; these rituals include bathing, the worship of Śiva, and so forth, as well as the mudrās and other elements present therein, along with their sequence and procedure.
The remainder of the sentence is:

"I shall clearly compose that which illuminates and reveals it. Regarding that, he states what must first be done among the eternal [mantras] and so forth that are about to be described, beginning with the word "prātaḥ": p. 5) ...the remainder is: "I shall clearly compose that which illuminates and reveals it. Among those things to be described, such as the eternal [mantras], he states what must first be performed with the words beginning with "prātaḥ"—

By the word "having meditated" (*dhyātvā*) and so forth, [the author] states that the morning ritual (*prātassamaya*) pertains to the early morning; he will describe the characteristic of this time in the section on the *saṃdhyā*, where it says, "at dawn, when the stars are still visible. Therefore, having risen within the five-nāḍī interval prior to that—while those five nāḍīs remain—one should, being pure, perform the ablution.
In the phrase "purely" (*śuciḥ*), two particles (*vā*) are used to indicate that both [conditions] are primary:

being endowed with purity as far as possible, and being accompanied by the washing of the feet and so forth appropriate for that time. Here, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding whether [one should sit] in the heart-lotus or at the *dvādaśānta*, according to the difference in the qualifications of the practitioner, as in the case of the meditation on *saṃdhyā* which will be described later.

It should be understood as "accomplished" (kṛta); that which is auspicious and peaceful has been so described because of its peace, its being the agent of all, and its existence as the supreme cause. In the Mahātantra, those who know the tantras have called Śiva "Sadāśiva."

(As it is stated in the Smṛti: "The Great Tantra is remembered as having three doors for its meaning and four feet")—having meditated in the manner taught by the Guru; for otherwise, it would be impossible to perform it—this is the sense. This...
One endowed with the power of *samādhi* and the power of *yoga* should perform meditation on the partless Śiva (*niṣkala-śiva*).
One devoid of that [power] should always meditate on Sadāśiva and others; by the word "and others," one should meditate on Him in the form of the five-faced, fifteen-eyed, and so forth.
Thus it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Then, at the rising of the dawn, the practitioner, composed in mind, should arise and [visualize] the Supreme,
who is beyond the supreme, as either situated within a lotus in the heart or in the form of light.
One whose mind is solely fixed on Śiva [should contemplate] the subtle deity residing in the *bindu*, the supreme, imperishable syllable;
or else, one whose mind is solely fixed on Śiva [should contemplate him] eternally in the void within the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*).
According to one's qualification, the knowledge of Śiva bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one who is unawakened should meditate on Śiva as Sadāśiva within the lotus of the heart.

Thus [ends the section]. Now, he describes the going outside for the purpose of bathing, stating "accompanied by a staff and so forth. The staff (*daṇḍa*) is made of bamboo (*vaiṇava*), because it is prescribed specifically as being made of that material; thus it has been stated [on page 7].
For lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and those who have bathed after completing their studies (gṛhasnāta), one should have a bamboo staff made with a span of the hand;
or rather, the excellent bamboo staff should be carried at all times.
Thus [it is said]. By the word "etcetera" (ādipada), the substances for bathing are indicated. Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
"Heartwood, cow dung, flowers, sesame seeds, and likewise myrobalan."
Having collected kusa grass, ashes, and other such items, one should go to a river that flows to the ocean.

Thus, accompanied by a staff and other such items, and equipped with a staff and so forth, having gone to a suitable place—that is, a place fit for the disposal of feces, urine, and the like—he must perform his necessary duties (*āvaśyaka*) there. "Necessary" (*āvaśyaka*) refers to the action that must necessarily be performed by him in that very place; it excludes the transformations of the great elements (*mahābhūta-vikāra*). [The transformations of the great elements are...]
Regarding "caves in the earth" and so forth—how they are to be avoided:
one should not face the sun and so on; by the word "and so on," [the avoidance of facing] Brahmins and others is intended.

In their absence, having gone to a suitable place, one should void excrement, urine, and so forth on ground covered with grass or on ground distinguished by grass; as it is stated in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*:
"Having gone to a proper place, one should discharge feces, urine, and the like."
Facing north, observing silence, he should always practice during the day and at both twilights.
Facing south at night, with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose,
his mind absorbed in the hair at the crown of his head, he should remain upon the ground covered with grass.
"And for the twice-born and others who have not undergone the [initiatory] consecration, the sacred thread is worn over the right ear"—
thus it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhu-paddhati*. Also, [one should avoid facing] the sun and moon while facing Brahmins, Arka-liṅgins, or women.
"Let [the practitioner] avoid the transformations of the great elements (mahābhūta) and let [the deity] emit impurity. Thus it is stated in the Kāmika-tantra.

The obligatory rites (*āvaśyaka*) must not be performed facing the sun, a cow, a Brahmin, or one bearing sectarian marks (*liṅgin*), nor while facing the moon, nor during the transformation of living beings. Thus, the prohibition against going to unsuitable places is stated in the *Suprabheda*.

A man should not perform both [acts] in a field, in the shade of a tree, within rivers or streams, near a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), on the shore of the great ocean, at a crossroads, or in the middle of a house.

Thus it is said elsewhere: "If a person voids urine, excrement, and so forth in these places— a temple and the like, near an anthill, a cremation ground, or a grove, on ashes, during a fire sacrifice, on *dūrvā* grass, or in a courtyard slippery with water— "
"He is cooked in a most terrible [hell] until the dissolution of all beings.
Now, he states the rule for purification: "With clods of earth, etc. By the word "etc.," grass and other such items are included;
as it has been said:
"One should clean the anus with grass unfit for sacrifice or with a clod of earth, or by means of a brick;
one should not clean it with cow dung, nor with stones, nor with wood. Thus [it is said].
Holding the penis with the left hand— *śepha*, *meḍhra*, *meḍhra*, *mehana*,

and *śephalī* are synonyms according to Amara— and with the other [hand], having gone near water, one should perform purification (*śauca*) using water drawn up in a vessel as prescribed by the scriptures.
As it has been said:
"Having grasped the penis with the left hand and a lump of clay in the right hand.
[One should take clay] from a cremation ground, a path, an anthill, sand, or pure mud.

"A wise person should fetch earth for the purpose of purification from a pure place, avoiding soil that is defiled by worms, insects, husks, charcoal, ashes, leather, or bones, or that remains after another's cleaning, or that is merely dusty."
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"Having withdrawn his penis and stood up, he should perform purification without haste, using earth and water drawn from a source,
until the odor and the smear are removed."
"Having left the water for only a night, one may perform purification in that which has not been drawn out;
afterwards, one should clean the bank, for otherwise one would become impure. Thus it is said.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara and the Jalatītra: having placed the cleansing clay and sprinkled it with water,
one should first purify the clay by drawing it up with the hollow of the right hand.
Taking water with the right hand and holding it in the left, one should wash the anus three times with intervals of water, repeating this five times.
One should wash the penis with one application of clay and the left hand with ten;
one should rub both hands and the two knees with water using seven applications of clay.

One should wash the feet and hands with water using each lump of clay individually. This is the purification for householders; it is double for students, triple for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
This purity is prescribed for the daytime; at night, one should perform the acts as previously stated. For those who are ill, it is ordained that two or three parts [of the requirement] may suffice.
Thus, through purity of being, there is being. Having performed purification in the manner described above,
as long as there is an absence of purity of mind— that is, until the mind becomes pure— one should continue the purification.
One should perform [the rite]. By this, the intention is clearly to increase the stated number, and not to decrease it;
for if that were the case, the injunction of the specific number would result in being rendered meaningless.

"In another place, having performed the double sipping of water (dvirācamya)": this means that in a location other than the one where purification was previously performed, one should first sip water without reciting mantras, and afterwards perform the sipping of water with mantras as will be described in the section on *ācamana*. Regarding the cleansing of the teeth, he says: "The wood for the purpose of cleaning the teeth..."

The tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) possesses the characteristics previously described; it may be produced from either permitted or prohibited trees. Among the permitted trees such as the mango (*cūta*), it may also be produced from those belonging to the class of *piśāca*, *dhava*, *nīva*, *niṃba*, *eraṇḍa*, *kāśa*, *kuśa*, and other trees associated with sacrifice (*yajña-sambandhin*); these are the sacrificial trees (*yājñiya-vṛkṣa*). It should be produced from among them.
The tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*). "Fingers" is well known; by the word "etcetera," other prohibited trees are also excluded.

Having avoided the prohibited tooth-sticks, one should take another tooth-stick that is not forbidden. On those days mentioned as prohibited, when it is said "with twelve mouthfuls of water," one should perform the cleansing of the teeth by rinsing the mouth twelve times,
or by using the mouthfuls of water from pure trees such as the mango (*cūta*), or by means of [other] substances for cleaning the teeth.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"With śairīṣa, arjuna, kārañja, bilva, and khadira wood—
of equal thickness, with half the bark removed, free of joints, straight, and without blemishes."
Those seeking liberation should perform the purification of the teeth by using a tooth-stick eight finger-breadths long, moistened with water from an arishta tree.
With loose flowers from the Aśoka, Jambū, Kakubha, Cūta, Plakṣa, and other trees, along with Campaka and Apāmārga blossoms, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length.
"Cleaning the teeth for those desiring to eat"—thus it is stated in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*, p.
"One should use the *dhātrī* (myrobalan), *vairaṇḍa*, *kṣīrī*, *nimba*, *ākuli*, or *tṛṇa* [tooth-sticks]."
Nor indeed with a bamboo splinter, water-demons, grass, kusa-grass, or finger-nails.
One should avoid performing the cleansing of the teeth on the ninth, the new moon, the sixth, and the first lunar days;
however, one who desires to eat may do so using purifying leaves.

"Alternatively, purification of the mouth may be achieved by rinsing with mouthfuls [of water] equal in number to the sun (twelve), even without brushing the teeth; having performed this, one should carry out the bath.
Thus it is stated elsewhere as well.
"One should always make [the tooth-stick] from grass or leaves, except on the new-moon day and the eleventh lunar day;
for those two days as well, one should use [sticks from] the *jambu*, *plakṣa*, or *sāla* trees.
Now, he states the rule for bathing: "One should bathe," and so forth.

In that regard, "having gone to one of the [sites] such as river confluences" means: having reached any one among those, namely, the confluence of a river with the ocean, the confluence of rivers, and—by the word "etc. (ādi)—rivers, streams, ponds, and so forth.
Thus it has been said:
"Bathing at the confluence of rivers, in lakes,
ponds, streams, pools, and even in small puddles, is exceedingly excellent."

"In a *nālikā*, a lotus pond, and so forth, [the bath is] middling; furthermore, in a large tank (*vāpī*), a reservoir (*kuṇḍa*), or a well (*udapāna*), it is inferior; whereas bathing at home is unsurpassed.
Thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*.
Whether in a river, a pond, a lake, or even a well—there are four types [of bathing sites].
One should not perform a well-bath when rivers and the like are available.
But if [such water] is not available, one may perform a bath in a well without incurring any fault;
nor, O Gajānana, should one bathe in tanks when a river is present.

A step-well is ten times more meritorious than a well; a pond is ten times more meritorious than a step-well; know that a river flowing to the ocean is ten times more meritorious than that; and water—whether pure or impure—that flows near a temple of Śiva is ten times more meritorious still.
"It is renowned as Śivagaṅgā because it sprinkles the waters of the abode of Śiva.
Thus [it is said]. There, in the case of rivers and so forth, there are those known as Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Divya, Vāyavya, and Mānasa. (p. 16)

Among the five types of baths (*pañcavidha-snāna*), the *vāruṇa-snāna* is twofold, consisting of the procedure for the bath for removing impurities (*mala-snāna*) and the formal ritual bath (*vidhi-snāna*).
First, he describes the bath for removing impurities: "Having taken earth with the *astra-mantra* from below [the knees] at a depth of eight finger-breadths.
Regarding this, it has been said:
Bathing is of five kinds: Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Divya, Vāyavya, and Mānasa.
Vāruṇa bathing is performed with water, and Āgneya bathing is done with ashes.

The bath by rain accompanied by sunshine is the divine (divya); that from wind is the aerial (vāyavya); that arising from cow-dust is the earthly (gauraja); and that performed with mantras is said to be the mental (mānasa). Thus, the bath is of five kinds.
Now listen, O Sātvata, to the two-fold Vāruṇa bath:
having first performed the bath for removing impurities, one should then perform the ritual bath.

The extraction of dirt from the limbs and minor parts using powdered *rajanī* and clay is called the "impurity bath" (*malasnāna*); however, the "prescribed bath" (*vidhisnāna*) is performed with mantras. Thus, having dug the earth with the *astra-mantra*, one should take the clay situated eight finger-breadths below with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having placed [the substance] in hot water and divided it into three parts,
one should smear all the remaining limbs with one part.

Having performed the preliminary rites such as the invocation of the Six-faced One (*Ṣaṇmukhī*), the intended meaning regarding the eyes, ears, and nose is stated as follows: "Having dug eight finger-breadths deep into the ground, one should purify it with a sword."
Having taken up the clay with the heart mantra, one should fill it again with that very same [mantra].
Having lifted up the grass and other debris with the *śikhā* [mantra], one should then divide it with the *varma* [mantra];
having washed from the feet to the navel with one [mantra], one should do so again with another.
Having smeared his entire body with the blazing weapon-mantra consecrated by recitation, he should,
with a focused mind, purify his eyes and hands and restrain his vital breaths within the water.

Having thus performed the bath for removing impurities while recollecting the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) in his heart, which has the brilliance of the wind of destruction, he emerges from within the water.
Having performed the *astra-saṃdhyā*, one should then carry out the ritual bath (*vidhi-snāna*). Thus is described the characteristic of the six-faced [mudrā]:
with both thumbs, [one should touch] the two ears; then with the two index fingers, the two eyes.
One should firmly bind the pair of side-locks with the two middle fingers;
this is indeed the "six-faced" method, which one should employ during the ritual of bathing.

Thus [it is said] by the twice-born; thus by the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. The other, the Śūdra, performs the *brāhmī* [sandhyā] as prescribed in the Vedas, because he lacks the entitlement to Vedic rituals. Now, if it is asked how the *saṃdhyopāsana* can take place in the midst of the ritual bath, it is replied: "The *saṃdhyā* performed with reference to the *astra* (weapon-mantra) is proclaimed as the *astrasaṃdhyā*."

Since it is stated thus in the Āgamas, one should offer three *arghya* libations preceded by sprinkling with the *Śivāstra-mantra*, recite [the mantra] as much as possible, and then present [the offering]. Alternatively, one may perform the sprinkling and other rites with the *Astragāyatrī*. This is because sprinkling and the other rites are prescribed in this manner as constituent parts of the ritual bath for removing impurities (*malasnāna*). As for the Vedic [rite], it was previously...

"Having performed [the Śaiva rite], one should then perform the Śaiva [practice]. Thus, certain Vedic rites such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*) and others must be performed even before the Śaiva observance.

Because it is something that must be performed, there is the presence of Vedic rites such as the *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) and the recitation of hymns even at the time of bathing; thus, what has been stated is without fault. He speaks again of the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*): "The remainder," meaning the portion remaining after one-third has been used; "having consecrated with the *saṃhitā*"—that is, [the *saṃhitā*] in which seeds (*bīja*) are joined together.

For those for whom the *sakala-prāsāda-mantra* constitutes their *saṃhitā*, it is said to consist of three hundred and fifty [verses] together with the root mantras and the limbs (*aṅgas*). On the other hand, for those for whom the *niṣkala-prāsāda* is [the basis], the *saṃhitā* is simply the collection of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and limbs as taught in the *Kālottara* and other scriptures, numbering two hundred. Therefore, this *patyāti* consists of three hundred and fifty.
Because they are the root, the mantras that express the root-limbs of Brahman are called *saṃhitā*.
"One should contemplate them like the Śiva-tīrtha" means [the ritual] is joined with the Śiva-tīrtha.
As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Taking one-third of the clay with the *saṃhāramudrā*, the practitioner,
standing in water reaching up to his navel, faces north with his left hand [holding the clay].
Having divided it into three parts with the Kavaca mantra, one should consecrate those portions.
And in the *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said:
"The eastern [direction] should first be consecrated with the Astra-mantra; the southern with the Brahma-mantra;
and the northern with the Śiva-mantra. They should perform these separately, one by one."
The weapon-mantra (astra) should be recited in all ten directions in due order;
then, by means of the application of the iron-arrow weapon (nārācāstra), one should cast it again into the midst of the water.
One should smear the body with a portion consecrated by the Brahma-mantra;
then, having meditated upon the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā), one should again contemplate the nectar of immortality.
Then, O Six-faced One, one should draw back the water with a portion consecrated by the recitation of the Śiva-mantra; by this rite, it becomes the Śiva-tīrtha.
It is the supreme merit of all sacred fords. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda* as well: "By all frogs, fish, and other aquatic creatures...
Therefore, one should always consume water, especially that which is impure;
for the sake of pacifying its defects, one should prepare a Śiva-tīrtha. Thus it is said.

"Having meditated upon Śiva"—that is, having properly meditated upon Śiva in the lotus of the heart; then, "the Moon and Sun," meaning one should meditate on the Sun and Śiva in the right hand, and the Moon and Śakti in the left hand. Thus it has been said:
In the Siddhāntaśekhara,
it is said: "Having meditated upon Śambhu in the lotus of the heart while standing amidst the waters of a sacred ford,
[one should perform the rite] with the hands in the form of Śiva and Śakti, using the *kumbhamudrā*."

One should sprinkle the head with those mantras ending in *vauṣaṭ*, or else with the root mantra; one should sprinkle water with the *astra* mantra for the sake of self-protection and for the pacification of the multitude of obstacles.
"Having cast [the water] in all directions," it says, "one should bathe. However, in the *Suprabheda*, it is stated:
"Having placed the eye within the water, one should not show any part of the body at all."
Or one may show half of it, or else recite the mantra while submerged up to the face.
"What is recited while the face is submerged becomes a hundredfold;
when half the body is submerged, it is a thousandfold; when the whole body is submerged, it is said to be ten millionfold. (p. 22)
The characteristic of the *kumbha-mudrā* has been stated:
having placed the right fist upon the palm of the left hand, one should conceal it;
with the fingers of the left hand, one should place two thumbs upward.
The Kumbha-mudrā is called "the sixfold," and it is the flowing forth of the nectar of the Praṇava.
Regarding the phrase "with the royal protocol of a Cakravartin":

the "royal protocol" (*rājyopacāra*) refers to the royal insignia such as the *cakravarti* umbrella, musical instruments, and so forth; [the phrase] "with fragrant *āmalaka* and the like" indicates that the use of *āmalaka* and other ingredients is mandatory and must be performed immediately following the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*).

In the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Immediately after the ritual bath, the practitioner, recollecting Śiva, should subsequently bathe with fragrant *āmalaka* fruits consecrated by the *gāyatrī*, while employing the [appropriate] mantras. Thus it is said.
(23) Regarding the phrase "by way of the metaphor of a universal monarch" (*cakravarty-upacāreṇa*): on this point, some hold the view that it applies only to householders. And it has been said:
"By way of the metaphor of a universal monarch, [one should bathe] with fragrant myrobalan and the like."
In that regard, one should first perform the bath; thereafter, the ritual bath (vidhisnāna) follows.
This very [bath] performed with clay and other materials is declared to be the ascetic’s bath (yatisnāna). Thus it is said.
Furthermore, some claim that this does not apply to fragrant *āmalaka* and the like, and that the specific manner for a householder’s position must be stated;

however, that is not so, because the procedure for emerging from the water is prescribed as "having bathed with fragrant *āmalaka* and so forth, one should emerge from the water. [This applies to] the householder.

Because that [interpretation] is untenable in this context. Here, by the word "fragrance" (sugandha), used figuratively, the recently born (*sadyojāta*) aspect of the earth-element is indicated, according to the statement: "The earth is to be known as *sadyas*. By the word "pure" (*amala*), consciousness (*bodha*) is meant;
and by the word "consciousness," the heart is expressed, according to the statement: "The heart is a synonym for consciousness. Therefore...

Since the word "with jars" (*kumbhaiḥ*) is to be supplied [from the context]— meaning jars consecrated with fragrant substances and the like, with the *sadyojāta* mantras and so forth, with *āmalaka* fruits and the like, and with the *hṛdaya* mantras and so forth— it is not illogical; so say the experts in logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*).

"Having sat down, he should perform the *ācamana* (sipping of water)" means that one should indeed perform the *ācamana* while seated, not standing or bent over. "With a short recitation, he should direct [the water] to the *tīrtha*"—it should be understood that "short recitation" refers to a specific mode of pronunciation. The *tīrtha*...

One should withdraw the Śiva-tīrtha imagined by oneself by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Now he states the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*): "Then" (*tataḥ*)—that is, after the performance of the bath; "water clinging to the limbs" (*aṅgalagnajalam*) means water adhering to the body; "with a pure, washed, non-damp garment" (*anārdavāsasā*)—it is called "non-damp" (*anārda*) because it does not become wet.

"Anārdra-vāsaḥ" means that which is both not wet and a garment; having wiped or rubbed [himself] with that, he should put on two clean garments (*śuddha-vāsasī*). Here, because of the dual number in the word "vāsasī," [it refers to two garments].
Having put on two garments, one should perform the rites such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*);
one should not do so with only a single garment. Thus it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"One should not perform a ritual with only one garment, nor naked, wearing merely a loincloth."
During bathing, worship of the deity, sacrifice, and eating,
a wise man should wear two washed garments— unbroken, pure, and auspicious.

"There is no fault for a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin) who wears a loincloth. Likewise, Śumati says: "Equipped with a lower garment, one should perform one's duties without sloth."
"That action becomes futile; it is purified by bathing again.
And elsewhere:
"If one, having bathed and wearing wet clothes, voids feces or urine..."
"Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one becomes pure again through bathing. Thus it is said.
"Baddhacūḍa" means one whose topknot is tied; "anāvṛtaśiras" (p.
26) means one whose head is not covered by clothing or the like. Thus it has been said:
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Then, having tied the topknot with the [topknot-thread] upon the pure edge of the sacred thread,
and having placed the left foot in the water and the right foot on the ground..."
Facing either east or north, with both knees and both hands [placed together],
one should contemplate pure water, free from foam, bubbles, mud, and the like.
Placing [the hands] on the palm of the right hand with the thumb and little finger released,
one should meditate on the moon-form during the bright fortnight and the sun-form during the dark fortnight.

The knowledge of the Self is Śiva; with the principles (tattvas) ending in the "own-end" (svānta), beginning with the Praṇava, and with the heart, crest, and top-knot mantras accompanied by the seed-syllables, one performs three mouthfuls (culuka).
"One should drink [the water] with the *brahmatīrtha*, which is dear to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:
"Having washed the feet up to the knees, or the hands up to the wrist (*maṇibandhana*)."
Having tied his topknot, he should face either the east or the north.
Having formed the hand like a cow’s ear, one should drink water in which a *māṣa* bean has been submerged.
Having sipped it three times with the root-mantra using the *brahmatīrtha*, one should wipe the mouth three times.
One should touch the lips with the root of the thumb; the eyes, nose, and ears with the union of the ring finger and the thumb;
and the arms, chest, navel, and head with the [thumb and] index finger.
One should know that the mind is accompanied by mantras; having drunk water with the auspicious *ātman-vidyā* and *aṇu-mantras* ending in *svāhā*, one should wipe the lips with the *hetin* mantra.
One should perform the touching of the eyes with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) in the order starting from the left; and in the Parākhyatantra it is said:
"Then one should touch the limbs—the head, the two eyes, and the two nostrils."
Then, one should perform the touching of the ears, the heart, the navel, and the head;

thereafter, the touching of the limbs should be performed with the thumb joined [to the fingers]. The thumb shall always be the Lord (Īśa), while the nameless finger (the ring finger) is the immortal digit (amṛtākalā).
"By that [offering] which consists of the deceased self, the gods become eternally satisfied and free from ailment;
such is the ritual action of the performer, whose state of being is indeed Brahman. Thus it is said.

(28) But surely, in another scripture, the touching of the eyes by means of the fingers is prescribed; how then [can it be said] "by the thumb and the ring finger"? This has been stated in the *Suprabheda*:
Having wiped the two lower lips twice with the base of the thumb three times,
and having touched the mouth with the hand, one should sprinkle the feet and the head.
The wise man should touch his two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger;
he should then touch his nose with the thumb and the index finger.
Then one should touch the two ears with the thumb and the little finger;
the two arms with the thumb; the navel with the thumb;
the heart with the tips of the fingers; and one should touch the head with all five [fingers].
Satisfaction is desired through the threefold drinking of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
By wiping his mouth twice, one attains the lower Veda;
by wiping it once, the face of Gaṇeśa becomes pleased.
The sages do not desire satisfaction through the mere sprinkling of water;
nor would it be pleasing to the Moon and the Sun if their eyes were touched.
Touching the nose brings pleasure to Aśvinī;
touching the ears brings delight to the Quarters (Dik); and touching the arms, the navel, and the heart brings pleasure to Indra, Viṣṇu, and Agni, respectively. Thus it is said.

Even though it has been stated thus—"In brief, this division of the Tantras is distinguished by the differences of ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth"—because the distinction of ritual action and the rest is the cause for the division of the Tantras, let it be so there. However, here, since there are many scriptures, it must be performed according to the lineage of one's own Guru; this was stated because such performance is established by the conduct of former masters. Now...

In this context, he describes the method for bathing at home as an incidental point: "Or else, having bathed with earth as before"—that is, as previously stated in the section on bathing. This refers to the case of one who is a *prabhu* (a master or householder). Thus it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"Alternatively, in one's own home, [one may bathe] with pure water or cool [water]."
Standing on a seat placed upon ground smeared with heated [ashes], one should perform the ritual bath.
Thus [it is said].
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"With nine, eight, or five jars consecrated by the *śiva-mantra*..."

"Even at home, the bath must be performed by the initiated on ground that has been smeared. Thus it is said. Regarding the inability to perform the bath due to illness and so forth, he says "one capable of the Vāruṇa bath. According to one's capacity—that is, in accordance with the strength of one's own body—one should wash [the body] up to the neck, or up to the waist, or up to the feet.
One should wipe the remaining part of the body with a wet cloth. Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Due to the inability [to bathe fully] caused by headaches and other ailments, one should wash the body up to the neck;
this is declared to be 'throat-bathing' (*kaṇṭhasnāna*), which becomes reddish through the use of earth and water."
"Having wiped away the washed soft cloth, or indeed the Vāruṇa [garment] of the woman," thus it is said.
Likewise, elsewhere also:
"The divine [purification] is by a shower of rain, and the purification of the body is through the Kāpila [fire]."
"And another with a moist garment, [and] mental contemplation on Śiva.
31) "With the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*": [this means] with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [the dust] raised from the big toes of the feet of the virtuous beings.

"Not with fire" means that one should contemplate the external impurities located in the body as being burnt by that fire, since it is well known in the scriptures that Kālāgni resides in the left thumb. "With pure water flowing from the agitated Śakti" means that one should bathe the body with the water described in the section on the mental bath (mānasasnāna) which will be explained later.

"One should recite the *saṃhitā* once. One should recite the *saṃhitā* for the purpose of expiating the failure to perform the ritual bath. For it has been stated: "If one who is ill is deprived of the bath, he should recite the *Śivaikādaśikā*. Furthermore, since the *vāruṇa* bath alone is prescribed everywhere in the case of touching those who are untouchable (*aspṛśya*), and as it has been said:
If one is touched by crows, herons, camels, donkeys, cocks, or vultures,
or by village dogs and the like, or by the bodily excretions produced from them;

If one is touched by outcastes, ghosts, or those who have fallen [from their status], or by people who consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya), or by a woman in her courses, a woman recently delivered, and so forth, one should perform the Vāruṇa rite.

"One should bathe with water in the event of contact above the navel—excluding the hands—with any other bodily excretions such as feces or urine; otherwise, one should merely wash the affected part and remain pure.
Having thus described the method for the *vāruṇa* (water) bath, he now states the method for the *āgneya* (fire) bath: "Now..."

Regarding the "procedure for the ash-bath" (*bhasmasnānavidhi*): now, following the water-bath (*vāruṇasnāna*), the procedure—that is, the method—of the ash-bath is being stated; this is the remainder of the sentence.
Because this ash-bath is most excellent compared to bathing with water, it [should be performed] by Brāhmaṇas and others.
Householders who have renounced the world must necessarily perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) as appropriate;
for it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "The Āgneya [initiation], which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is not truly purified except by means of ash."
The ablution with fire and water brings about incalculable fruit;
just as the water of the Gaṅgā is pure, so too is the sacred ash (bhasma) purifying. (p. 33)
Because it illuminates itself while emitting ashes, and because it shines forth as something auspicious,
it is celebrated as "Bhasma" (ashes) due to its consumption which destroys all sins.
Bringing prosperity and purity, as well as necklaces and ornaments,
this meritorious ash-bath brings the world under one's control day after day;
it [protects] those afflicted by fever, epilepsy, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas.
Merely by the application of ashes, she was seen standing healthy upon the surface of the earth.
Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of one’s teacher, having committed theft, and even having committed the murder of a Brahmin—
one who is covered in ashes, lying on a bed of ashes, and meditating upon Rudra, is liberated from all sins.
A bath with ashes possesses ten million times the merit of a bath in water.
One should perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) three times a day, twice a day, once a day, or even just a single time, as is appropriate.
Freed from all evil, one should accomplish the desired fruit;
having entered the householder stage of life, one should constantly maintain the threefold merit.
A wise monk should always wear the sacred thread made of human hair on his forehead,
on his upper arm, and likewise upon his chest.
One should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
whether by means of the leaves of the sacred trees or by means of the various stages of life, and whether through the recitation of mantras or even without them.

The application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) have been proclaimed with reverence by Jābāla. The best of sages, the Śvetas and the followers of the Śvetara branch, respectfully regard both the smearing with ashes and the Tripuṇḍra as the very means to liberation through knowledge.
The best of sages, established in the Atharvaśiras, prescribe the smearing of ashes (uddhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the cessation of the bond of Māyā; likewise,
the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be worn constantly by the twice-born and others along with the ashes.
"Because it is enjoined by the Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen"—
thus [it is stated] in the *Smṛtisārasamuccaya*. Or, even if there is impurity or improper conduct, one might commit sin with the mind.
"One shall always remain pure by wearing the *tripuṇḍra*. Thus it is stated in the *Dharmasārasudhānidhi*. (p. 35)
One should always apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes purified by mantras, according to the procedure declared in the Vedas; thus one shall attain union with Śiva.

By such statements as these, although the bath with ash (*bhasmasnāna*) supersedes the bath with water (*jalasnāna*), there is no fitness for performing the bath with ash without first having performed the bath with water; therefore, householders (*gṛhasthāśramin*) should perform the bath with ash after first having performed the bath with water.
And it has been said:
"O best of sages, one is entitled to the ash-bath daily, constantly, once [per day], according to one's ability, in one's own water; not otherwise."

The phrase "established since the beginning of the kalpa" includes the *anukalpas* and *upakalpas* by means of the word "beginning. Having first performed the consecration (*saṃhitā-mantraṇa*) of the ashes of the *kalpa*, *anukalpa*, and *upakalpa* according to the prescribed rule, one should wear them. [The term] "the state of being a non-kalpa" refers to—
p.

36) By the phrase "the *kalā*-mantras beginning with *nivṛtti*," the *kalā*-mantras of *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, *śānti*, and *śāntyatīta* are included. Having purified—that is, having performed the cleansing—the *saṃhitā*.
One should wear [the ashes] after consecrating them with mantras.
One should perform the Āgneya rite with ashes; the ashes are said to be of four kinds:
the first is designated as the Kalpa, and the second is the Anukalpa.
The third should be "almost fit" (upakalpa), and the fourth should be "unfit" (akalpa);
there should be a distinction for each preceding one based on the difference in the fire and the cow-dung.
Having taken cow dung situated in the sky, having formed it into a ball and dried it,
one should purify it by burning it in the fire of Śiva while reciting the Sadyojāta and other mantras.
Ash purified by the root mantra is proclaimed as "kalpa";
or alternatively, ash produced from the *agnihotra* sacrifice is called "kalpa."
As an alternative method in the forest, one may use dry, pure wood burnt by the fire of Śiva;
or in a wilderness, a house, or a cow-pen, one may use dry bricks and the like.
It is burnt with fire and purified by a cloth of ashes;
then it is formed into a ball with cow's urine and consecrated as before.
That third is called Upakalpa, and it is known as Bhasma.

"That which is devoid of the ash-mantra is a ritual-less [act], yet it remains unblemished. Thus, regarding the bath with ashes (*bhasmasnāna*), there are two types due to its form as both the procedure for the bath of impurities (*malasnāna*) and the [ordinary] bath. First, he describes the bath of impurities:
"Having taken a mere handful of ash with the right hand..."
Having purified it through the yoga of concentration and meditation, it is rendered supreme.
Having performed [the ritual], one should always purify the root mantra along with the Brahma-aṅga mantras;
then, placing the ashes in the left hand with the mantra beginning with "agniriti" and so forth.

"Having performed the 'dirt-bath' (malasnāna) starting from the head with the Astra-mantra using the right hand, one should then perform the ritual bath (vidhisnāna) with the dust of ashes. Thus it is said.
He describes the ritual bath [beginning with] "Īśāna": *īśa* refers to the Īśāna-mantra.

The *puruṣa* is the *tatpuruṣa* mantra; "for each limb" (*pratyaṅgam*) means that, having performed the purification of the hands with the *astra* mantra for each limb, one should remember (or perform) the smearing (*uddhūlya*) with the remaining ashes using the mantras of Brahmā, Īśa, and Īśāna.

One should perform the consecration on the head with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). This *uddhūlana* (smearing with ashes) is prescribed in other scriptures according to the distinction of the qualified practitioner (*adhikārī*): a Brāhmaṇa should perform the smearing on all his limbs; a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should smear above the navel; a Śūdra, however, should omit the smearing altogether.
One should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) consisting precisely of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*); this pertains to Śūdras, excluding those who are ascetics (*tapasvin*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"If an ascetic should perform the ash-bath according to the rules"—
by the word "etcetera," the procedure for the impurity-bath and the two types of bathing consisting of smearing with ash have been stated according to the distinction of eligible practitioners.
Likewise, Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas should also perform the ash-bath in the form of the *tripuṇḍra* on their foreheads.
Alternatively, (p.

39) the four [classes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇas who follow the dharma of the householder stage of life, if they are unable to perform the smearing of ashes (*uddhūlana*), [may do so by other means].

One should apply the ashes specifically in the form of the *tripuṇḍra*. According to certain Āgamas, a renunciant (*yati*) should smear his limbs with ashes, whereas for those in the householder stage (*gṛhāśrama*), he should apply the *tripuṇḍra* and so forth; this is because smearing (*uddhūlana*) is declared in those scriptures to pertain to ascetics (*tapasvin*).
Such are the positions stated in the Āgamas.
Furthermore, in certain Āgamas, regarding the intention of the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) consisting solely of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*),
it is stated that the quantity of ash— namely one *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, half of that, and half of that again— is prescribed according to the status of the recipient, such as Brāhmaṇas and others.
Thus, from among the positions taught in the scriptures, relying upon whichever position has been established by the conduct of former masters—
whether at five locations such as the forehead, or eight locations, or sixteen locations, or thirty-two locations— with the index, middle, and ring fingers.
Alternatively, one should apply the *tripuṇḍraka* on the forehead using the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb. And it is said:
"O Śrīmanmṛgendra, [one should apply it] from the head, face, heart, and private parts, starting with Īśa and the others."
"One should effect the purification of the hand of action for each limb with the weapon-mantra. Thus it is said.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The wise one should successively apply ashes with the five mantras beginning with Īśa;
this is declared to be the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*). Now the triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) is described."
Taking the ashes with three middle fingers consecrated by the root mantra,
the Brahmins [apply it] to the forehead, the heart, and the two shoulders while standing in the house.
One should not scatter [ashes] upon those [joints]; one should remember these deities in sequence:
Śiva and Īśvara at the feet, Rudra and Viṣṇu [at the knees], and Brahmā at the five joints.
It is said that there is a *puṇḍra* of five limbs, or alternatively, a *puṇḍra* of eight limbs;
[these are applied] on the head, forehead, neck, shoulders, heart, navel, and back.
Brahmā, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Umā, Īśa, Savitṛ, Anala,
and Śaśin— these are said to be the eight limbs; now the sixteen limbs are described.
Likewise, one should place [the offerings] on the plowshare, the neck, the two upper arms, and the two elbows.
One should declare that the deities at the two wrists are Śambhu; at the chest, the belly, the navel, and the two sides, as well as on the back, they are Īśa, Rudra, and Prajāpati.
Viṣṇu, the nine beginning with Vāmā, and the Aśvins—these sixteen are applied in sequence.
The thirty-two lords of the joints are said to follow the order of the *tripuṇḍra*:
on the head, forehead, throat, and the asterisms (the eyes), as well as on the nose, mouth, head-veins, and so forth.
On the two shoulders, on the pair of arms, likewise on the two elbows,
on the two wrists, and on the chest, navel, penis, and anus;
In these—the thighs, knees, shanks, feet, and toes of the rider—reside the deities:
the Mūrtis, the Vidyeśvaras, the Guardians of the Quarters (Dikpālas), and the four groups of eight Vasus.
"The thirty-two positions are declared, along with the triple-tilaka belonging to the Lord of the Three Principles;
one should perform them according to what is possible, taking into account the place, time, and other factors. Thus it is stated in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*.
During the three junctions of the day, at midnight, at the beginning and end of the twilight periods,
after sleeping, after eating, after drinking water, and after performing the necessary bodily functions such as voiding;
A woman, a eunuch, a Śūdra, a cat, a bat, and mice—
Having created [the dust] in that manner, one should perform the appropriate ritual bathing;

however, one should not perform the rite of smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) in the presence of the gods, the fire, the guru, or the Veda, nor upon seeing an outcaste, nor on impure ground, nor on a path. Thus it is said.
He states what must be done immediately thereafter with the word "tataḥ" (then)—that is, as previously described in the section on *ācamana* (sipping water).

Regarding this, some maintain that even after the bath of ashes (*bhasmasnāna*), one should perform the washing of the feet, *ācamana*, and so forth. He now describes the procedure for the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*): the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) is the *prāsādamantra*, which denotes Paraśiva.
The definition [of this] will become clear later in the section on the worship of Śiva.
"Ending with the Nāda" means up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); here, having performed inhalation and retention, one should agitate [the breath] by mentally reciting the root mantra.
One should contemplate one's own body as being consecrated by streams of nectar flowing from the circle of the Śaktis. And it has been said:

Standing before the root mantra, one should perform the mental bath by sprinkling the nectar-stream of the Śakti upon oneself externally and internally. This mental bath should be performed in all cases whenever there is a doubt regarding impurity. Furthermore, the divine (divya), wind-born (vāyavya), and other types of baths should also be performed daily, or as the case may require.

To this he says: "Of the divine and so forth"—because even the divine and other [types of baths] are occasional (*naimittika*), since they are obtained by taking time and so forth as the occasion. One should perform that occasional [bath] at the very time [prescribed]; among all baths, this one dedicated to Varuṇa and this one dedicated to Agni are constant (*nitya*), while the others are [occasional].
It has been stated that these are occasional (*naimittika*). In the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
"The baths of Varuṇa and Agni are declared to be the daily (*nitya*);
the fourfold set beginning with the mental (*mānasa*) is remembered as the occasional (*naimittika*)."

The signs (*nimitta*) such as rain and sunshine have already been explained previously. He describes the method for the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) on the hands and limbs with the words beginning "Then" (*tataḥ*): "Then," that is, after the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*), follows the process of making [the self] complete (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
The *sakala* [mantra] is the *śiva-mantra* accompanied by the *kalās* and the mantras beginning with *Īśāna*; one whose body and so forth have been infused (*vinyasta*) by that is *sakalī*.
Because it makes the *niṣkala* (partless) into the *sakalī* (endowed with parts), it is called *sakalīkaraṇa*.

That is threefold, according to the divisions of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). Among these, [the sequence is] from *Īśāna* and so forth, and from *astra* and so forth.

The placement (*nyāsa*) which follows the sequence of Sadyojāta and so forth, as well as the Heart and so forth, is of the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). The placement which follows the sequence of Brahmā and so forth for the [five] limbs is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). The placement which follows the sequence of emanation for the [five] Brahmās and the sequence of withdrawal for the limbs is of the nature of maintenance (*sthiti*). Here, in this world-dharma, there is the mundane [practice] of the initiated householder.
The form of emanation (sṛṣṭirūpa) belongs to the celibate student, the householder seeking enjoyment with his wife, and also to the forest-dwelling practitioner.

For one who is without a wife, a forest-dweller seeking liberation, a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), and a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), it is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). For a householder seeking liberation at the end of the body, as well as for a material celibate of that same kind, and likewise for a forest-dweller with a wife of that same kind, it is also material (*bhautika*) and lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*).

The state of being a *samaya* consists of the mode of abiding for both the householder and the teacher; for even by the lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*), initiation (*dīkṣā*) must be performed. Regarding the funeral rites and so forth of the teacher, it takes the form of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); regarding initiation, it takes the form of fitness for the disciple. It should be understood that what is described here as "making complete" (*sakalīkaraṇa*) is the state of existence within these three types.
The statements regarding these [mudrās] have not been written here because they are numerous. Regarding the "right and left hands," this refers to the limbs of the hands;

for it is prescribed that after performing the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) at the time of the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), the placement of mantras follows immediately thereafter.

First, for the purpose of purifying the hands, with the right hand, one should [touch] the palm and the back of the left hand, from the wrist to the tip of the thumb, individually with the *astra-mantra*. (p. 46)
Having wiped [the hands] twice, one should thereafter contemplate the two hands as being joined together. And it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The palm of the left hand [should be purified] twice with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*."
Beginning from the wrist,
one should wipe the right hand together with the thumb using the right hand itself, following the prescribed path up to the heart;
then, with the left hand, one should rub both hands as if they were burnt ropes.
"Having washed those two hands as before, one should form the lotus-mudrā.

Thus, "of the palms" (*talayoḥ*) means of the two hand-palms (*hastatalayoḥ*). "Hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the Head"—in this application for the Brahmās, after pronouncing the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should then pronounce the respective seed-syllable (*bīja*).

The gurus maintain that one should subsequently recite the mantras read in the middle [of the ritual], beginning with "To the head of Īśāna" and so forth, which pervade the sky (*vyomavyāpin*). Likewise, it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati* (p.
"One should thus conclude the *homa* with the words 'Brahma-bīja-pada'.
For this very reason, the application of the mantra is performed in the *paddhati* as follows:

"By means of the power that pervades both hands (*sakala-hasta-vyāpti-śaktitvena*). The term *sakalau* means "accompanied by the *kalās*" (energetic digits). And those two are the hands (*tau ca tau hastau*).
The two hands are complete. The pervasive power (*śakti*) of those two, consisting of the forms of Īśāna and the others, has been so described; its state is "thatness" (*tatva*).

By that—namely, by the pervasiveness of that power within the middle (of the hands)—the temple (*prāsāda*), which is the Śiva-mantra, exists as the pervader of that power. Its state is "thatness," and by that [it is established].

Having invoked Him with "Hṛdayāya Namaḥ" and so forth, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of all the limbs except for the eyes, reciting all the mantras ending in "Namaḥ. However, in the performance of rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*), one should recite them joined with the six ritual suffixes (*jāti-ṣaṭka*), such as "Namaḥ," "Svāhā," and so on. Thus, in the section on the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra-prakaraṇa*) in the commentary on the *Mṛgendra-paddhati*.
As stated in the *Śivārcanācandrikā* (p. 48): "At the time of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras, all these mantras..."
Having performed the binding of the directions preceded by the three *tāla* gestures with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
the definition of the *tāla-mudrā* is stated in the *Ajita*:
"The striking of the palm of the left hand with the fingers of the right hand."
"The *sātala* mudrā, excluding the thumb, bestows purification.
Furthermore, the characteristic of the *nārāca* mudrā is stated in the *Parākhyatantra*:
"Then, having formed a very firm fist with the right hand..."
And having firmly pressed the tip of the index finger with the tip of the thumb.
"One should extend the index finger when there is a separation and the arising of sound;
this is known as the Nārāca weapon-mudrā for the rite of binding the directions. Thus it is said.
Regarding the instruction "one should display the Mahāmudrā," the definition of Mahāmudrā is given in the *Samāna-tantra*:
One should touch those two feet with both hands and lead them up to the head;
this is the Mahāmudrā, for the ritual action of consecrating the hands. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific ritual procedure, it is stated:
"Then one should touch with both hands from the beginning of the feet to the end of the feet;
this mudrā is called Mahāmudrā."
He describes the sequence of *prāṇāyāma* with the words beginning "afterwards" (*paścāt*), etc.

*Prāṇāyāma* is the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*); its *āyāma* is its coming and going, that is to say, the specific [processes] known as inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kuṃbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*). And this is to be understood according to the distinction of time. As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
One should exhale the impure air residing within the body and situated in the ether,
while gradually drawing in pure air through inhalation (pūraka).
One should remain like a completely filled pitcher and then exhale;
[the breath] deficient by twelve *mātrās* is considered the lowest, while that with double [that duration] is considered the middling.

The middle duration for each [of the breaths], such as exhalation (recaka) and the others, consists of three *guṇas*. The measure (*mātrā*) is defined by the time it takes to snap the fingers three times while rotating the knee-circle.

Having thus performed that breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the *saṃhitā* mantra, first exhaling the air within the body, and subsequently drawing in the external air by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), one should mutter the *saṃhitā* mantra during the retention (*kuṃbhaka*) and then exhale. Likewise: "The practitioner of mantra, with his breath restrained, should mentally mutter the *saṃhitā* three times."
"This shall be the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) prescribed for all rites.
Immediately thereafter, he states what must be done next: "From the location of the drop," meaning having drawn the nectar from the location of the drop by means of the goad-gesture (aṅkuśamudrā).
The characteristics of the goad (aṅkuśa) mudrā have been stated: having formed a fist with the right hand, excluding the index finger, and then hooking [the thumb] with that index finger—
this is proclaimed as the goad mudrā.

"When that same [mudrā] is formed with the index finger extended, it is called the *sṛṇi* (goad) or the *udbhava* (arising); this mudrā is recommended for the rite of installation (*sthāpana*). Thus [it is said].

Having established that nectar in the water with the *utthāpana-mudrā* and having protected it, one should seal it and transform it into nectar. As it has been said: "Then, having drawn up the nectar from the center of the earth by means of the [mudrā] called the goad (*aṅkuśa*)."
"One should establish [the deity] with the mantra consisting of all the preceding [syllables], known as the 'Emergence' (udbhava).
The binding of the ten directions is performed with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and the snapping gestures (choṭikā-mudrās).
Protection is performed with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra). The veiling (avakuṇṭhana) consists of the circling of the right index finger."
The consecration by means of nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is performed by displaying the *dhenumudrā*.
The definition of the *dhenumudrā* has been stated:
having placed the hands in the *veṇībandha* position with the two thumbs joined together.
The index finger is merged with the middle finger, and likewise the little finger with the ring finger.

Thus, the pair of four [fingers] which rains down divine nectar is this Surabhi mudrā; it is taught for the purpose of purifying substances. He describes the method of performing the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana): having meditated upon the twilight, one should perform the salutation.
He establishes that very point with the verse beginning "raktabhūṣāmbara... and ending "prātastārakitambara..."; and it has been said:
"The morning twilight (prātassandhyā) is proclaimed as being endowed with stars, the midday [twilight] as having its stars obscured, and the inferior [twilight] as accompanied by the sun.
Regarding "midday" (madhyaṃ dinaḥ): it refers to the time of midday, and that occurs after twelve *ghaṭikās*.
The intended duration is up to six *ghaṭikās*. Regarding "half-set and reddish": this refers to when the sun is half-set; and it has been said:
"That which is accompanied by the sun is the best, while that during which the sun has disappeared is middling."
"The lowest [sandhyā] is accompanied by stars; thus the evening sandhyā is considered to be threefold.
Having stated the individual characteristics of the powers (śaktis) beginning with Brāhmī, he states their general characteristic:
"All of them wear black antelope skins. He then describes the division of these [powers] according to the qualities of sattva and so forth.

"Conjoined"—thus it is said. In this regard, it should be understood that Brāhmī is conjoined with the quality of *rajas*, Vaiṣṇavī with the quality of *sattva*, and Raudrī with the quality of *tamas*.

In this context, he states that it is Śakti alone who is to be meditated upon in the form of Brāhmī and the others, by saying "divided by the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) which are the causes such as Brāhmī.

The meaning is: that Śiva-Śakti which has attained division—that is, become differentiated—by the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts of the Lords who are the causes such as Brahmā, namely [the functions of] creation and so forth. This...
In response to the inquiry "Of whom is this complete meditation? he says: "of one who possesses equanimity" (*samadhinaḥ*).
This refers to both the one possessing general equanimity and the one possessing specific equanimity. And it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The action inseparable from that [equanimity] is declared to be Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī."
Through transformation, these very [energies] consist of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
Endowed with the three qualities (guṇas), these three powers— Brahmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Īśānkarī— are meditated upon by the wise during the three junctions of the day.
"By the power of temporal adjuncts (*kālopādhi*), the colors, vehicles, weapons,
and forms [of the deities] are to be meditated upon as supreme (*alam*) in sequence within the heart, the *bindu*, and the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*).
Having thus described the meditation on the junction (*saṃdhyā-dhyāna*) between the *samādhi* and the *viśiṣṭa-samādhi*:

55) He speaks of the "sons" and so forth, saying "putrakādyāstu": the *putraka* is one who is endowed with merely the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for liberation; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya* are included. The essential nature of the *putraka* and the others [is described] in the section on initiation (*dīkṣāprakaraṇa*).

Clearly, we shall explain this: "In the manner of a lotus fiber," and so forth. Like a lotus fiber (*mṛṇālatantu*), she is thin—meaning subtle in form—and red, to be meditated upon at dawn; she is white at midday.

"Thin like a lotus fiber," meaning she is dark (sitetara) [or black]. She is to be meditated upon in the evening; she who is to be meditated upon at midnight is the radiance (*vibhā*) that is contemplated. She is devoid of both form and formlessness, or she is black in color. Among these powers (*śaktis*), three powers are associated with the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and so forth. The power is fourfold.
She is devoid of qualities (*guṇa*). Thus it is said in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*:
"Now, the supreme twilight (*saṃdhyā*) of the knowers is declared to be fourfold;
though it is one, it attains multiplicity through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the forms of Śiva and Śakti."
Slender like a lotus fiber, clad in red silk, and white as the opposite of black—
she who is perceived at night as having the form of the fourth state, or as being dark.
"These [energies] reside respectively in the heart, the bindu, the brahmarandhra, and the supreme state;
three of them are conjoined with sattva and the other qualities, while the fourth is devoid of qualities.
Thus it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Those powers known as Kriyā, Dṛk, and Icchā on the pure path are said to be subject to time; these are the three intermediate junctions (saṃdhyās) that are both supreme and non-supreme.

"It is to be meditated upon by those initiated into Nirvāṇa within the cavities of the heart and the *kāla* [the time-organ], and it is proclaimed as the *Parā*; it extends to the end of the *Turya* and *Unmanā* states.
Thus, even for the *putraka* and others, the meditation on the *saṃdhyā* [junction] follows from the context of the *yogin* and the *jñānin*.
It is written here, having been extracted from another work:
"The two twilights at the end of the sun and the moon are for those who possess vital breath and movement;
but that which is the supreme awakening of Śiva is called the supreme twilight."
The commentary on this verse is now provided:
(p. 57) Of the sun and the moon, which are the forms of the upward and downward vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
And so it has been said: "The sun is the upward-moving breath, while the moon is the downward-moving breath."

At the end of those two—that is, when the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels, known as the Moon and the Sun, have ceased their activity—for the practitioners of breath (*prāṇa-yogins*) who are practitioners of the *haṃsa*: according to the statement, "The letter *ha* is traditionally held to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which takes the form of a *haṃsa* during its own activity," the *prāṇa* itself is the *haṃsa*. Therefore, "yoga" [here] means union with the *prāṇa-haṃsa*.

Those who possess this yoga of breath are called *prāṇayogins*. For them, two junctions (*saṃdhyā*) are prescribed— those who perform the recitation (*japa*) of the root-mantra in the form of sound, which is higher than the highest, by means of the practice of inhalation and exhalation from the navel up to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Then, at the conclusion [of the day], those practitioners of breath-yoga (prāṇayogins) are told:
"The two junctions (saṃdhyā) of the sun and the moon are indeed remembered by them to be at the end. Thus he speaks of the knowers: "The awakening of Śiva," and so forth.

(58) Śivabodha is the experience of the consciousness of Paraśiva, who resides at the *dvādaśānta* and is free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In that state, the union (*saṃdhi*) of the self and Śiva, their meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), or their state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), is *saṃdhyā*. [This is superior] to all the [other types of] *saṃdhyā* mentioned above.
It is supreme. And so it has been said:
"In reality, that Śaivī power alone is the stainless, supreme [energy], which is inseparable from the Lord Śambhu, just as heat is inseparable from fire."
Thus, the union of the Self and Śiva is the realization of Śiva, which is higher than the highest.

Regarding the statement "She who is called *sādhyā* is this very one": here, for those [practitioners] in a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the description beginning with "red ornaments and garments" refers to the gross twilight (*sthūlā saṃdhyā*). For those initiated into *nirvāṇa*, the description beginning with "slender as a lotus fiber" refers to the subtle twilight (*sūkṣmā saṃdhyā*). For those yogins, the description beginning with "of the sun and moon," as stated in other scriptures, refers to the supreme twilight (*parā saṃdhyā*).
"The awakening to Śiva for the wise," and so forth, up to "the supreme twilight.
It should be understood that four types of twilight (saṃdhyā) are prescribed according to the distinction of those qualified [for them].
He states the procedure for purification with the words "tatra" and so forth:

therein, among the previously mentioned meditations (*dhyāna*), according to one's qualification— that is, in whatever meditation one is fit to be qualified— one should perform that which is appropriate for the time, such as the morning and other times.

"Standing in the midst of their circle of light" means: one should contemplate oneself as standing in the midst of that circle (*maṇḍala*), which is the collection (*samūha*) of the radiance and brilliance of those [rays]. "With the right hand [pouring] water into the left hand," and so forth, is clear. He states the *adhamarṣaṇa* (the rite of cleansing): "Furthermore, that which remains"; that which remains...

The water remaining after the cleansing (mārjana), held in the left hand, should be cast upon a diamond-stone (vajraśilā), or else into water, on the ground, or in front [of oneself]. And it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having placed that water on the palm of the left hand at a gentle (saumya) bathing-place..."
Having consecrated it with the heart-mantra, [he should do so] with water flowing from that sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
One should perform the cleansing with the *saṃhitā* mantras using the right hand,
having placed the palm of the left hand within the hollow of the right hand.
Having led that white form of Dharma, which is slightly more than a span in height, one should contemplate it;
drawing it up by means of inhalation through the iḍā, one should hold it within the bindu-maṇḍala.

Then, by means of *kuṃbhaka*, one should draw out the accumulation of *pāpa* (sin), which pervades all limbs and resembles the color of a lamp-flame from the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*), and having taken it up, [expel it] through the right [nostril].

"One should angrily cast the sin from one's hand onto a stone in front, like a thunderbolt, with the *āgneya-tīrtha* [finger-tip]; this is the *aghamarṣaṇa*. Thus it is said; and it is also stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:

"Sprinkling [with water] while reciting the Saṃhitā mantras, and gazing at the water with a mind fixed on Śiva. Regarding its commentary: "gazing at the water" means the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite; "sin" (*agha*) is explained as evil, and "removal" (*marṣaṇa*) is its destruction.

Because it has been stated: "The Naiṛtīya [mantra] was spoken by Śiva; by its name, it removes sin," therefore, from the beginning of the recitation until the conclusion at the head (of the text), [it should be applied].

Having unified the sin inherent in the self and drawn it in through *recaka* (exhalation), one should cast it upon the ground or into water while reciting the *ghora-mantra*, and then perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). However, in the commentary on the *Mṛgendra-paddhati*, regarding the statement "one should cast that evil into water upon a diamond-stone slab," the casting of the water is directed toward the southwest (*nairṛti*).
It has been stated that [the water] must be poured in a specific direction. Among these aforementioned options, the pouring of water should be performed in one of them.

He states what is to be done immediately thereafter, beginning with "tataḥ" (then): "Then," meaning after performing the *aghamarṣaṇa*, [one should perform] either without mantra (*amantraka*), i.e., devoid of mantra, or with mantra (*samantraka*).

"Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) accompanied by mantras, one should perform the *sakalīkaraṇa* as before. This means that although the *sakalīkaraṇa* was already performed previously according to what was stated in the section on *sakalīkaraṇa*, it is performed once again. Wherever the ritual sipping of water is performed, there too it must be done for the sake of the success of the mantra. And it has been said:

"Whenever one performs the ritual rinsing (ācamana), at those very times the practitioner of mantra should perform the placement upon the hands and body for the sake of attaining the goal of the mantra. Thus it is said.

By means of the armor [rite] (*kavaca*), that is, by the armor mantra (*kavacamantra*), one should meditate upon Sadāśiva situated in the center of the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍalamadhyastha*) according to the method of meditation to be described hereafter.

Having meditated upon the red form by means of this method, through the influence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the substratum, one should perform the offering of *arghya* and more. Alternatively,

having meditated upon the Gāyatrī or the Śiva-Gāyatrī according to the described manner— beginning with "having the luster of molten gold"— one should offer three *arghya*s to Sadāśiva residing in the solar orb, either with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) or with the Gāyatrī.
Having given according to one's capacity, one should recite [the mantra]. And it is said in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"Having meditated upon Sadāśiva in the solar disc, one should offer [the oblation] with the root mantra (*mūlāṇu*).
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the ritual assignment of mantras to the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), one should offer three oblations of water (arghya) with red flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other materials, using the root mantra, to Śiva as the Sun.
"One should recite the three-eyed Gāyatrī in the morning, standing facing the east. Thus it is said.
p.

63) "One should satisfy [the deities] with the *saṃhitā* ending in *svāhā*," because in the ritual procedure for the satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*) of the deities of the mantras, it is prescribed that they must end precisely with *svāhā*. Thus it is stated in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
Having sipped water again, one should satisfy the mantra-deities with the names of the deities of the limbs of the mantra,
preceded by the syllable Om, ending in "svāhā," and using the dative case;
the sages [should be satisfied] with the tips of the darbha grass held in the hand hanging down to the throat.
With the sacred thread over the left shoulder, using the *tīrtha* located at the base of the little finger,
one should worship mortals with mantras ending in "namaḥ" as before, and the *bhūtas* at the joints of the fingers.
"Accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* [mantras], one should offer to Sanaka and the others in due order with the mantras,
using the base of the ring finger and the thumb while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), as if offering to the ancestors.
Thus, [the offerings begin] with "Svāhā to all the gods," and so forth.
Because the accomplishment of that fruit occurs even when performed as a collective whole. Alternatively, "in detail" means:
one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇas*) either by way of the detailed method, excluding the collective position, or according to the sequence stated in the *Paddhati*.

"Mantras beginning with the root mantra (mūlamantra)" means that even in the extensive version, one should first satisfy the mantras headed by the root mantra using the tip of the finger as the *devatīrtha*, and only afterwards perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods and others. It is well known in the scriptures that the tip of the finger is the *devatīrtha*. And it has been said:
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The excellent Āgneya-tīrtha is located on the palm of the right hand;
the Daiva-tīrtha is at the tips of the fingers; and the Brāhma-tīrtha is at the base of the thumb."
The *paitra* [tīrtha] is at the base of the index finger;
the *prājāpatya*, belonging to the sages (*ṛṣis*), is situated at the base of the little finger; and that which is at the joints of all the fingers is for the ancestors.
"The gentle [tīrtha] is on the palm of the left hand, and Bhauma is at the base of the fingers; these sacred sites (tīrthas) of the wise reside within the space between the hands. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the term *upavītī*: after performing the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors, one becomes *upavītī* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder).
