By the phrase "Gaṇapati, Ambikā, and so forth," Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and others are included.

Regarding the phrase "having the sun as his form" (*ādityamūrtayaḥ*): the sun is the form, that is, the body, of him [the deity]. One should recite the prayer according to one's capacity. In performing the recitation, one should recite for the duration of one fortnight (*pakṣa*) with whatever number of repetitions corresponds to one's own strength. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Kiraṇa*, it is stated: "One should recite [the mantra] a full hundred times by means of one's own power, or otherwise.

It is said that this should be done "intensely at the time of twilight (*saṃdhyākāla*). It is also stated: "Endowed with the Mother and the Star," and so forth. When the prescribed time has passed—that is, when one has fallen away from the three periods of twilight—one should recite the *Śivaikādaśikā* three times.

Because it is stated in the *Prāyaścittakāṇḍa*: "In the event of a lapse at one time, one should recite [the mantra] once. Now, he describes the procedure for one returning home after performing the rites of bathing and so forth:
"Then, situated within the cage of weapons (*astra-pañjara*)," meaning a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) consisting of the binding of the ten directions by means of the *astra-mantra*.
Having meditated upon this, one should go to one’s own home and so forth, having entered into its center. Thus it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"Having expelled the obstacles, situated on the path, and possessing a body consisting of the *vimāna*, he should go to a temple or to his own excellent home.
Thus, the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth are impure; [these include] earth and the others, totaling thirty-one.
One should contemplate the state of the pure *vidyā* as the locus of worship, wherein the principles (*tattvas*) abide otherwise than their true nature; and it is said:
"Then, by way of purification, one should conceive of the earth and the other principles according to their [purified] state."
"Śuddhavidyā-tattva is my abode, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus, the place of worship consists of the essence of Śuddhavidyā-tattva. By this, it is indicated that even the performance of worship for one's own sake (ātmārtha) must be carried out according to the method prescribed in the scriptures; and that [place] is in the northeastern direction of the house.

It may be made of stone, baked brick, pure wood, or clay; it may be square, oblong, or circular; and its length should be three times the middle joint of the middle finger of the sacrificer, according to the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior as described in the *Rūpa*.

67) Having ascertained the constriction of the site and other factors by means of the hand measurement known as the twenty-four finger-breadths with separated fingers, one should [construct] according to one's wealth [a temple] measuring three, five, seven, nine, thirteen, seventeen, or twenty-one [cubits].
Having constructed a shrine hall measuring thirty-two cubits in one dimension, consisting of one, two, or three stories,
and having divided it into five parts, one should— avoiding the stone foundation in the central portion—
construct [the main area] out of clay or brick, square in shape, free of pillars, and sixteen or eight finger-breadths in height.

Or, having constructed a railing (vedikā), one should prepare on its western side a space serving as the sanctum (garbhagṛha), measuring one *tāla* in width and length and five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height; and on its eastern side, a space serving as the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇḍapa*), with dimensions for its base equal to those [of the sanctum]. Then, of that...

In the eastern part, one should prepare a space corresponding to the pavilion for the image (beramaṇḍapa), measuring five tālas in length, four tālas in width, and eight aṅgulas in height. Therein, in the space corresponding to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should provide a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, which may be square, oblong, or circular.

68) One should install the *veṭaka* (canopy). In the location corresponding to the temple pavilion (*beramaṇḍapa*), having placed a canopy measuring two cubits in length, one cubit in width, and twelve finger-breadths in height, adorned with lotuses, one should place something beautiful upon it.
Having spread out that measuring cloth, such as silk or other fine fabric, and having placed upon its center a pedestal made of ivory or similar material,

one should then place on top of that a lotus-pedestal made of gold or other precious metal, complete with a halo fashioned at its western side, and spread a cloth over it. One should also prepare the worship pavilion.

One should adorn [the place] with scattered flowers, the fragrance of incense, sandalwood paste, canopies, strings of pearls, banners, flags, mirrors, lamps, and so forth. In the absence of such a worship pavilion (*pūjā-maṇḍapa*), one should mentally visualize the very site of Śiva’s worship as being such a pavilion; having thus entered such a place of worship—

Regarding that, he first states what must be done: "Facing east, one should worship the Sun"—meaning that, facing east, situated between Indra and Agni, one should constantly worship Ravi. Thus it is said.

Because of the scriptural statement: "Indra is in the eastern Amarāvatī, Hutāśana (Agni) is in Tejovatī, and between those two, Divākara (the Sun), the witness of the world, is in Bhānumatī," one should worship [him] in that place. There too—

Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka, Āditya, Śaktya, and so forth—according to the injunctions for the worship of the Vāstu deity, one should worship Bhāskara (the Sun) in his own place, facing oneself. Now, alas! Is this not improper for the Śaivas? [For] the Sauras and Vaiṣṇavas...

The divisions of the Śaivas are established as such; for it is stated that "there is no fruit in the mixture even for the Kālabhairava-Śāktas," and because it will be stated later in the section on the procedure for the worship of the *pavitra* (sacred thread) that "in deed and in thought, there is no other refuge for me but You."

Furthermore, since even the eight forms (mūrtis) beginning with Earth are specifically the forms of Śiva, when the worship of one form is performed, it would follow that the others must likewise be worshipped. This is true; it is said:
"Having abandoned all these gods, with Brahmā at their head,
one should worship Virūpākṣa, who dwells within the sun"— so says the scriptural statement.
Furthermore, according to the statement: "Nandin and Mahākāla, Daṇḍin and Piṅgala—
these are known as Śiva, Sūrya, the limbs of Śiva, the mantras, the Vidyēśvaras, and the planets," one should know Īśvara to be Bhāskara (the Sun) and Skanda likewise to be Aṅgāraka (Mars).
Because of such statements by Bodhāyana, there is no fault here, as Śiva alone is worshipped through the relationship of the container and the contained (*ādhārādheya*).
If it is asked, "In that case, let worship be performed only in the solar form (*sūryamūrti*), why is it performed in the *liṅga* and other forms as well?"—
it is because the worship of Śiva in six substrates (*ṣaḍādhāra*) is prescribed as the essential extraction (*niṣkarṣa*) in the Āgamas, including the worship of the Sun.
And because it is declared to be an object of desire. As it has been said:
"Worship of the Sun, self-sacrifice, the Linga, fire, the Guru, and the book—one should constantly perform this sixfold worship of Śiva."
(As stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā* and other texts:
One should worship Śambhu in the form of the solar disc for the increase of fame and intelligence.
Good fortune, prosperity, and complete success proceed from the daily performance of the fire-oblation.
"The practitioner of mantra should worship the deity of the *liṅga* even mentally; it is not desired [otherwise].
Some say that this worship of the Sun is to be avoided by those seeking liberation because it is an object of desire (*kāmanā-viṣayatvāt*). That is not so, for it says:
"One should worship [it] constantly, even once."
Because it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā* and other texts, the teachers maintain that this must be performed by those seeking worldly enjoyment as well as those seeking liberation.

Thus, it is said: "Having performed the purification of the body with the root-mantra of the Sun. Likewise, in the *Makuṭa*: "O Maheśvara, I shall now declare the root-mantra and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of the Sun."
The Praṇava, conjoined with fire, is that six-syllabled imperishable.
That [syllable] is the root of the Bindu and is long; it is again joined with its head.
Preceded by Vyoma and ending with Visarga, it is the Sūrya-mantra ending in Namaḥ.
One should place the heart-mantra, joined with the peaceful bindu (sānta-bindu), upon the heart.
For the head, one should place [the mantra] for Arka on the crown; one should place the *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ* as the tuft (*śikhā*) on the top of the head.
Having performed the placement of the armor (kavaca) with *hrūṃ* and the eye-mantra (*netramantra*) with *auṃ*, one should perform the placement of the three Vedas (*trivedī*).
One should worship the imperishable Śiva with the seed-syllable of fire ending in the visarga, joined with the solar weapon *phaṭ*, and endowed with the nasal bindu.
Having uttered the single *abindu*, and then reciting *khaṣolka* ending with *sūrya*, one should cause the offering of perfume and garlands of flowers with this mantra. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that he whose purification of the body has been performed by means of the root-mantra of the Sun (Sūryamūlamantra) should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); he should contemplate his own body as being the form of the Sun according to the method of solar meditation to be described hereafter,
thus visualizing his own physical frame as the Sun.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"One should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the hands and limbs with the Sūryamūla-aṅga-mantras;
having effected the purification of the body through the state of the Mūla-śaṃbara."
One should meditate upon one's own self as the supreme Sun in the form of the sun.

At the time of performing the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should place [the mantra] on the heart at the thumb, and for the head, crest, armor, and weapon, on the little finger and the others respectively.

"One should place that [syllable] on the index finger"—this is stated in the *Uttuṅgaśivapaddhati*. Therefore, the teachers have also performed the practice in exactly that manner. Having thus explained the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth, he describes the procedure for the offering of water (*arghyavidhāna*), beginning with the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*):
"in a copper vessel," meaning [the vessel] which is of the same color as the cloth, fragrance, and other offerings belonging to the Sun who is being worshipped.

It has been stated that the *arghya* vessel and other implements should also be made of that same color. By the phrase "having prepared the *arghya* with water, red flowers, and so forth in a copper vessel," one should fill the *arghya* vessel— purified by the *astra-mantra* as will be described later—
with water in the form of red-colored nectar (*amṛta*) flowing from the *bindu*, along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other materials.
The worship with mantras should also be performed.
On a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)— that is, on ground prepared with cow dung and other materials— one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
The altar (*vedi*) is the consecrated ground, the leveled sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or the courtyard (*catvara*), as these are declared to be the abodes of the immortals.
Regarding "on the right side of the door": one should know that the door faces inward, while the door-keepers face outward.
According to this statement, the southern direction itself constitutes the right side (*dakṣiṇapārśva*). Likewise, it is stated in the commentary on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"One should worship Daṇḍin and Piṅgala on the right and left branches of one's own [body]."
"Having displayed the *visphura* mudrā. Regarding the definition of the *visphura* mudrā, it is stated in the *Aspaṣṭapadabodhinī*:
"With the thumb [touching] the tips of the fingers in order, beginning with the little finger..."
The touching of these two hands should be a throbbing [contact], as well as that of the two [feet].
"Drawn from the forehead" means from the middle of the forehead;
drawn forth—that is, brought forth—the throbbing, reddish drop situated at the *jāli* (the junction) by way of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The meaning is "having meditated. Likewise, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The term *raktabīja* refers to the Sun, which is of the nature of radiant energy (*tejas*) and perfectly pure.
"One should visualize [the deity] emerging from the center of the *bindu* and entering the handful of flowers. Thus it is said.
Regarding the characteristics of the mudrās for invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, Bhojadeva stated:
"Having formed a hollowed palm (*añjali*) with both hands, the *āvāhinī* [mudrā] is formed by joining the two thumbs at the bases of the ring fingers."
This same [mudrā], when placed facing downwards, is the *sthāpinī*. With both hands joined in fists with the thumbs raised, it is the *saṃnidhānī*.

Those same two [hands] with the thumbs tucked inside are the *niṣṭhurā*. Having formed the shape of a lotus and placing the two thumbs in the center in the form of a pericarp, it is the *padmamudrā*; [it is also] the *prasāritā* when the two thumbs are joined and extended.

The *bimba-mudrā* consists of the tips of the middle fingers joined together. Regarding "unity at the base"—this refers to the non-manifestation of the limb and the possessor of the limb (*aṅga-aṅgin*)—it is the *khaṣolkinī*. The application of that is: *oṃ khaṃ khaṣolkāya sūryāya namaḥ*.
Regarding the *dhenu-mudrā* for the heart and the other limbs, it is stated likewise in the *Somaśambhu*:
The *dhenumudrā* is for the heart and other [limbs], the *goviṣāṇa* for the two eyes,
the *trāsanī* for the weapon (*astra*), and the salutation (*namaskriyā*) for the [four] abodes (*gṛha*).
Thus, their characteristics have also been stated by Bhojadeva:

77) We shall explain the method [of worship] more thoroughly later on, at the conclusion of the Śiva-pūjā. Immediately following that is the method for the Caṇḍa-pūjā. Then, as for the passage beginning with "in the northeastern direction," etc., or else [it refers to] the conclusion of the Śiva-pūjā.

Regarding the instruction "one should dismiss [the deity]," one should remove the flowers and other offerings from the worship of the Sun, perform the washing of the feet and so forth, and then perform the worship of Śiva. Otherwise, one should dismiss Caṇḍanātha at the conclusion of the worship of Śiva.
Having thus described the procedure for the worship of the Sun, he now describes the worship of Śiva with the word "atha" (now).

After the worship of the Sun, the worship of Śiva should be performed; that [mudrā] is the *goviṣāṇā*, formed by the sudden extension of the middle and index fingers of the right hand while the fist is clenched.
By the sudden extension of the middle and index fingers of the right hand while the fist is clenched...

It is of many kinds, distinguished by the "half-horn" (*goviṣāṇārdha*) and "supreme limit" (*parārdha*) divisions, by the distinction of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), by the external and internal divisions, by the distinction of time, and by the distinction of worship. Thus, it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The worship of Śiva is twofold, according to the distinction between that for the sake of others (*parārtha*) and that for one's own sake (*svārtha*)."

One should know that the worship performed for the sake of others (parārtha-yajana) at a *liṅga* installed in a village or elsewhere, or one that is self-manifested (*svāyaṃbhuva*) and so forth, brings welfare to all living beings.
At the time of initiation, one receives from the Guru the insignia of one's own [deity] for the sake of one's own purpose;
the performance of sacrifice for the sake of accomplishing one's own goal is declared to be "for one's own purpose" (svārtha).
The supreme preceptor, who is a primordial Śaiva, should perform sacrifice for the sake of others;
all others, such as initiated Brāhmaṇas and the like, should perform it for their own sake.
One who is uninitiated, even if he has mastered the four Vedas, should neither touch nor worship [it].
Likewise, it is stated in the Kāmika:
"Now I shall describe the procedure for worship, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
that is proclaimed to be of two kinds: for the sake of others and for one's own sake."
The worship of Śiva for the sake of others must be performed constantly by Brahmins;
for others, it would be only for their own sake, as they have no authority for the sake of others. Those who perform the sacrifice to Śiva are born from the mouth of Brahmā.
They are equal [to others] in that they are entitled to perform sacrifices for the sake of another;
yet, if through delusion there occurs the destruction of the king's kingdom, that is their standing [as a fault].
If ordinary Brahmins worship Śiva for the sake of gain,
they fall [from their status] within six months; therefore, one should avoid them.
"For the wise Brahmin initiated by Śiva,
who is Śiva himself, knowledge that leads to fault regarding the welfare of others occurs only under the power of Śiva’s command.
Thus is the characteristic of the Ādiśaiva stated in the Vīra-tantra.
Īśvara said:
The first is the Anādi-Śaiva; the second is the Ādi-Śaiva;
the third should be the Mahā-Śaiva; and the fourth is the Anu-Śaiva.
The fifth intermediate [lineage] is Śaiva; the sixth is called Pravara;
and the seventh is the final Śaiva. Their distinctions are now declared.
The Śaiva [tradition] is to be known as beginningless; I myself am that, without a doubt.
But the twice-born who are devoted to Śiva, O best of Brahmins, are proclaimed as the original Śaivas (Ādi-Śaivas).
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bharadvāja, Triṇa,
and Gautama— these five were initiated into the five faces.
O Śiva, those twice-born ones born in the lineage of these most excellent sages are great devotees of Śiva (mahāśaiva), O brahmins, and are endowed with the initiation of Śiva.
One who is uninitiated, even if he has mastered the four Vedas, should neither touch nor worship the Supreme Lord for the sake of gain; such people are devoid of initiation.
They fall into degradation after six months and are remembered as *devalakas*.
If one who is not initiated (*adīkṣita*) should worship a fixed linga for the sake of livelihood for three years, O Brahmins, he indeed becomes a *devalaka*. Thus it is said.
The characteristics of other Śaivas should be understood from that very same source.
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*:
"Those born from the creation of Śiva from the four faces of Brahmā..."
Those Brāhmaṇas who were born on the earth are known as Śiva-Brāhmaṇas.
However, those who are born solely from the mouth through the creation of Śiva are called ordinary Brāhmaṇas; one should lead them to Śiva by means of initiation (dīkṣā).
Those who were created as Śaivas by Śiva, the Supreme Self,
those Śaivas came from the mouth of Brahmā to the world of mortals.
"They are celebrated under the names of Kāśyapa and others, appearing in the form of sages.

Thus [ends the section]. The distinction between the external and internal [forms of worship] is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Worship is declared to be of two kinds, according to the division into external and internal."
That twofold [practice] shall be the mental worship for ascetics who desire enjoyment.
The nature of the external sacrifice for all [of these] is now described. Thus.
Regarding the distinction of time, it is stated in that very same [text]:

"The worship performed during the seven watches starting from dawn is said to be the highest; the worship performed during six watches is said to be the middle-highest. Thus, the highest, the middle, and the lowest are described according to the number of watches.
The purification is to be known as fivefold; that which is taught in the middle [section] of the Āgama is the supreme.
Morning, midday, evening, and midnight constitute the middle [category].
Sacrificing at dawn, midday, and evening is middling-inferior;
not sacrificing during the morning and the beginning of the night is inferior-superior.
"The worship of Śiva in the morning is to be known as the lowest; worship at whatever time is available is indeed the lowest of the low. Thus it is said.
Indeed, they say that worship of the All-pervasive One is ninefold through the division of time;
others, according to the division of time, say it is sixteenfold. Where there is a period of two muhūrtas, at that time one should worship Śiva.
Some declare that worship should be performed according to thirty-two divisions of time.
"In that context, the time [required] would be a *muhūrta*; thus it is stated in the Śivāgama.
All this should be understood as being for the sake of others due to the abundance of accomplishments. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the distinction regarding worship is also found in that very same source:
Worship through the various types of *pūjā* is proclaimed to be fivefold:
namely, *ārādhā*, *arcanā*, *pūjā*, and *yāgārhā*. Thus it is fivefold.
For ascetics, worship ending with the offering of lamps bestows liberation;
for one desiring worldly enjoyment, worship ending with the offering of sacrificial food (havir) bestows both enjoyment and liberation.

The festival of worship (*pūjotsava*) should be known as bestowing all happiness upon villages and other such places; the conclusion of the sacrifice and the dance (*yāgonṛttāntaka*) should be known as bringing prosperity to kings and kingdoms.
"Ending with the feeding of the Brahmins, this [rite] bestows all peace upon the Arhats. Thus it is said.
He states what is to be done immediately thereafter, beginning with "having sipped water" (ācamya) and so forth;
here, it should be understood that the sipping of water (ācamana) is for the purpose of removing the impressions of the previously performed solar meditation (saura-bhāvanā).

It was previously stated that after the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), the ritual of "making [the body] complete" (*sakalīkaraṇa*) must also be performed, according to the rule: "Whenever one should sip water, at that very time the deposition upon the body (*dehanyāsa*) should be performed.
Here, he describes the preparation of the *arghya* offering in common for all the deities, beginning with the door and ending with Caṇḍa:
With the words "the general arghya vessel," and so forth: "general" means collective; "arghya" refers to the water offering; "vessel" (pātra) means a container for that purpose.
Having purified it with the *astra* [mantra], that is, having performed the cleansing by means of the *astramantra*.
Having filled that vessel with water—the nectar flowing from the *bindu*—using the Heart Mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should worship it seven times with the *praṇava* or the Astra Mantra. (p. 84)

Furthermore, having consecrated it seven times with that same mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). As it has been said:
"The general *arghya* for the doors and so forth [is used] until the end of the worship of Caṇḍa."

The general consecration of the *arghya* is performed with either the *praṇava* or the weapon-mantra (*astra*). Thus, he describes the sequence of the worship of the door with the words beginning "the door" (*dvāram*).
Here, one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) should worship the doors and the door-keepers at the eastern door. [One should worship] Kīrti, Vijaya...

One who desires good fortune should worship at the southern gate; one who desires liberation alone should worship at the western gate. However, according to the scripture, worship should not be performed at the northern gate. Having sprinkled the door with ordinary water using the *astra-mantra*, one should first worship the guardians of the outer quarters, beginning with the one on the upper part of the threshold to the south.

The *ūrdhvodumbara* refers to the two wooden planks situated above the two side-branches of a door. Regarding the southern part of the *ūrdhvodumbara*, that is, the southern direction, it is stated thus in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
On the upper *udumbara* branch to the south, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Kamalāṅgiras;
and on its own southern branch, Nandin together with Gaṅgā.

"One should worship Mahākāla, situated on the left branch, along with Yamunā. Thus, the worship of the foremost Gaṇapati and others must be performed for the sake of removing obstacles and for the sake of success. As it is stated in the Pauṣkara and other texts:
First, there should be a sacrifice to Gaṇeśa for the sake of removing obstacles;
one should worship Vāṇī for the attainment of mantras, and Mahāśrī for the attainment of wealth.

The worship of Nandin and the others as gatekeepers is established by the rule: "One should request protection from them. This means one should pray to the gatekeepers that the removal of obstacles be performed. Regarding the phrase "with the root-mantra placed," it refers to that [deity] in whom the root-mantra has been placed; "divine" (divya) means those who exist in heaven (divi).

"Situated in space" means as follows: "On the threshold"—the threshold is the *ayodumbara*; on that [threshold], one should perform the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*) preceded by the meditation on the weapon (*astra*) which will be described later (p.

The meaning is "as will be described. As it has been said: "These [deities] are to be worshipped in due order with the [mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with *namaḥ*, according to their respective forms, postures, and dispositions, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in sequence."
Then, having offered the general arghya, one should pray to the gatekeepers as follows:
"O gatekeepers of the Lord, protect the door from this point on."
"Having warded off the hosts of obstacles—such is the command of the Supreme Goddess."
By the falling of divine vision, those who follow after the divine—
those moving through the atmosphere— cast flowers with blazing iron arrows as weapons.
The mantra-practitioner, desiring prosperity, should dispel the three kinds of obstacles located within the sacrificial hall by striking with three blows from the right heel.
Without touching the threshold and keeping slightly to the left side,
the Guru should enter the interior of the palace with his right foot first.

For the purpose of warding off obstacles, one should place a sword upon an udumbara post, having worshipped the Self-born One with the mantra: "Obeisance to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site (Vāstoṣpati)."

The worship of these [deities] consists of offering a seat, mounting [the vehicle], establishing [the presence], and causing them to remain; it concludes with the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful oblation (*arghya*), perfumes (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), and finally, food offerings (*naivedya*) and betel (*tāmbūla*).

Each [deity] should be worshipped individually. If one is unable to perform the worship individually, one should worship all the door-keepers together in the center with the mantra "Obeisance to all the door-keepers (sarvebhyo dvārapālebhyaḥ namaḥ)," using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. This method of worshipping Gaṇapati and the others at the *ūrdhvoduṃbara* and other locations applies when there exists a temple of Śiva or similar structure possessing the characteristics as previously described. [This occurs] prior to the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*).

In the absence of that [physical site], one should mentally visualize such a place of worship, namely a pavilion for worship (*pūjā-maṇḍapa*). Seated near the Śiva-pīṭha, the Preceptor (Deśika), having worshipped the door in the western part of that very chest, performs the worship of the gatekeepers (*dvārapāla-arcana*) prior to the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*), according to the manner previously described.

Or one may perform it later. Now, he describes the method for fetching water and other materials for the ritual bathing of Śiva, beginning with the words "for the purpose of bathing" (*snapanārtham*). [One should fetch] jars (*gaḍḍuka*) and pots (*ghaṭa*), having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), and sprinkling with water (*abhyukṣaṇa*). The definitions of inspection and the other rites have been stated.
In the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra* (p.
"With the thumb and ring finger, [the practitioner] should perform the placement with the root mantra while looking with the eye."
That by which there is the perception of a substance is called "observation" (nirīkṣaṇa).
Sprinkling with water from the palm of the hand while reciting the *huṃ phaṭ* weapon-mantra is known in the scriptures as *abhyukṣaṇa*,
for the purpose of purifying ritual substances.
If worship is performed with materials that have been stolen, purchased, or otherwise improperly acquired, it shall be fruitless;
one should worship Śiva only with substances that have undergone purification through inspection and other rites.
By means of the eyes of the Sun, Fire, and Moon, which consist of vision, action, and will,
[the body] is respectively dried, burnt, and joined with the immersion of nectar.
Then, for the sake of purification, the spear (śakti) is sprinkled with water and struck with the *teja* mantra;
thereafter, it should be grasped while performing the rite of sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) and endowed with the proper disposition (*bhāva*).
Just as wood attains the nature of fire through contact with it, so too does a substance fit for the worship of Śiva become one with Him when consecrated by the Śiva-mantra.
p. 89) Likewise, by means of the mantra: "This illusory substance has the nature of power.
By the word "and" (*ca*), water and cloth [are included]. Having also washed the water-jars with the *astra*-mantra, [one places them] at the location of the *bindu*.

Having filled the vessels for the sake of sacrifice and worship with water in the form of flowing nectar—either by means of the heart-mantra or the Gāyatrī—preceded by the arrangement of the cloth; "all substances" such as flowers and so forth are mentioned, where the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to all materials for worship, including perfumes, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and the rest. Thus it was said by Somaśambhu:
In the manual (paddhati): Having taken up the water-pots purified by the rites of inspection and so forth according to the scriptures,
and having obtained the auspicious permission, one should proceed silently toward the Ganges or other sacred waters.

One should fill those vessels, purified by the Astra-mantra, with water that has been consecrated by recitation over the Pavitra and strained through a cloth, using either the Gāyatrī or the Hṛdaya-mantra.

"Having gathered all the materials, such as fragrant substances, seeds, flowers, and so forth, for the purpose of worship, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Thus [it is said].
By the words "to the right of the deity," and so forth, the manner of the worshipper is described in relation to the deity being propitiated.

90) Because, on the southern side of Śiva, the northern direction is untenable due to its being unfavorable to the gods situated in the other [northern] part. Regarding "on a seat such as a *vṛsī*": by means of *darbha* grass and so forth, for the purpose of protection (*vṛti*).

Regarding the seat that has been prepared, its name is *braśī*; Amara states that "the seat of those observing vows is called *braśī*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), items such as the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) are included. Facing north—that is, with one's face turned toward the north—one should assume a comfortable posture (*sukhāsana*) on a soft-surfaced object such as a black antelope skin, or else by means of the *padma*, *svastika*, or other postures prescribed in the Yoga scriptures.
Having remained in such a way that one is able to abide in comfort, as it is said in the Kāmika:
"On a seat of kuśa grass, on a mat of *brasya* grass, or on the skin of a black antelope—
having assumed whatever posture is desired, with the body straight and the face turned toward the north."

"Astra-prākāra" means that the *astra-mantra* itself is the wall (*prākāra*), the enclosure; the *kavaca-mantra* itself is the wrapping (*avakuṇṭhana*), like a tent or similar structure. By those two, the sacrificial hall—the place of worship—is encircled.
(91) "Having protected" means having performed protection against obstacles. Now, in order to explain the sequence of the five purifications—
The purification of oneself is the first act; the purification of the place is the second;
the purification of the ritual substances shall be the third; and the purification of the mantra is the fourth.
The fifth is the purification of the *liṅga*; thus, the five purifications are described.

Having said this, he first explains the method of self-purification: "becoming Śiva" (*śivīkaraṇam*). Becoming Śiva means attaining the state of Śiva (*śivatva*). This state of Śiva is defined as omniscience and omnipotence. And by that—

The Supreme Lord Śiva is designated as such because of his union with that which is eternal and unconditioned. However, because that state of Śiva-nature is veiled by impurity (*mala*), which is a synonym for beginningless impurity, it does not manifest with regard to all objects. For the purpose of removing that [veiling], the realization of one's own Śiva-nature is brought about through the purification of the body, preceded by the purification of the self.
The task [to be performed] is as follows; likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having performed this correctly, one becomes Śiva; not otherwise.
"One should first purify the body by means of the five *dhāraṇās*;

having thus become one whose body is purified, one should then apply oneself to the mantras of Śiva. Thus, even if the body has been generally purified by bathing and so forth, it must first be specifically purified by the [methods] that will be described hereafter.
Having purified [the body] by means of the *pārthiva* and other *dhāraṇās*, one should subsequently perform the rite of *śivīkaraṇa*.
Now, an objection may be raised: this is untenable, since purification has already been accomplished through initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself. That is true;
however, even though the body is thoroughly purified during initiation, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśodhana*) every day for that body.
The rite consists of mantra. Thus, in the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra*:
"The elements residing within the body must be purified day after day;
for the self whose enjoyments have been experienced and whose lineage has been completely consumed by fire."
For one whose accumulated future karma has been incinerated and who is of a stainless nature,
it is impossible to remain within a body produced from the impurities of mother and father.
Therefore, every day, one should perform the ritual action consisting of mantra.
Thus.
Furthermore, regarding the powers (*śakti*) that reside in all mantras to be accomplished through meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
which manifest as obstacles and are obstructive— here, their "burning" (*dāha*) is intended; and this burning consists of their non-production or their cessation.
Regarding the phrase "then it is remembered":

for those initiated into *nirvāṇa*, even though the karma of the body that has begun its fruition (*prārabdha-kāya*)—which was not exhausted during initiation—is being consumed day by day through experience, the possibility of a residual trace (*vasanā*) remains; and it is in accordance with that [residual trace] [that the memory occurs].

It has been stated that for one who remains [in this state], the impurity (*mala*) which is the cause of attachment toward the state of being an enjoyer, and the *māyā* which is the cause of the body and senses that are the means for that [enjoyment], are each divided fivefold daily, part by part. This is explained in the *Sūkṣmasvayaṃbhuvavṛtti*: "Having thus stated the purpose, [one performs] the purification of the body..."

Regarding the purpose of the ritual, he first states the procedure for the placement of the hands (*karaṇanyāsa*) with the words "Therein," etc.: "Therein, at the time of commencing the purification of the body, as before, [one should perform it] as described in the section on the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).
Having performed the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) on the two hands, one should proceed as stated in the *Kāmika*:
"One should purify the two hands smeared with sandalwood paste by means of the *astra* mantra;
having thoroughly purified the palms and the backs of the hands against each other."
Having rendered them nectar with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
and having meditated upon their supreme nature as the body of Vidyā, up to the limit of Śakti;
Having invoked Śiva with the root mantra, one should assign the Brahmāṇīs and the limbs [of the mantra].
Thus, the two hands are consecrated as Śiva and become capable for all ritual acts.

"Karanyāsa (the ritual placement on the hands) must be performed during the sakalīkaraṇa, at the time of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), as well as during the sipping of water (ācamana), and also according to its specific rules.
Now, [this applies] when the nature of the Suṣumnā and other channels is not fully understood, for the sake of purifying the body... [of that which is being performed].

Since practices such as *prāṇāyāma* cannot be performed [in that state], he describes their essential nature with the words beginning "the big toes of the feet" (*pādāṅguṣṭha*), etc.: starting from the two big toes of the feet (*pādāṅguṣṭhau*).
As far as the *mūlādhāra* extends, [the channel] has two forms; above that, up to the end of the *brahmabila*, it has a single form.
By the phrase "in the heart, throat, etc.," the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the *brahmarandhra* are included.

Having visualized the Suṣumnā nāḍī as being joined by the Iḍā and Piṅgalā— which are situated on the left and right sides starting from the kanda located at the Mūlādhāra— as being hollow in form and possessing internal openings, [one should meditate] upon it.

Within and without the *suṣumnā*, she whose form is the supreme void (*paramavyoman*); that is to say, she whose form is the supreme void, the supreme ether known as *kuṇḍalinī*; through her, [one attains] the Self.

One should meditate on the subtle body as its presiding deity; then, one should meditate upon Śiva-Śakti, who causes the rain of nectar to flow through that [nectar] which has been set in motion. Thus it has been said:
"The pair [of feet] is in the two feet, the aperture is in the body, and the one [the head] is in the heart and other locations."
It is endowed with five knots and situated within the central channel, the suṣumnā.
And in the midst of that, one should place the external power, the flowing drop of nectar, whose nature is action and knowledge, and which has the form of space. Thus it is said.
"Having meditated upon the blazing syllable *hūṃ* in the midst of that"—
meaning, having meditated upon the seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā-bīja*), namely *hūṃ*, in the center of that power (*śakti*) which resides within the aperture; immediately thereafter,
he speaks of the inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kuṃbhaka*) for the purpose of causing the lotus situated at the heart-center to blossom.

Having done this— first performing inhalation (*pūraka*) measured by twelve *mātrās* and retention (*kuṃbhaka*) measured by the same duration— and subsequently fixing the mind on the previously mentioned syllable *HŪṂ*,
one exhales the breath upward as far as the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*), causing it to proceed upwards.

At the time of the upward movement of the breath, with the Śiva-weapon mantra accompanied by the seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā*)— namely *huṃ phaṭ*— and by means of a continuous, uninterrupted recitation, one [should place] the lotus-buds, which are the hearts, in their respective locations while remaining face-downward.
Having made the lotus buds— which were previously described as facing upward— open by piercing them,
and having turned back, one should exhale through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*), thereby withdrawing the upward-moving wind that was formerly [present].
Having placed the syllable *hūṃ* in its proper place, one should exhale through the *piṅgalā*.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having drawn in the radiant fire through the *iḍā* channel by means of inhalation (*pūraka*)."
One should hold the syllable HŪṂ in the middle of this aperture by means of the kumbhaka breath-retention.
One should pierce the knots situated in the heart, throat, palate, eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahma by means of the *hūṃ* syllable ending with *phaṭ*, using the exhaling breath (*recaka*).
"Therefore, having withdrawn [the breath], one should place the syllable *hūṃ* in the navel-maṇḍala.
Thus it is said in the *Samāna-tantra*:
"Then, having pierced the membrane with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should enter upwards."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the illustrious *Trayodaśaśatika* [Tantra], it is declared that the sixth seed-syllable (*bīja*), endowed with a vowel, belongs to Śiva.
Therefore, O son of Pārvatī, she [the goddess] becomes accessible through this alone.
That which is joined with the essence of Śiva is proclaimed as "yuktā" (the united).
"O child, you shall become the impeller of the great-souled weapon.

Then, he describes the method for the conjunction with the Self (*ātmayojanā*) in order to perform the purification of the body, beginning with the words "again by the filling breath" (*punaḥ pūrakavāyunā*), etc.; immediately thereafter, by the filling breath on the left...

By means of the wind drawn in through the *nāḍī*, consciousness (*caitanya*) is withdrawn; "consciousness" refers to the power characterized by perception, pleasure, and pain, and that which belongs to it is the self (*ātman*). The meaning is that consciousness, which pervades the body, is withdrawn—i.e., the self is contracted.

Residing in the heart-lotus, situated within the lotus of the heart, having the form of a shimmering star, resembling an exceedingly luminous constellation, consisting of the *sānta* seed-syllable (*am*), joined with the *bindu*, and denoted by the letter *ha*—
it is so called because it cannot be grasped as a pervasive self; rather, through its expressive medium (*vācaka*), it is the *jīva*, for it is the cause of life.
The *puryaṣṭaka*, which is denoted by the word "birth" (janman), acts as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that delimits [the Self];
it is encapsulated within the heart by means of the Heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*). The *puryaṣṭaka*... [p. 99] ...is thus enclosed within the heart.

Having extracted [the self] from the body and encapsulated it, one should contemplate the Person—the Self—whose form (*vigraha*) consists of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), specifically the seed-syllable ending in *saḥ* (*sāntātmaka*). This solitary Self is being released even from that subtle body; for this very reason, it is free from affliction (*nirāmaya*) and devoid of defects. It resides within the crest of the *hūṃ*-syllable, that is, within the *hūṃ*.
Having placed the seed-syllable of the *śikhā* upon the region of the navel and having enclosed [the breath] with it,

one should perform *kumbhaka*, meditating on the supreme cause in the form of a drop (*bindu*), which has become a subtle point through the process of dissolution by extremely subtle and high-pitched utterance, while causing the vital air to move upward.
Having drawn [the breath] upward by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* while purging, one should withdraw it; here the definition of the *mudrā* is stated:
"Extending the right hand, one should then contract the fingers starting from the little finger in sequence; this is considered the *saṃhārikā-mudrā*. Thus it is said.
since movement is impossible because the self is all-pervasive,
it is here accepted that movement occurs by means of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body).
How is it possible for one who is devoid of that [support] to be led upward?

Alternatively, it is said [to be] "accompanied by the *puryaṣṭaka*"; this is because the body of the *puryaṣṭaka* is that which is to be purified, and because it has been stated, "having meditated on [the Self] alone and free from affliction. Furthermore, it is called the "seed-form" (*bīja-vigraha*), and because it is presided over by the power of *nāda*, which is the effect of the *bindu*, it is derived from that *nāda*.
Even in the absence of the *puryaṣṭaka*, there is an inseparable concomitance. As they say:

"The light of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jyotis*) within, which is subtle and never departs from the body—[the wise] call that 'immortal' (*amṛta*) in the case of the Puruṣa who is [otherwise] a mere fragment. Thus it is said.

One should gradually abandon the causal deities— namely Brahmā, Acyuta, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— who reside in the locations of the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), as well as the letters beginning with 'ka' and so forth.
(101) By a single upward thrust— that is, by a single effort made with the upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), meaning by its upward transport— it is said:
"When the [lower winds] are properly restrained, the wind moves upward."
"She is known as 'Sodghātā' because she is ejected by her own will at the desire of the younger [initiate].

This means that for the sake of experiencing the *bhogya-karma*—the karma not exhausted during initiation which remains to be experienced while in the present body—for the purpose of enjoying that karma, she returns once more; however, unlike the one who has ascended by her own will (*svecchotkrānti*), she does not return no more.
This is the intended meaning. Now, an objection may be raised: "If there exists karma to be experienced (*bhogyakarman*), there can be no purification of the body;
for the body is caused by karma, and since it has been stated that bodies are diverse according to their respective karmas.
Alternatively, if you consider the body to be pure, then karma to be experienced must also be destroyed."

Because here, by means of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśodhana*), the burning of the body is taught, according to the statement: "One should burn the body with the fire of yoga from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.

This is truly said: here, the burning of the body or rather the burning of karma is declared to be by the fire of yoga. However, because it has been stated that this does not occur through the unmanifested [state] but rather through karma, one should unite [the self] with Śiva—the partless essential nature—at the end of the twelve [fingers] (dvādaśānta) or at the end of Unmanā. For it is stated that "union" means the individual soul (*jīva*) is led upward by the Power (*Śakti*). Upon the abandonment of that [body]:

But by means of the function of the seed-mantra (*bīja*), having become a point (*bindu*), one should contemplate the entry of the self into the state of Śiva together with the presiding power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*). Then, entry there occurs. And so it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
Having withdrawn [the breath] by means of inhalation (pūraka), the knower of mantras should, with the heart-mantra,
place the life-force consisting of the seed-syllable of peace upon the head of the syllable *huṃ*.
Having meditated upon the Person situated at the crest of the syllable *hūṃ*, whose form is the seed-syllable— solitary, subtle, having become a drop (*bindu*), and free from affliction.
Then the yogin should unite [the self] with Śiva, the supreme cause,
who transcends Śiva, within the end of existence, as pure as a flawless crystal.
"By means of a single emission alone"— here, the conjunction at the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths) should be understood as being like the twilight meditation (*saṃdhyā-dhyāna*),
according to the distinction of the qualified practitioner (*adhikārī*), because it has been taught [to occur] even in locations such as the heart. As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Having made the self the object of withdrawal by means of that [breath], and having placed the *bindu* within the center,
one should subsequently burn the body"—
thus it is stated in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*.
"One who knows the ritual procedure should place [the deity] in the heart-lotus for the purpose of experiencing the karma to be enjoyed,
or in the hollow of the palms, or else at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta). Regarding this,
in the commentary *Durbodhabodhinī*, it is stated that placement at the end of the twelve constitutes liberation (*nirvāṇa*).

It is well known that this applies only to those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*). Now, following the application of the self (*ātma-yojanā*), since the body is twofold according to the distinction between the subtle and the gross, [the author] first states the purification of the subtle body with the words beginning "in this way" (*evam*): "In this way," as previously stated... (p. 104).

In this manner, by way of the function of the seed, the mantra-seed is dissolved into Śiva; having attained identity with Him through the form of pervasion—as it is heard that "dissolution is indeed equal conjunction"—the principles (tattvas) such as earth and the rest, namely the thirty-six principles, are [withdrawn] in reverse order according to the sequence of dissolution, in the manner to be described: "earth into smell, water into taste," and so forth.
The world-sphere (bhuvana) of the Śiva-tattva situated within the Tattvāṣṭaka is thus described.
One should bring [the elements] up to that extent to dissolution for the sake of purifying the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha).
It is said that one should purify it as follows:
Dissolved into Śiva by way of the seed-syllable (bīja-vṛtti), and remaining there within the body by means of the mind,
[one dissolves] the principles beginning with earth (avany-ādi-tattva) in reverse order into their own causes.
"One should purify [the elements] by leading them to dissolution up to the level of the Śiva-tattva. Thus it is said. He states another alternative with the words "or else" (yadvā):

Having performed the recitation of the root mantra (mūlamantra) according to the procedure for invocation (*āvāhana*) to be described [later]— either by means of the recitation of the *prāsāda* mantra or by the departure of sound from the lotuses of the heart and other centers where Brahmā and the other Lords of Causes reside— one should effect the purification of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).
By the phrase "sound and so forth," touch, form, taste, smell, mind, ego, and intellect are included, because it is stated in the *Kālottara*:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth; mind, intellect, and ego—this is declared to be the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city). Now, what indeed is this *puryaṣṭaka*?

The subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), which is common to all individuals, consists of thirty principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth and ending with *kalā*; it is fixed for each person from heaven until the end of the cosmic cycle (*kalpa*) or until liberation (*mokṣa*). If it is asked how sound and the other [objects] constitute the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), the answer is found in the explanation given by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha, who uses the term "thirty principles" to denote it.

It has been explained by her as follows: it is "become" (bhūta) because it is composed of the eightfold group [of letters], which consists of the five sheaths beginning with *kalā*— individually distinguished by the breath-inhalation (*pūraka*) and its causal quality, along with those known as the *mātrās*, the *śuddhis*, the *indriyas*, and the *antaḥkaraṇas*.
Therefore, for the sake of its purification, one should offer it to Brahmā and the other deities.
As it has been said:
One should renounce sound and touch in Brahman;
one should renounce form and smell in Rudra; one should renounce intellect and pride in Īśvara;
and one should renounce mind and the *bindu* in Sadāśiva for the purification of the *puryaṣṭaka*.
He explains how one should purify the elements that constitute the gross body for the sake of purifying the gross body itself, beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*):
"Then," meaning immediately after the purification of the subtle body, one should purify the gross body, which is the elemental body. And here—

Just as one practices the meditation on Garuḍa for the sake of removing poison from those situated within the gross and subtle bodies, so too is there a purification—like a state of dissolution—for the sake of removing the quality of bondage from the principles (tattvas) residing therein; however, this is not a direct withdrawal.
The earthly sphere (pārthiva-maṇḍala), which pertains to earth, is yellow in color and solid.
(Vajra) having the intrinsic nature of a thunderbolt, adorned with a vajra;
because it is the Maheṃdra-maṇḍala, it is marked by a vajra and characterized by the weapon. Likewise, in the Sarvajñānottara:
"Square, yellowish-green, marked with a vajra, hard, and heavy—the yogi should contemplate the maṇḍala of Mahendra starting from the crown of the head.
Now, one might ask: how can the element of earth and so forth, which occupies only a single location, extend from the feet up to the crown of the head?
If it is asked, "Why is this so?", it is said: because she is presided over by the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti* and the rest, the following intention is expressed here.

Here, Speech (*vāk*), whose form is sound (*śabda*), although established as the bestower of enjoyment for those abiding on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) as Mahāmāyā, is also said in the *Āgamas* to abide in the impure *dhvani* of Māyā in the form of *nāda*. For thus [it is stated]:

In the daily worship and other rites, as external purifiers, there are the five elemental principles (tattvas) beginning with earth which constitute the body; specifically, it is their respective powers (kalās)— the presiding principles and the objects of their governance, namely the kalās such as Nivṛtti and the rest—
that are here denoted by the words "earth" and so forth.
As it has been said in the venerable *Viṃśatikālottara*:
"Nivṛtti is to be known as earth; Pratiṣṭhā is said to be water."
Vidyā is said to consist of splendor, while Vāyu is proclaimed to be peace.
"Beyond Śāntyatītā is the supreme ether; beyond that is the peaceful and imperishable.
Starting from the feet up to the crown of the head—having attained this, it is the same even in the mandalas and so forth, because they too pervade the body. "By means of the fivefold *udghāta*":
When the breath is properly restrained, it moves upward;

this is renowned as the *udghāta*. According to the statement "by one's own will, however, [it may be done] with fewer [repetitions]," one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kuṃbhaka*) without exceeding twelve *mātrās*, while meditating mentally on the syllable *HĀM*.

Or, having performed the utterance and led [the breath] to the *dvādaśānta*, one should return and exhale. In this way, for the destruction of the five qualities of earth, five *udghātas* are prescribed; for the others, however, (p.
One should know that the number of *udghātas* (expirations) corresponding to the number of one's own qualities is for the destruction of those respective qualities.
One should contemplate the earth as being overcome by its opposite, air, because of the mutual opposition between earth and air, as well as between water and fire. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
water, air, fire, and earth; water, fire, earth, and wind; and water-earth, as well as wind-fire.

"Neutral, enemy, and friend [are arranged] in groups of four, two by two. Thus, at that time, having abandoned the form of the *kāra* (the letter *ka*) and so forth, one should contemplate (*bhāvayet*, i.e., visualize) the form of the enemy, such as air (*vāyu*), and so on; for the letter *ā* is inimical to all of them. Otherwise—

He says that what is to be purified is the "sphere of space" (*nabhomaṇḍala*); it has the form of the void, appearing as the space well-known to worldly people as such because it is formless; it is empty, yet adorned with the power of the *bindu*, meaning it is presided over by the crooked power (*kuṭilā śakti*).

(110) Regarding the phrase "overcome by the supreme space" (*paramākāśābhibhūtam*): the lower space (*aparākāśa*) is that which is joined with planets, constellations, and so forth, while the supreme space (*paramākāśa*) is devoid of those; thus, the twofold nature of space is taught in the *Āgamas*. Likewise, in the *Ratnatraya*:
Furthermore, they say that the sky is eternal and possesses even more darkness than night;
yet for those who possess equal sovereignty, it serves as the basis for both their enjoyment and their authority.
"Ether is the cause of the qualities of light, of Śiva, and of the elements. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"It is devoid of qualities, beyond the manifest, and free from planets and constellations."
"One should contemplate the supreme ether (para-vyoma) resembling pure crystal.

Therefore, setting aside the elemental ether which possesses qualities such as impermanence, one should contemplate the nature of the Great Ether (mahākāśa), endowed with qualities such as permanence. He states what is to be done immediately after that, beginning with "then, by means of the weapon-mantra" (tato 'streṇa): "Then..."
Immediately after the exhaustion of the qualities such as smell residing in the elements beginning with earth, one should [proceed] with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
By the fire raised from the big toe of the right foot— that is,

the fire arising from the big toe presided over by the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti), which is the Kālāgni— the external body, composed of a collection of elements whose power has waned due to the exhaustion of the *guṇas*, is said to be dissolved. Its impurities are consumed.

Having meditated upon that ash and having removed it with the *navāyu* (the new breath), one should then perform the ritual immersion (*āplāvana*) in the manner to be described hereafter, beginning with the words "the bound void" (*baddha-śūnya*). Now, he states another method for the purification of the gross body (*sthūla-deha*), beginning with "or else" (*yadvā*).

Alternatively, without performing the previously mentioned method, one should purify by meditating upon the gross body in the form of a banyan tree. One's own body is the external body; it is that whose seed consists of the five elements, earth and so forth, because Brahmā is the creator and Viṣṇu [is the sustainer] of them.

That from which a sprout has emerged—that is, arisen—due to those two being the agents of protection; namely, passion and hatred (rāga-dveṣau), which are well-known as desire and aversion, and as merit and demerit (dharma-adharmau); and delusion (moha), which is a particular kind of impurity. Delusion and intoxication (mada).

For it has been stated: "Passion (*rāga*), despondency (*viṣāda*), stagnation (*sthāna*), emaciation (*śoṣa*), and variety (*vaicitrya*)—these seven are the impurities (*mala*) along with [the others]. That which has these [impurities], beginning with passion, as its roots—that is what is meant. Therefore it was said: "Knowledge (*vidyā*), the lords of knowledge (*vidyādhipati*), the mantras (*mantra*), and the lords of mantras (*mantreśvara*) protect the [principles] beginning with *kalā*. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), *vidyā* and *rāga* [are included].

That whose essence and stable core consists of the principles known as Time (kāla) and Necessity (niyati); so it has been said—that which possesses great branches and minor branches; likewise, that which possesses the perception of objects through the operations of the sense organs such as the eyes, which are its cowherds and tender sprouts; so it has been said—the various states of being (bhāvas).

The eight qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*), beginning with virtue (*dharma*), have fivefold manifestations as their flowers; joined with these, this jar—which is the object determined by the intellect—is fixed in its nature as "this is a jar" and not as "a cloth. (p. 113) How [could it be otherwise]? It is immovable.

Form (*rūpa*) is the activity; *saṃkalpa* is the activity consisting of mental synthesis. That which has this very [activity] as its fruit is described as such. The "person" (*puruṣa*) is the self (*ātman*; *sa eva*). Because the body has been described as being in the form of a tree, the self is figuratively expressed by the word "bird" (*vihaṅga*) due to its being the enjoyer of that fruit.

Having meditated upon the form of the great banyan tree (*vaṭatara*), which has the nature of the enjoyer as its sap, the object of enjoyment as its sap, joined with that [enjoyer], with its root directed upwards and its branches extending downwards— having thus contemplated it in the form of a *nyagrodha* tree— thereafter, by means of the first part of the inhalation (*pūraka*), that is, for the duration of twelve *mātrās*.

The duration is six *mātrās*; within that time, by means of the fivefold utterance of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) for the dissolution of the five qualities of earth—uttering "Hlām" five times—one should contemplate [the tree] as being devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruit, and rendered rigid, because it is stated in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*: "It is endowed with the yoga of the destruction of the leaves."

First, having meditated upon a form like a pillar, devoid of leaves and so forth, one should afterwards recite the seed-syllable of the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, "Hvīṃ," four times for a duration of six *mātrās*— that is, half of a *parārdha* of the *pūraka* breath.

One should visualize [the tree] as being endowed with glossy, pleasing leaves, flowers, and fruits. Then, having performed *kumbhaka* (breath retention), one should recite "Hrūm"—the seed-syllable of the *vidyā-kalā*—three times, using the first syllable for a duration measured by the time of the *parārdhya* (the supreme) *mātrā*, and the second syllable for a duration measured by the time of the *parārdhya* [of the previous]. Thus, [one should meditate on it] as dry.

Having contemplated [the tree] as burnt, during the first half of the exhalation (*recaka*), one should likewise consider the duration to be measured by twelve *mātrās*. Having uttered the seed-syllable of the *kalā* of Peace (*śānti*), namely *hyaiṃ*, twice,
and having visualized the burnt tree as reduced to ashes and dissolved into the directions, one should [utter] *haum* during the latter half of the exhalation.

Having recited the seed-syllable of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*) once, one should contemplate the body as having the appearance of pure crystal. Thus, it is said in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*: "One's own body is the seed-syllable of the elements..."
The Nyagrodha tree— composed by Hari and Vidhi, having its own sprouts as its roots in karma, auspicious with time and other factors as its core,
possessing the objects of the senses as its leaves, branches, and sub-branches, with all states of being as its flowers,
bearing excellent fruit hidden within, enjoyed by the bird of the human soul, and rooted above while its sap is directed downward toward the objects of the senses.
"And one should contemplate the possessor of branches.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "The field is Māyā; the seed of the youth (Māṇava) is the power of dharma and adharma."
The principles beginning with *kalā* have ignorance as their root; they are like passion, devoid of essence.
The soul, the person, and so forth constitute the great tree of activity;
the sense organs are its branches and the like, while the objects of the senses are considered its sprouts.
In the same way, that tree of existence, consisting of phenomena and the rest,
has its roots above and its branches below, bearing the two fruits of pleasure and pain.
The practitioner of mantra should thus contemplate his own body as being like a banyan tree;
first, by means of the previously described filling-in (pūraka) breath-control, he should identify it with the earth element.
"O Bhava, become that tree, provided with leaves, flowers, and fruit;
[and] by the latter half [of the mantra], [become] the one endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruit through Vāruṇī."
During the Āgneyī retention (kuṃbhaka), one should contemplate [the body] as being neither merely dried out nor merely burnt;
then, during the Vāyavī exhalation (recaka), one should contemplate it as having been reduced to ashes throughout the ten directions.
One should contemplate the pure, stainless sky as dissolved otherwise;
one should utter the mantras of the other elements, beginning with earth, according to their respective qualities.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"Having visualized the tree of saṃsāra as having its roots above and its branches below,
by means of the inhalation (pūraka), one should discard the notion of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted regarding the earthly element."
It was nourished by the water from the rear portion of the *pūraka*,
rendered glossy with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and [cleansed] by the weapon of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Having thus offered it into the fire and dried it by means of *kumbhaka*,
one should burn the beautiful [substance] starting from the big toe with the fire of knowledge (*jñānānala*).

Then, by means of the *recaka* [exhalation], one should contemplate the ten directions as reduced to ashes and dissolved; otherwise, purification is not achieved— one should meditate on the stainless sky.

Thus, he says that one should immerse the body whose defects caused by the *bhūtas* have been dispelled; this is expressed by the words "then," and so forth. Then, immediately after performing the purification of the body, one should contemplate the entire body—consisting of both gross and subtle forms and bound in nature—as being empty (*śūnya*), considering it to be inactive and as if non-existent because it acts as a fetter.

When the conceptualization of a self as a self, which depends on the expectation of forms as objects, ceases to exist, there remains only consciousness— devoid of support, free from bonds, and identical to the nature of the Self— which resembles the orb of the sun. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
One should burn away the animal form with that which touches the state of Sadāśiva;
then, by the wind of those ashes, the Śākta [form] should be removed and one should not look back.
"Having the form of the solar orb and adorned with the orbs of vision and action—that very body of his is intended to be called 'the unmanifest-limbed' (avyaktāṅga). Thus [it is said].
(p. 118) Then, just like the voluntary departure [of the vital breath], because the body— consisting of both gross and subtle aspects— is not destroyed in any way,
and because that body is worthy of being touched by the Supreme Lord, [one performs] the worship of the Supreme Lord and so forth, without [the need for such destruction].

Because the residual impurity has not been removed due to the cooperation of *prārabdha-karma*, and because at the time of purification it is entirely abandoned through separation from even a mere trace of rays; [this refers to] the Supreme Lord’s power, which exists as the warp and woof of all things, which is eternally the substrate, and which is of the nature of supreme nectar.
Because the supreme bindu (parabindu) exists as the support of all, one should perform an immersion with the nectar arising from it, ending with *vauṣaṭ*. Beginning from the *mūlādhāra*,

one should utter the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*— as will be described in the section on invocation— and [perform the immersion] with the streams emitted by the circle of power (*śaktimaṇḍala*) situated within the downward-facing lotus at the end of the resonance (*nāda*).
One should cause [the practitioner] to be bathed by streams of nectar entering through all the gateways of the channels, such as the *suṣumnā*.

Now, he describes the preparation of the seat for the purpose of again placing the Self, which resides at the *dvādaśānta*, within the heart, beginning with the words "In the heart" (*hṛdaye*) and so forth.

In the heart—that is, in the location of the heart—there is a form consisting of a stalk, petals, and pericarp, which is composed of the three principles (tattvas) beginning with the Self (*ātman*). For this very reason...

One should install the seat, which consists of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) and has the nature of Pure Knowledge itself, by means of the *praṇava* alone— which is all-pervasive, whose essence is Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), which is joined with the three measures beginning with the letter 'A', which consists of the triad of solar and other mandalas, which is the essence of the triad of digits (kalā) beginning with Nivṛtti, and which takes the form of the triad of mantras beginning with Sadyojāta. As it has been said:
In the *Trayodaśaśatika*:
"One should know the Ātmatattva, which is immediately joined with eight digits (kalās), arises from the letter 'A', and is endowed with twenty-four principles."
The bulb and the stalk arise from that; thus it is proclaimed.
One should know the left [channel] as being born from the syllable *U*, endowed with thirteen digits (*kalā*).
The principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is declared to be situated upon the support of Śiva;
it is established within the pericarp, in the midst of the filaments of the lotus petals.
"The principle of Śiva (śivatatva) is proclaimed to be the letter 'A', which possesses manifold forms. Thus [it is said].
In the *Samānatantro* as well— beginning with: "The letter A, which arises from the self, is indeed like the orb of the sun," and so forth.

By means of the syllable *oṃ*, the lotus and the yoga-seat (*yogapīṭha*) likewise come into being. In the location of the heart, one should recite with a long pronunciation the seat of the Self (*ātmāsana*), beginning with the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) and ending with Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), extending up to the palate and ending with the letter *m*, pervading [the entire body] from the letter *a* to the point (*bindu*).

Having performed the placement with the *praṇava* using a short pronunciation, one should then contemplate the pure *puryaṣṭaka*— ending in the *bindu* and all-pervading— within the pericarp of that lotus, as having descended by means of the *praṇava* of four parts consisting of the letters from 'A' to the *bindu* with a long pronunciation; thereafter, within that *puryaṣṭaka* body...

Situated at the end of the twelve finger-breadths, for the purpose of performing the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), it is joined to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] and has the nature of the seed-syllable previously described.

One should establish the Self, which consists of Śiva, is presided over by Śiva, and is of the nature of Śiva, by means of the letter *ma* and so forth, joined with the five *kalās* ending in *da*, through a protracted (*pluta*) utterance. One should then perform the immersion in nectar for that Self using the *Śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Thus it has been said:
Having caused the root mantra to flow as a stream of nectar from the liquefied power,
one should bathe [the deity] within by sprinkling it upon the lotus of the heart.
The preceptor, having invoked the form of the Self with the Mūrti-mantra,
should take that Self from the heart and unite it with the Dvādaśānta.
One should consecrate that body with nectar for the sake of unification;
the body is to be known as Sadāśiva, for the individual soul (pudgala) is indeed Śiva himself.
"In this way, for the sake of meditation, one should contemplate non-duality through the placement of mantras.

If it is asked, "Since it is stated in another scripture that the invocation of the Self (ātmāvāhana) should be performed with the *prāsāda* mantra, how is it done here with the *praṇava*?"—there is no fault, because of the statement: "One should conceive of no difference between the *prāsāda* and the *praṇava*."

Having explained the internal placement (*mantar-nyāsa*), he states that for the sake of accomplishing the body of the Śākta Vidyā, the placement of mantras (*mantra-nyāsa*) must be performed upon the external body. Having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) in the same sequence as before, "as before" means...
As stated in the section on the *saṃdhyā*: when there is an opportunity and no mental agitation occurs,

one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Daṇḍabhaṅginī, Muṇḍabhaṅginī, and Vaktrabhaṅginī— as will be described in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*)— as well as the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa and Vyomavyāpin, which are taught in other Āgamas.

One should also perform the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth. Thus, having attained the state of Śiva through one's own nature and form—having first purified the vital breath (*jīva*) and the body, and having the body invested with the placed mantras—one becomes fit for the worship of Śiva. This is because of the scriptural statement: "One who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva. In this way, if one is unable to effect the purification of the vital breath and the body, [one should perform] *nyāsa*.

One should perform at least this much. Even for one who has performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), if there is an inability to perform it fully, one should perform at least the five-fold Brahma-nyāsa and the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) nyāsa (p.

To that extent alone, the purity of the nature of Śiva belonging to both the body and the self is established; by that much, one becomes fit for the worship of Śiva. Now, he describes the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*) and so forth, stating: "The heart, the navel, and the station of the *bindu*. But why is there an internal sacrifice here?

If it is argued that this is because one begins with external worship in this manner, it is said in reply: even by those who perform external worship, internal sacrifice must first be performed, and only thereafter should external adoration be carried out.
And it has been said:
Having first performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), one should then perform the external worship;
that very same Jyotirliṅga residing within the heart is worshipped externally.
Therefore, for that reason, the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) is said here to be what must first be performed;
for he who performs the external sacrifice without having performed the mental sacrifice [is ineffective].
"It is certain that the labor of that scripture is in vain.

Thus, having worshipped Śiva with flowers and other offerings brought forth through mental visualization— beginning from the seat and invocation up to the end of the recitation (japa)— in the external worship according to the sequence to be described hereafter:
The navel itself is the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); it is well known that the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) resides within the belly as something spontaneously established.
Having performed the oblation (*havana*) therein, one should likewise [offer] the partless (*niṣkala*), all-facing reality in the center of the *bindu*.

In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "One should meditate on the partless [reality] between the eyebrows"—thus, worship should be performed in the heart, the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the navel, and meditation in the space between the eyebrows. Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:
"Having thus attained the state of mantra, [one resides] in the divine body according to the sequence."
One should designate the locations for worship, fire-offerings, and meditative absorption.
One should meditate on Īśvara, the granter of boons, who faces all directions, upon the forehead;
there, one should prepare a seat according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
Having invoked the deity Śiva mentally with perfumes and other offerings, one should worship him;
then, in the navel-cavity which arises spontaneously, one should gratify him with the supreme nectars.
Having kindled one's own internal fire and restrained the downward-moving breath (apāna),
one should meditate upon the Linga, brilliant like crystal, at the station of Sthāṇu.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "One should [meditate upon] Śambhu, together with his limbs, within the lotus of the heart, according to the procedure for the external sacrifice."

"One should worship with those things brought forth through the intellect. Thus, the internal sacrifice and so forth have been described here in general for those who possess the Śiva-initiation; however, as it is relevant, that which is taught in other Āgamas according to the distinction of qualified practitioners is also written here.
O Guha, the teacher should be wise, a knower of reality, and born of a distinguished lineage;
even if he lacks all [other] auspicious marks, O Guha, he must be a knower of the meaning of the Śiva scriptures.

An *ācārya* characterized by such marks as being skilled in half a *pāda* of the *Vidyā* and so forth, should perform the internal worship (*antaryajana*) and other rites according to the methods prescribed for worship and praise. For example: having mentally conceived, within the space of the inner heart, a divine pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) for the worship of Śiva composed of red light, therein—

Having mentally brought forth the substances required for the worship of Śiva and purified them, one should offer the *arghya* with a stream of nectar flowing from the lunar disc situated at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths].
Having performed the filling of the vessel and other such consecrations (*saṃskāra*), and having conducted the worship of the gatekeepers (*dvārapāla*), one should,
with the permission of Gaṇeśa and the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*) according to the sequence to be described and preceded by prayer,
[visualize] a lotus with a pericarp the color of rubies and gold, ten rising petals of blue color, and eight petals of the color of barley.
