Having meditated upon the *liṅga* consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which has the form of a flame and the nature of sound (*nāda*)— to be perceived through the union of the ear and the thumb— situated within the yellow pericarp of the heart-lotus as the *bindu* and having the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) upon its pedestal; and [having meditated] upon the powers beginning with Śakti on that pedestal in the sequence to be described hereafter.
Having worshipped the Śivāsana at the end, and having worshipped the form of Śiva and the Vidyā-deha in the Liṅga,
one should worship Paramaśiva there through the sequence of consecrations beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of water (arghya).
Having bathed Him with a profuse stream of nectar falling from the Dvādaśānta, [one should worship Him] with garments, ornaments, and so forth, [and contemplate] detachment...

Having adorned [the deity] with sandalwood paste, one should offer the flower of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth— in this manner, by means of the eight flowers consisting of non-violence, restraint of the senses, forbearance, compassion, knowledge, austerity, and truth.

One should perform worship. Then, having conceived the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the fire, and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) as the flame of the incense within the mental vessel, one should offer incense. Having conceived the knowledge of Śiva as the lamp, one should offer it. Contemplating the mind withdrawn from sense-objects as the food offering (*naivedya*), one should present it. [The path is] Suṣumnā.

One should contemplate the very coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) along its path as the act of recitation (*japa*). One should adorn [the self] with ornaments appropriate for that state, fashioned through meditation on Sadāśiva—the constituent parts of whom have been stabilized by the fivefold concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) beginning with the earthly element. This is the offering of the self (*ātma-nivedana*), consisting of the contemplation of identity with Śiva in the form "I am Śiva."

And one should perform [this]. Or else—immediately after the consecration—one should offer the subtle elements of smell, sound, touch, form, and taste in the form of sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, and food offerings.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: preceded by the recitation of the root mantra, [one says]: "Oṃ hlāṃ, to Śiva Sadyojāta, I offer the fragrance consisting of the subtle element of smell, hraum; to Śiva Īśāna, I offer the flower consisting of the subtle element of sound, hyaiṃ; to Śiva Tatpuruṣa, [I offer] the touch..."
"I offer the subtle element of fragrance (gandha-tanmātra) as incense. HŪM! To Aghora Śiva, I show the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) as a lamp.
HVĪM! To Vāmadeva Śiva, I offer the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) as the food offering (naivedya). Then...

After offering water for washing the hands and mouth-perfume, one should contemplate: "I offer betel-leaf, which consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Then, having prepared the ritual eye-ointment (nīrāñjana), one should present a mirror fashioned by the wind residing in the intellect, as well as auspicious objects.
The manifold activity of the mind has been fashioned by you in the form of this dance.
Sound exists in the form of song through the union with resonance (dhvani), and as a variety of musical instruments;
Suṣumnā exists in the form of a banner, and the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth exist in the form of chowries.
The ego is described as the elephant, the body as the chariot,
the mind in the form of the reins, and the intellect in the form of the charioteer.
"Everything else has been offered by me, with my very self as an instrument of austerity. Thus [he said].
One should offer everything belonging to oneself—the intellect, the mind, the vital breaths, and so forth—as instruments for the worship of Śiva.

At that time, one should also perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*) in the form that will be described hereafter. Then, having made Śiva favorably disposed toward grace through circumambulations and prostrations, one should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) by His command.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: one should visualize a fire-pit with three enclosures at the navel; having visualized the fire there as self-established, one should kindle that fire with the *astra-mantra*. Then, having conceptualized a certain ember within that fire as the "flesh-eating" portion (*kravyādāṃśa*), one should discard it in the southwest corner (*nairṛtikoṇa*) and [take up] the fire remaining in the pit.
Having purified [the fire] through gazing and other means, in order to establish its status as the Śiva-fire, one should lead that fire (i.e.,
its consciousness) to the *dvādaśānta* by means of exhalation (*recaka*), unite it there with Paramaśiva, and make that mass of light intensely radiant.

Having brought back that form of the fire of knowledge, one should establish it in the navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*). When this has been done, it becomes the Śiva-fire without requiring any further consecration; that Śiva-fire is red in color.

Having meditated upon Sadāśiva, who has five faces, ten arms, and a form identical to his own, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seat (*āsana*), the form (*mūrti*), and the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) within the lotus of his heart. Then, having invoked Śiva, one should offer as oblation (*ājya*) the stream of nectar flowing from the end of the twelve [fingers] through the *suṣumnā*— acting as the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*)— by means of the *iḍā*, using the root mantra one hundred and eight times.

Having offered oblations one hundred and twenty-eight times, or eight times, and having visualized the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) as the *suṣumnā* channel— marked by the heart-lotus and having its bowl filled with the nectar of power (*śāktāmṛta*) and clarified butter— one offers the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with it, [causing] Śiva, who was satiated by delusion, [to emerge] through the path of the channels (*nāḍīmārga*).
Having united that [consciousness] with Śiva, who is worshipped in the heart-lotus, and having honored Him with the eightfold flower-offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should conclude the worship.
Then, [one should contemplate Him] in the middle of the eyebrows as devoid of all distinctions of limbs.
One should meditate on Śiva with a form resembling a pure lamp.

Everything described here, beginning with "within the space of the heart," is perceived directly by one endowed with a subtle body through the power of yoga; for one devoid of that [subtle body], everything must be accomplished through mental visualization.
He in whose waking state all objective phenomena dissolve as if in deep sleep—his realization is complete; by him the three steps have been transcended.

Thus, the manner of worship for the Knower endowed with such characteristics is described. *Bhūtaśuddhi* (purification of the elements) is the absence of the conceit of identity with the body as a material form; *dehaśuddhi* (purification of the body) is the absence of desire for sense objects.
Alternatively, *bhūtaśuddhi* is the perception of the eightfold form (*aṣṭamūrtitva*), and [the purification of the body] is the penetration of Śiva into all substances.

Vision is the purification of substance; self-purification is the state of abiding as one with that [Śiva] after perceiving one's own true nature through the knowledge of Śiva. In the five-syllabled mantra, having set aside the two supreme syllables pertaining to the category of *pāśa* (the bonds), one takes the two supreme syllables pertaining to the category of *pati* (the Lord) and the single supreme syllable of the *paraśu* (the axe).

Having understood this and having abandoned both vocal and mental [repetition], the purity of mantra (*mantra-śuddhi*) consists in the continuous contemplation of that which is expressed by the single vehicle.
It is the realization of Śiva as the indivisible form of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), known solely through direct experience.
Purification of the Liṅga:
The Self is the seat of Śiva; the form is truth, knowledge, and the unobscured;
the root is supreme bliss. Now, the invocation is described.
In this context, the very manifestation of Śiva is traditionally known as the invocation (āvāhana);
purity is the installation (sthāpana), and facing [the deity] is the presence (saṃnidhāna).
Absorption (laya), distraction (vikṣepa), and withdrawal (haraṇa) are called "suppression" (saṃnirodhana).
The dissolution of the duality of māyā is likewise [called] the foot-water (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamana).
There shall be the destruction of the three karmas; the arghya is the liberation from ignorance.
The great consecration is purity, the cleansing of the garment is freedom from obscuration.
The removal of attachment is the sacred sandalwood paste; the renunciation of dualities is the flower;
the destruction of the latent impressions of ignorance is the incense; and self-luminosity is the lamp.
Having brought the offering of food (naivedya) experienced by Śiva, well-perfumed,
along with the dripping of its delicious flavor and likewise the wiping of the hands;
The straining of decoctions has been described; betel-leaf is for the fragrance of the mouth.
The *layastotra* (hymn of dissolution) has been proclaimed for the Lord known as Āhata;
it constitutes a circumambulation everywhere, being coextensive with Śambhu.
Just as water becomes of one uniform taste through its union with the ocean,
so too is the union of the Self and Śiva proclaimed as the true salutation.
Just as that which is known and unknown becomes submerged within the object of knowledge,
so too they say that the offering (arghya) presented with averted face is an offering to the Self.
Thus, having explained the internal sacrifice and so forth, he speaks of the external worship and the request for Śiva’s permission: "I worship externally.

The meaning is that, having made the request, "I worship you who have been worshipped internally even externally," and having received the response, "Do so," he then performs it. He states what must be done immediately thereafter: "One should perform the purification of the place."

Even though the place of worship has previously been purified by means of fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth, it must be purified through mantra. Thus he says, "by means of the weapon-mantra" (*astreṇa*).

One should perform the three *tālas* with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). The definition of the *tāla* and the *aṅganyāsa* (placement of limbs) were explained for the purpose of understanding [the procedure] in the section on *coṭikā* and so forth; their characteristics have been stated right here. One should contemplate that protection has been established everywhere against obstacles by means of the *parighas* (crossbars), the *aghāthikās* (spear-protectors), and the *śakti-jāla* (net of spears), which is a multitude of spears. This is the preparation of the *arghya* for Śiva.
He says: "Constructed from gold and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," silver, copper, and others are included.
Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "It may be made of gold, silver, copper, coral, pearl, or conch."
A vessel made of palāśa leaves, lotus petals, wood, or clay.

Alternatively, whatever vessel has been prescribed for the worship of Śiva, such as one made of yantra and so forth—one should perform its cleansing with the *astra-mantra*, ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Here, because of the singular number in the word "vessel" (*pātram*), there is only a single vessel for the *śivārghya* offering. Thus it is.
In the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī* (p. 135):
"One vessel among the vessels, such as gold, is purified with water consecrated by the Weapon-mantra (*astra*). By that very [water],"

The water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the water for rinsing (nirodha), and the offering water (arghya) should be presented. When resources permit, each of these should be prepared individually for each [deity]. Thus, it is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"One should wash the four arghya vessels with the Astra mantra."
Therein is a triad of mandalas, known by the names Soma, Sūrya, and Agni.
One should prepare the special *arghya* in the *arghya* vessel using the heart-bīja;
one should fill it with drops of water resembling nectar while reciting the Śakti mantra.

Having placed the substances prescribed in the scriptures separately within those [vessels], in that very context it is said: "In the absence of vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings, one should prepare two *arghya* vessels."
In the case of two *arghya* offerings, there should always be a special *arghya* for the Lord;
the general *arghya* belongs to the gateway and so forth, ending with the worship of Caṇḍa.

Thus: "With perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādipadena), [it is meant]: water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice grains, *sumanā* flowers, and sesame seeds. (p. 136)

Regarding the statement "the *arghya* consists of eight parts," the eight substances are taken according to the scriptural injunction: "along with barley and white mustard seeds. In their absence, one should add fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Having prepared the *arghya*, he states what must be done immediately thereafter: having sprinkled oneself with those waters while reciting the *astra-mantra*, [one offers] fragrance and so forth.

One should also sprinkle the articles of worship with the *kavaca* [mantra]. *Paramīkaraṇa* (the act of supreme unification) is the visualization that the various colors of the installed *kalās*— such as those of the heart, the crest, and so forth— attain that same color through the white radiance brought forth by the invoked Supreme Śiva.
One should touch [the body] from the head down to the feet with both hands in the manner of Mahāmudrā. Furthermore, having recited the Astra mantra twice, one should purify the left hand;
likewise, one should purify the right hand with the right hand and the left hand with the left hand.
Having recited it once, O Nandikeśvara, one should purify.
One should contemplate the two hands, endowed with the splendor of missiles, up to the wrists;
then, having formed a hollowed cavity with the two hands, one should place the two thumbs between the middle fingers.
One should meditate upon the supreme circle of Śakti with the seed-syllable of nectar;
reciting "Oṃ hāṃ śaktaye vauṣaṭ," it should be immersed within the hollow of the joined palms.
One should visualize the form of a lotus within the cavity; in its center is the seat of Śiva.
Having placed the subtle form there, one should subsequently recite the mantra.
In this manner, O Nandikeśvara, one should install the form of Sadāśiva.
In the Vīratantra:
"Then one should place the five mantras, beginning with Īśa, on the thumb and the other fingers;
then, having meditated upon the body of the Vidyā, one should [place] the supreme [mantra] ending with Śakti."

Having placed the *netra* (eye-mantra) on the palm of the hand, one should subsequently perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*). Then, while contemplating the one called Viśvasāda, one should perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), beginning with the little finger and the thumb.
The placement of mantras on the heart and other centers constitutes the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the process of making [the deity] complete).
In the *Kālottara*:
"Having performed the placement with the fingers in the center, one should enclose it with the *kavaca* [mantra]."
Then, one should place the temple upon all the fingers of the hand.
The ritual placement on the limbs (*karanyāsa*) has been fully explained; after this follows the ritual placement on the body parts (*aṅganyāsa*).
With the right thumb and ring finger, one should perform the placement on the heart, the seat, and the form.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) upon the body according to the rules, one should then place the five Brahmans.
One should place Īśa on the crown of the head with the tip of the thumb;
Tatpuruṣa on the mouth with the fist-grip of the index finger and the thumb joined together.
One should likewise place the Aghora mantra on the heart using the union of the middle finger and the thumb;
and one should place the Vāma mantra on the private parts using the union of the thumb and the ring finger.
By joining the little finger and the thumb at the feet, one should place Sadyojāta;
with the thumb and the tip of the ring finger, one should place Vidyā on the body and Hṛd at the heart.
One should place the eye [mantra] at a distance of three finger-breadths between the two eyes;
having placed the *prāsāda* mantra in the heart, one should subsequently place the limbs (*aṅga*).
Likewise, one should place the Aghora mantra at the heart by joining the little finger with the thumb.
One should place [the mudrā] on the head with the tips of the thumb and ring finger;
one should place it on the topknot with the tips of the thumb and middle finger.
One should assign the heart and other limbs to the body, and the armor (kavaca) between the breasts;
then, one should assign the throat as a covering with the two index fingers.
One should place the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) upon the palms with both ring fingers;
likewise, one should perform the triple-clapping (*tālatraya*) and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the weapon-mantra.
Having meditated upon the *sādākhyā* [tattva], perform the binding of the ten directions with this *uṣṇīṣa-mudrā*.
As it is said in the *Ajita*:
Striking the palm of his left hand with the fingers of the right hand,
excluding the thumb, is the *sātāla* mudrā, which bestows purity.
Having again formed a fist with the right hand,
one should properly press the tip of the index finger against the tip of the thumb.
One should extend the index finger when piercing, so that the arising of sound occurs.
This is known as the Nārāca weapon, employed in the rites of binding with mudrās and the directions.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having purified the two hands with mantra, one should protect them with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
Then, one should perform the touching (*ālaṃbha*), beginning from the feet up to the head."
Having performed the consecration with the root mantra, one should then sequentially form the Mahāmudrā.
As it is stated in the *Samānatantro*:
"One should touch the feet with both hands and lead them to the left side of the head."
This is the Mahāmudrā seal, employed in the ritual action of purifying the hands.
The specific cause has been stated:
since one should touch the feet with both hands from the letter *ka* to the end of the feet,
this is the Mahāmudrā, which is the purification of the hands in the Western [tradition].
The purpose of this has been set forth in the Pauṣkara:
"If there were a purpose for those whose natures are utterly distinct... (p. 141).
"That indeed is the immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) of the limbs together with the possessor of the limbs. Thus it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara* regarding the ritual action:
"One should contemplate within oneself the very form that Śiva possesses;
always perform this installation (*nyāsa*) of the Śiva-mantra upon yourself."
Thus, the practitioner whose body is armored with mantras is not afflicted by any obstacles for the sake of protecting his body.
Thus it has been said:
"The heart-armor (*hṛdayāvaraṇa*) is like a protective bandage;
the head-armor (*śīrṣāvaraṇa*) is the wrapping around the head."
Wearing a helmet for the protection of the head and a breastplate for the protection of the limbs,
he stood like a warrior with a terrifying weapon grasped in his hand.
One should [use] those items that are small yet unassailable, like those of Tārkṣya and Dyusravas;
immediately thereafter, having consecrated those substances with the heart-mantra and veiled them with the armor-mantra, [one prepares] the water for the *arghya*.

One should drop a drop of bathing water together with a flower into the jars. Thus it is said in the Kāmika: "With those waters, while reciting the Kavaca mantra, one should likewise sprinkle the kuśa grass, as well as the sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamp, arghya, and the food offering."
One should sprinkle curd, milk, ghee, and so forth with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should consecrate each substance prepared for the purpose of worship with the heart-mantra; this includes the water for the *arghya* offering and the flowers that have been gathered.
One should pour [the water] into all the bathing jars for their purification.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should sprinkle with that [water] the substances prepared for the sake of the sacrifice."
One should not give what has not been sprinkled with water, nor should one give anything that lacks excellence to Śiva.

In its commentary: "And the 'distinctness' of substances is the production of their capacity [for action] through means such as consecration with mantras, sprinkling, consecration by recitation, and enveloping.

"Contrary to worship" (*pūjā-viruddham*) means that one should remain silent until the conclusion of the worship. Likewise, it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "One should worship oneself with such substances in their proper order; having maintained the silence desired [for the rite], one should then purify the mantras. Thus it is said.
In the *Kriyākramāvalī*: Having offered a flower upon his own seat and having applied a tilaka on his head, he should join the flower [to the deity] with the root mantra during bathing,
worship of the deity, fire-offering (*homa*), eating, and both types of sacrifice (*yāga*).
"The wise should always maintain silence during the obligatory recitation (*japa*).
Thus [it is said]. He speaks of the purification of the mantras with the words "the mantras" (*mantrān*);
here, because of the plural number, the five Brahmans, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the root-mantras (*mūlamantra*)—both short, long, and protracted—are intended.
"In sequence" means:

"The Brahmans are said to be short, O Six-faced One, and the Aṅgas are long," according to this statement. [The sequence is] from the end of Bindu to the end of Nāda, and from the end of Layā, for the five Brahmans and six Aṅgas.
The root mantras begin with *oṃ* and end with *namaḥ*.
Those which have *oṃ* at the beginning are "beginning with *oṃ*"; those which have *namaḥ* at the end are "ending with *namaḥ*. (p. 144)

"One should perform the purification of the mantras. Their purification, however, consists in [the practitioner] casting off the body—characterized by touch, which is produced by being manifested through the words of the *māyīya* level—and taking refuge in the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*). Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Just as copper becomes pure gold through the application of alchemical elixirs,
so too do these mantras become pure and fit for use through union with Śiva.

The knower of reality, being a practitioner of mantra, should recite the mantras— consisting of short, long, and protracted vowels followed by the bindu— ending with Śiva in the aperture of Brahmā, according to this sequence.

Now, he describes the purification of the *liṅga* with the verse beginning "paryuṣitām" and so forth: one should withdraw the previously arranged offerings— such as perfumes and flowers— placed upon the *śivaliṅga* or other supports, using the root mantra or the *prāsāda* mantra ending in *svāhā*, accompanied by the seed-syllable of the heart (*hṛdaya-bījākṣara*), along with the Brahmans such as Sadyojāta and the rest.
One should perform the recitation once, having entered the fivefold [sequence].
145) Some say that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the tips of the little fingers; that is not correct, because [it would be] upon that which is to be worshipped.

Because it is stated, "having placed the hand," [the procedure continues]: by means of the *liṅga*, that is, taking the perfume (*gandha*) and other offerings previously prepared and placed upon the *liṅga* with the *astra-mantra*, [one places them] in the northeastern direction (*aiśānī-diśi*) on the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) or similar surface.
"Oṃ hāṃ, I offer this to Caṇḍa at the conclusion of the Śiva-pūjā"— with these words, one should set it down. Thereafter,

having performed a cleansing of both the liṅga and the pedestal with the Astra-mantra for the purpose of removing the previously offered perfumes and other substances, the purification of the liṅga is accomplished through sprinkling with the general arghya water.
And it has been said:

"The purification of the *liṅga* has been declared according to the sequence; now it is described as it truly is. The *liṅga* is said to be threefold: manifest (*vyakta*), unmanifest (*avyakta*), and consisting of both."
The self-existent [deity] appears in many ways—as divine, as a weapon, as a ṛṣi, as human, and so forth;
likewise, he may be a stationary liṅga, mobile, or a maṇḍala, or even a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Whether it be a cloth, a wall painting, or a seat upon which the mantra is recollected;
or else, a forest stream, a venerable tree, and so forth— this is the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
Specifically, a stone that is naturally formed, or even a jewel, or another type of linga—
such as one made of sand— is said to be especially [auspicious].
Having arranged all this for the sake of the worship of Śiva according to the proper method,
one should perform the worship directed toward the form of the Liṅga as previously prepared.
Having worshipped with the Gāyatrī, one should offer the general arghya;
then, having recited the five Brahmans and having withdrawn the worship from the liṅga.
Having placed the pedestal and so forth in the eastern direction according to the ritual procedure with the heart-mantra,
one should cast the *piṇḍikā* [pedestal] with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra while reciting "To Caṇḍeśa."
Having purified the Śivaliṅga with his right hand,
the practitioner should likewise purify the water for the weapon-mantra (astra-ambu) as well as the Śivaliṅga together with its pedestal.
"Afterwards, one should perform the consecration with the waters of the general *arghya*," so it is stated in the *Kāmika*. Likewise, elsewhere as well (p.
Having slightly removed the previously offered worship by joining the little finger and the thumb,
one should [place] the flower upon the top of the *liṅga* with the Astra-mantra and the Gāyatrī.
One should place [the vessel] with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb turned upwards;
then, with the left hand using the Astra-mantra, one should wash the pedestal with water.
"By means of the *liṅga*, one should perform the rite of removing scents and other substances with the right hand;
one should not touch it with the left, nor should one touch the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).

Thus, immediately after performing the purification of the *liṅga*, [one should proceed] preceded by the worship of the stable seat (*sthirāsana*) beginning with the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*).

Following the ten consecrations beginning with invocation (āvāhana), the great ablution (mahāsnapana) such as the oil massage (abhyaṅga) and so forth is obtained by applying it to both mobile and immobile [liṅgas] alike. He shows this specifically by saying "in the case of a mobile liṅga":
here some, having worshipped the sixfold raised seat (ṣaḍutthāsana) upon the bathing altar, meditate on the form of the Bull (Vṛṣabha).

Having worshipped the Śivāsana, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) for the two guardians of the sacrifice in the pavilion worship, just as one does for the Śivakumbha and Vardhanī vessels. (p.
They say that after worshipping Śiva with offerings ending with *vauṣaṭ* and flowers, performing the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth,

and placing [the deity] upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should again worship the *ādhāra-śakti* and the rest up to the *sthirāsana*, and then perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites. Others, however, because this is a mobile linga (*calaliṅga*), maintain that the entire seat should be worshipped right there on the bathing altar (*snānavedikā*).

First, having performed the thirty-eight-fold ritual placement (*kalānyāsa*) and other preliminaries as in the case of a fixed linga (*sthiraliṅga*), and after the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*),

one should perform the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, wipe it with a cloth, place it upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and offer perfumes, flowers, and other articles. Both of these types [of worship] are likewise [to be performed].

Because it is not approved by the Teacher (Ācārya), [the option] "with the *iṣṭapuṣpikā* for the mobile liṅgas, the seat, the image, and the root mantra" has not been accepted here in this manual (*paddhati*). It was stated as an alternative; therefore, the position stated in the manual itself is superior. Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
At this time, when the liṅga is mobile, one should offer the eightfold flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā).
One should perform the bathing with products of the cow (gavya) and other substances after the vehicle has become stable. Thus it is said.

"Arising from the five nectars and so forth" means: the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are milk, curd, honey, sugar, and clarified butter; [the bathing] arises from these. One should perform the bath with those five nectars and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the coconut juice and other substances, as well as flowers, gold, and red water, mentioned in other scriptures, are included.
Thus it has been said: "Milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar [should be offered] according to one's capacity,
in measures starting from one *kuḍupa* up to an *āḍhaka*, or even increasing by one *kuḍupa* at a time."
"With coconut water, or with other juices containing wine,
with flower-water, gold-water, red-water, and scented water"— thus it is said.

One should contemplate these as the constituent parts of the bathing ritual, such as anointing, rubbing with unguents, immersion, and so forth, according to the procedure described later in the *Paddhati*.
Since these will be described later, they too should be performed whenever possible prior to the bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth.
Having performed an anointing with cow’s ghee and oil, [one should apply] flour and turmeric powder.
One should perform the ritual rubbing with a mixture. Thus it is said:
"Having worshipped Śiva with cow's ghee or with fragrant oil drawn up by the hand using a mechanical device, [one should do so] with the mantra of Śiva ending in 'namaḥ'."
Having rubbed [the body] with auspicious rice flour mixed with turmeric and powdered black gram (*māṣa*), one should then perform the immersion. This is done "alternating with water,
incense, and eight flowers"— that is, at the time of offering the oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) and other services, in the intervals between them.

Having consecrated it with water in the center and worshipped it with the eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should remove the incense and lamp as well as that worship with the *astra-mantra*. Then, one should consecrate it with another substance in such a way that the head [of the image] becomes empty while still possessing the flowers and other offerings; this is done five times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), with the Brahma-mantras, and with the limb-mantras (*aṅga-mantras*)—the word "and" (*ca*) implying these.

One should perform the recitation of each of these five times. Having bathed [the deity] with the Śiva-kalaśa, according to the injunction, one should worship a single *kalaśa* in the manner prescribed in the *Snapanakalpa*.
With that, one should perform the consecration. As it has been said:

"One should bathe the deity with auspicious sounds, using the Saṃhitā mantras ending in *svāhā*, or with the Brahma-mantras, or with the limb-mantras (*aṅga*), or with the root-mantra, or with the heart-mantra."
Thereafter, one should perform the consecration with jars that have been bathed;
and having removed the flower previously placed there with the Astra-mantra, [one should proceed].
Having washed his hands with his own mantra, he should bathe the Supreme Lord with water that is not moving, using conch-mudrās and pouring it over him.
One should sprinkle the collection of sacrificial materials with bathing waters;
one must never leave the head of Śarva devoid of flowers.
Having wiped all his limbs with a very fine, pure cloth, using the armor-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, for the purpose of declaring himself bathed and ready for drinking water.
O Sovereigns of the World, one should place [the image] upon a pedestal covered with divine garments.
He summarizes the aforementioned point with the words beginning "evam" (thus):
"In this way," that is, by the method previously described, the purifications of the self, the locus, the substance, the mantra, and the *liṅga* have been performed.

He by whom the purifications of the self, the locus, the substance, the mantra, and the *liṅga* have been performed should worship Śiva in the manner that will be described. Thus, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"In this way, having accomplished the purifications of the locus, the substance, the mantra, and the *liṅga*..."
Having performed the five stages and so forth, one should perform the worship.

With the words "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth, he describes the worship of Gaṇapati and the others. Regarding the phrase "the previously mentioned form": having meditated upon Gaṇapati and likewise upon Śrī in their forms as previously described for the worship of the gateway, one should worship them. "The sandals of the Master" (*svāmipādukā*) means the feet of the Guru, which express great reverence; it is to be performed according to the available materials. As follows:

Having described the manner in which the instruments (*kāraka*) and auxiliary causes (*upakāraṇa*) have come into being for him, [the author] now speaks of the worship of the *Śivāsana* (the seat of Śiva) as distinct from that of the supreme Guru Śiva and one's own Guru, beginning with the words "Then," and so forth.

"In the middle of the lower part of the deity's pedestal" means: the lower part of the pedestal—that is, the base—is its rear portion; [the rite is performed] from there, in the middle region of that.

Regarding the phrase "seated upon the tortoise-stone" (*kūrmaśilāsīnām*): the "tortoise-stone" (*kūrmaśilā*) is a stone shaped like a tortoise that serves as the substratum for the *ādhāra-śakti* (the foundational power). It is identical with the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīroda*), which possesses the form of a seed-sprout—that is, it has the appearance of a seed-sprout—since it is heard of as having the very form of a sprout, being of a curved nature.
For it is heard thus in the Śrīkālottara: "That primordial Kuṇḍalinī, joined with the Moon, Fire, and Sun,
is to be known as situated in the region of the heart in the form of a sprout."
Thus it is said. Likewise, elsewhere:
"Furthermore, having burst through the egg, she stands like a sprout from a bulbous root.
This is because it will be explained hereafter that dharma and the other [principles] consist of infinite potencies (*sāmarthya*).
Because it is impossible for those without support to remain stable, there exists that infinite seat consisting of a thousand-petaled *māyā*-lotus.

And he says that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) must be performed "upon the Brahma-stone" (*brahmaśilopari*). The Brahma-stone is the foundational stone; upon it is the form of the seat of Ananta. Regarding the phrase "the earth is the bulb" (*pṛthvī kaṃdam*): the earth itself is the bulb of that lotus. The "stalk" (*nāla*) consists of the principles from Water up to Kalā—that is, the thirty principles ending with Kalā—which constitute a single stalk for that [lotus]. These are the entities (*bhāvāḥ*).

That which has the fifty-fold qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) as its thorns; the definition of *bhāvanā* should be seen in the *Mṛgendra-tantra* and other texts. "Born from its bulb" refers to Ananteśa; here, Ananteśa is the first among the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s). He is the all-pervasive (*vibhu*) and omnipresent (*vyāpaka*), and for that very reason, he is below the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

It is situated here in the portion within the lotus-root, because it is stated that Ananteśa resides there; and his body, being born of *karman*, consists of pure causes. As it is said in the *Parākhyatantra*:
"His body is said to consist of pure origins and is not born of *karman*."

Then, [the seat] is to be meditated upon as consisting of the pure elements, earth and so forth, in their specific states; for it is heard in scripture that the lotus-seat of Śiva’s throne is adorned by Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
The state of being composed of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) belongs even to the stalk and other parts that constitute its limbs;

it is established as the nature of the arrangement of Pure Knowledge, existing as the support for pure earth and the other elements. With respect to the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), it is "consisting of Māyā" (*māyīya*) because it is the cause of limited knowledge and so forth, and because it is delusive. Therefore, [it refers to] the parts of the lotus.
Because the body-parts of all beings are infinite, because there is non-difference between the body and the embodied due to their oneness,
and because the embodied is primary, it is said that [the Lord] resides in the Infinite (Ananta). As stated in the Kāmika:

Ananta, whose essence is the sacred seat (pīṭha), abides there in the form of the agent; therefore, they are "of the nature of his power. This refers to the powers such as Dharma and the rest, which are of the nature of the splendor (tejas) that is the power of that Lord Ananta. As it is said in the *Śrī Parākhyatantra*: "His feet, limbs, and members are considered to be the directions, including the intermediate directions. The word "his" (tasya) refers to Ananta.
"Having presided over the directions of light and splendor, what are the powers?
Having presided over the directions beginning with the feet, they are the limbs"—this is stated in its commentary; this refers to dharma and so forth.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) should be understood as having the phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth as its basis, because it is the cause for activities such as retention (*dhāraṇā*).
They are like various manes and resemble various lion-manes; they are observers of one another's backs.
This state of observing one another's backs refers to the nature of the phenomena and so forth as being pairs, due to their mutual relationship of cause and effect.
This is stated figuratively: Kāśmīra is red in color, Kali is black, and Tāla is yellow.

Respective to their order, they possess white, red, yellow, and black forms. Among them, those located in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneyādi) upon lions, and situated in the directions starting from the east, are designated by the term *gātrakas*. In these [sections]:

One should contemplate the body situated in the eastern direction as being mixed with the lion-form located in the northeast and southeast corners; likewise, one should contemplate the nature of the panels extending toward the south, west, and north as being mixed with the lion-forms situated at both their sides.
(157) "The powers of Ananteśa" means forms of infinite capability, just like [the qualities] beginning with Dharma; or alternatively,
"limbs" is another interpretation, referring to the four limbs that resemble crystal, which are like crystal.

One should meditate [on them] as having lion-heads, being supported by lion-heads situated in the corners; their arms, heads, and necks are stiff— meaning their arms, heads, and necks are motionless— and their heads are attached to the sandals (*pādukā*), meaning they are fixed upon the sandals situated at the corners of the feet.

Furthermore, their heads: those whose limbs and feet are positioned at the front are "fore-limbed" (agragātraka); those whose limbs are situated in the portion of the *bhūpura* (the outer square), with their heads placed one upon another on their feet, are presided over by the qualities of *buddhi* (intellect) and *adharma* (unrighteousness). The qualities of *buddhi* are the *adharmas*; these are the "unrighteous-faced" ones (*adharmamukha*).
Ignorance, dispassion, and lack of mastery—these are the qualities of the intellect (buddhi-guṇas).
Likewise, those headed by unrighteousness (adharma) have been mentioned; their presiding deities are the aforementioned infinite [deities].
This means "those specific forms of fire. Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Dharma is situated in the direction of Agni; Jñāna is located in the direction of Vāyu; Rāga is in the direction of Nairṛti; and Śuddhi faces the direction of Īśāna."
Vairāgya stood upon the wind, dark-hued and facing the direction of Nirṛti;
he cast off those lions who had assumed their forms and rested at his feet, their fangs bared.
One should worship Dharma and the others, who are accompanied by their own forms and retinues,
whose bodies are firm, whose limbs are beautiful, and who can assume any form at will.
Their seats were shaped like wooden planks; their bodies were stiff with their left limbs extended, and they sat upon lion-heads with their heads joined together, resting upon each other's sandals.
[He visualizes] forms within downward-facing [lotuses], with the luster of stainless crystal,
possessing red, yellow, and black radiance according to the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
Well-restrained by stakes situated at the four corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya),
and firmly joined together by planks representing the union of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
One should sacrifice ignorance of dharma and lack of dispassion through these successive stages.

One should meditate on the lack of sovereignty in the four directions and within the bodies as residing in the *bindu*. Regarding this: the upper part of the neck of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is the portion above the upper rim;
the lower part is the region below it. Within that, one should contemplate the earth and the other elements as being agitated and approaching.
One should worship the lower face, extending down to the limit of the mixed māyā, and above that— the upper region of the upper belt— as the upper face. As stated in the Kāmika:
One should contemplate the downward-flowing [semen] as red and the upward-flowing [blood] as white;
because it is the cause of both bondage and liberation, this [central channel] consists of two powers.
"In the south-western and northern directions, joined above the two girdles"— thus,
"in its center" means in the central region of that pedestal (*pīṭha*), above, in the ten directions, [is] the eightfold Vidyeśvaras, beginning with "resembling rubies," and so forth.

The forms (*rūpa*) are the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), such as Ananta and others; their forms are white because they are produced from pure *māyā*. Some say that the forms of the Lords of Knowledge are the eight petals; in that case, the petal—

Because it would be contradictory if it were described as "resembling silver. The phrase "on top of the pedestal" (*taṃ mūlapīṭhopari*) refers to the upper portion of the *piṇḍikā* (the sacrificial cake) upon the pedestal;

that is, the elevated portion of the pedestal, its raised surface. Regarding the phrase "containing the fifty seed-syllables in its central cavity," the *Pauṣkara* states that it is indeed the fifty phonemes, beginning with the letter *a*.

"The letters end with the syllable *kṣa*, and there are exactly fifty of them. However, in the *Kiraṇa-tantra* it is stated: "The pericarp and the seed-syllables consist of Śiva and Śakti. [This refers to] "the pericarp and seed-syllables formed by the union of Śiva and Śakti," which are adorned by sixty-four filaments. [These are] excluding the letter *ma*.
The five groups beginning with *ka*, and those from *ya* to *ha*, each starting with their initial letter in sequence, [are joined] with the letter *ma* and the bindu (p.
It has been stated that sixty-four filaments are uttered twice from the [root] syllable; "or else" (*yadvā*) indicates an alternative view.
One should worship the lotus and the pericarp in their combined form, as previously described from the *kanda*.

Since everything previously mentioned is contained within the lotus, one should [worship] the presiding deities of the *vidyeśvaras*, beginning with "from there" (*tataḥ*), and so forth. *Vidyeśvara*...

The Śiva-śakti who performs the function of command (niyoga) is indeed differentiated into the eight powers beginning with Vāmā; in the *Mṛgendra*, these very divisions, Vāmā and the others, are declared by the wise according to their distinct functions. Thus, one should worship Manonmanī—the very Śiva-śakti, the power inherent in Śiva—who bears the name Manonmanī. Of these [powers]...
Regarding the meditation (*dhyāna*) beginning with "the radiance of the rising sun" and so forth: the redness of these [lotuses] represents sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

The deities presiding over the red ones are Ananta and the others; however, because Manonmanī lacks such a presiding deity, she is white. Regarding the description beginning with "the circle at the tips of the petals" and so forth, these are the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire.
p.

162) These are not established by worldly convention as the inhabitants of the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar; rather, they are the substrates for the manifestation of the powers of knowledge, action, and will, designated by the terms Ātmatattva, Vidyātattva, and Śivatattva.

It has been stated by the Gurus in the *Mṛgendra-vṛtti-dīpikā* that those [entities] which are transformations of the *bindu* are well-known in the world; however, because it is impossible for them to exist as the divine lion-throne (*divya-siṃhāsana*) of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), their presiding lords are not those well-known in the world, but rather specific powers (*śakti-viśeṣa*) who preside over them.

With the words "in the center of the pericarp" (*karṇikāmadhye*) and so forth, one should worship the crooked-natured Kuṇḍalinī in her essential form, as well as these mandalas of the Sun and others and their presiding deities, at the tips of the petals, the tips of the filaments, the tip of the pericarp, and the center of the pericarp, starting from the east and ending with the northeast. As stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
One should worship the solar mandala pervading the tip of the eastern petal;
one should worship Brahmā as its presiding deity in the southeast corner.
One should worship the moon-maṇḍala, which pervades the filaments, in the south;
one should worship Viṣṇu, the lord of that location, situated in the southwest corner.
One should worship the fire-maṇḍala pervading the pericarp upon the earth;
one should worship Rudra, the lord of that maṇḍala, located in the north-eastern corner.
One should worship the mandala of Śakti, which pervades the three images, in the north;
one should worship Īśa, the presiding lord of that mandala, in the northeast corner.

"Upon that," and so forth—meaning upon the Śakti-maṇḍala, [the elements] beginning with Earth up to the limit of Kuṭilā. Now, one might ask: "In another scripture it is stated that the seat extending from Earth up to the principle of Śuddhavidyā is the Vyāpaka-āsana; how is it that here it is said to extend to the limit of Kuṭilā? To this we reply: here, "Śuddhavidyā" is a synonym for Kuṭilā.
As it has been said:
"The supreme Vāgīśvarī is the Vidyā, and Māyā is remembered as Kuṭilā."
Therefore, the seat (pīṭha) should be conceived as being of such a nature that the entire path (adhvan) is fashioned within it; for according to the *Kiraṇa-śruti*,
the seat fashioned from all paths has the four ages as its great feet.
The tooth-stick should be one span long, with its tip containing a single fiber.
The principle of Māyā, adorned with the form of the bulb (kanda) divided into fifty states, possesses the Brahma-knot; the lotus of Śuddhavidyā is its form.
The circle of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) is beautified by filaments in the form of Śaktis;
it shines with the seed-syllables of the pericarp, which is formed from the union of Śiva and Śakti.
"One should meditate upon the *pīṭha* in this manner," so it is stated in the *Kāmika*.

And according to the *Śruti*: "Having contemplated the seat (*āsana*) which extends from the earth up to Mahāmāyā, one should worship the seat of Śiva. Having thus described the nature of the seat of Śiva, he states the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the form (*mūrti*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "mūrtim" and so forth: because of the traditional scriptural statement that "the mantra of the form (*mūrti-mantra*) is indeed the *Ṛk* encapsulated within [the syllable] 'Tva' and 'Jāta'," the name of the principle of the Lord (*Īśvara-tattva*) is "Form," which consists of the nature of light (*tejas*).

She is the complete form of supreme light, rod-shaped (*daṇḍākārā*), whose form is that of the resonance of the staff (*daṇḍānāda*). She is she whose limbs are undivided, being devoid of distinctions such as hands and feet; she is she who pervades the Supreme Bindu consisting of the *śivatattva*, which is the nature of the power inherent in Śiva.
The other Bindu is the principle of Īśvara. As it is stated in the Ratnatraya:
"It is born, it vibrates as the pure [Bindu], it persists, and likewise it dissolves;
that Bindu, called Paranāda, is the cause of Nāda and the phonemes."

The meaning is that it pervades the end of the *īśvara-tattva*. Having meditated upon such a form and having performed the recitation of the mantra (*mantroccāraṇa*), one should place it within the encasement of the *liṅga*, preceded by an offering of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). One should install it as stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
There, upon that divine lion-throne, she who has the brilliance of steady lightning,
who is a billion leagues in extent, and whose form is that of a single point—
Resembling a thousand suns, difficult to traverse even for the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, subtle, ending at the principle of Īśvara, it is well-established within the body.
Having meditated upon this supreme form of Śiva through the yoga of contemplation,
and having filled his joined palms with flowers, he placed them at the region of his heart.

Having uttered that mantra while sounding the *bindu*, having led it to the end of the *kūrca* and brought it back to the heart with joined palms (*añjali*), one should exhale it and place it within the handful of flowers. Thus, after the placement of the unmanifest form (*avyaktamūrti*) in this manner,
having first placed the self-form (*ātmamūrti*), one should then place the knowledge-form (*vidyāmūrti*).

According to this statement, he describes the conceptualization of the *vidyādeha* (body of knowledge): "In this formless [state]"— that is, in this gross form which pervades from the level of the *Īśvara-tattva* down to the end of the *bindu*, whose nature consists of the *liṅga-nāda*, meaning that its constituent parts are undivided.
Because this very form (*mūrti*) of the Supreme Lord—which consists of inherent power (*samaveta-śakti*)—exists as both cause and effect with respect to the fivefold cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*).

He states that "the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās* must be performed for the fivefold Brahman, beginning with Īśāna, which is divided according to the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of their respective functions and further subdivided"—this is due to the distinction [of the divisions]—in the verse beginning with "on the head, on the face," etc.
Here, the method to be described in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*) is as follows: "Īśāna is of all sciences..."

The placement [of mantras] beginning with "Śaśinī to this [face]" and so forth is the placement with the Śaktis (saśakti-nyāsa). The placement beginning with "Īśāna of all sciences, Īśvara of all beings, Īśvara of all prosperity" and so forth is the placement without the Śaktis (viśaktika-nyāsa). The method not mentioned here—beginning with "Śaśinī above the head" and so forth—is the placement of the Kevala-Śaktis (kevala-śakti-nyāsa) among the three aforementioned positions.
Since only the *śaktinyāsa* is prescribed here, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed upon the form of Śiva in this manner. (p.

He concludes thus: "It would be so"—meaning that in the manner described, if [the visualization] is performed by means of the five mantras beginning with Īśāna and the digits (kalās) beginning with Śaśinī, divided according to the parts starting from the head, then Śiva becomes possessed of power (śākta), having a body related to Śakti, because in the ultimate sense he has no physical body. As it has been said:
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra]: "I shall now explain how that [image] is to be fashioned;
for the sake of men, every undertaking concerns the Lord’s own perfect body."
That body of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) was instantly completed by the five mantras— Vāma, Aghora, Kṣut, Īśāna, and Sadyojāta— along with the [fifth] mantra.
"Completeness does not exist in reality for that [body], just as it does not for the Self; thus it is said.
In that very same [text]: 'In this way, these five mantras by which the body of Śiva is bound are, in reality, not distinct, because the primordial [Self] is not separate from its own power.'"
Thus, one should conceive of the form as consisting of the power of will (*icchāśakti*), according to the *Karaṇasiddhi*. In the *Mohaśūrottara* (p.
"Through ritual service, his auspicious form consists of the five Brahmans. Thus [it is said].

"The deity whose body consists of the five mantras is recited as *sakala* (with parts)," so it is stated in the *Mataṅga*. Furthermore, in its commentary (*vṛtti*), it is said: "The five mantras proceed together with their *kalās*, which take the form of internal subdivisions. For this very reason, it has been stated by the Teachers: "By means of this Śākta [power], he is to be known as *sakala*; Śiva is *niṣkala*. [And: "The mantra beginning with Earth and ending with Kuṭilā..."
The meditation on the body of the Vidyā, beginning with "seated upon the lion-throne," has been described.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with thirty-two marks," it is as follows:
five long, four short, five subtle, and six elevated.
It is said that [the face] has seven red parts, three deep, two fearsome, and two broad.
The two [distances] between the arms and the eyes, the knees and the nose, and the space between the breasts—these are declared to be the five long [parts]; likewise the neck and the shanks.
The middle of the back and the four [fingers] are stated by the wise to be short;
the joints of the fingers, hair, skin, nails, and teeth are subtle.
The two eyes, the belly, the chest, the two shoulders, and the forehead—
these six, indeed, all the attendant people declare to be the elevated parts.
The palms of the hands and soles of the feet, the corners of the eyes,
the nails, the palate, the tongue, and the lower lip— these seven are proclaimed to be red.
A deep voice, the seventh [note], and the navel are proclaimed as the three that should be deep;
a broad chest and a broad forehead are likewise praised as the two that should be broad.

"The thirty-two marks have been proclaimed, O Slayer of Men, exactly as they were seen. Thus, regarding "by power" (*śaktyā*) and so forth: the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord is of the nature of the state of dissolution (*layāvasthā*); it is indeed the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
The weapon called "Power" (*śakti*) is the power whose form is the state of enjoyment (*bhogāvasthā*). "Fearlessness" (*abhayam*) refers to those who have attained their own station.

The trident is the power whose nature consists of the states of will, knowledge, and action, which—due to the existence of the fear of returning [to saṃsāra]—is the state of fearlessness; it is the power that proceeds from the pure reality (śuddhatattva).
The khaṭvāṅga is the power that bestows desired enjoyments upon the self in accordance with its karma; it is the boon.

The power of activity (*pravṛtti-śakti*) belonging to the *māyā-tattva* (p. 171) is the seed-vessel (*bījapūra*). The power of activity belonging to the *prakṛti-tattva* is the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), beginning with *kalā*.

The power that initiates activity toward objects is the *nāga*; the power that initiates activity toward the five cognitive organs, the five action organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and the five gross elements is the *indīvara*. The power that initiates activity of the mind is the *akṣamālā*.
Thus it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatisahasra-kālottara*:
The supreme power, whose nature is consciousness, is known as Sādākhya and is considered fearless;
the trident, consisting of will, knowledge, and action, is situated on its right.
By means of transformation, those very [elements] become even a khaṭvāṅga (skull-topped staff) complete with its parts;
because they reveal the seeds, it is called Bīja-pūraka (the seed-filler).
Māyā is in the form of a hand-drum (ḍamaru), and she herself is the long double-tongue;
that which is called the blue water-lily (indīvara) is the senses, and it is the rosary of beads (akṣamālā).
One should meditate upon [the deity] endowed with the three eyes of the powers of will, knowledge, and action;
the moon, which is the form of omniscience, [radiating] toward the ten directions from its ten hands.

Because it is stated thus in the *Kāmika*: "The *aṇu* [mantra] of Sadāśiva possesses the same nature as the weapons of the guardians of the directions. Others apply this as follows: the weapon of Agni is the *śakti*, that of Īśāna is the trident, and [the weapon] of Varada is the downward-facing [face].
Because of the presence of the banner;

the weapon of Pāyu is the *khaṭvāṅga* because of its club-like form; and that of Abheras is the Vaiṣṇava *abhaya* [mudrā] because of his being the embodiment of stability (*sthiti-mūrti*). As it has been said:

"Holding the conch and discus in the left [hands], and the mace and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in the right. Because he possesses the weapons of Aghora, he is the presiding deity of Yama; because he holds a noose, he is Varuṇa; the rosary is external; the citron is Indra's because of its various colors, and the thunderbolt is likewise.
The blue lotus and the sword represent the darkness [of the southwest]; thus, [it is said]: "The wide-eyed one, possessing vision, action, and will, endowed with the digits of the moon of knowledge.
Starting from the lotus feet up to the crest of matted hair, these are the weapons held in the hands of this body of Vidyā.

It is determined that every particular attribute, such as the wheel-ornament (*cakrābharaṇa*) and so forth (p. 173), possesses the nature of Śakti; likewise, this form of Sadāśiva possesses the nature of *bindu*.
Some desire [the soul] to be so; others, however, maintain that it is one of the subtle *sadāśivas* whose bodies have arisen from the *bindu*.

Both of these views are untenable according to the method I have stated, and they contradict reason. In the former case, because that body is an effect, it would require another agent for its own creation.

If it were created by another, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress. In the latter case, since the Supreme Lord is common [to all], it would be directly contradictory for Him to be within the stainless *liṅga* prescribed in the scriptures. Therefore, it is rightly said that this body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) belongs specifically to Śakti; such a body of knowledge resides in both the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and the mobile *liṅga*.

"Śiva faces the practitioner; however, in the case of a stationary [liṅga] such as a water-pot (kumbha), he faces the door. According to this statement, in the case of a stationary liṅga, he should be meditated upon as facing the door itself.
That which is the face of the liṅga is considered its eastern door;
there, one should meditate upon the Tatpuruṣa face as being upward and facing forward.
"One should visualize the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), the bull, and the trident facing its [the door's] opening.
And:
"The door faces Śiva; Śiva faces the door."
One should designate as the east that direction in which the door is located;
there, the Tatpuruṣa face should be directed upwards and facing forward.

In such statements as these, because a fixed *liṅga* (sthiraliṅga) benefits the world, it is established that it faces the entrance; whereas, regarding a mobile *liṅga* (caraliṅga), since it is worshipped by the worshipper in a common manner, Śiva should be meditated upon as facing south, being the one who bestows grace upon that particular worshipper. Thus, in the *Suprabheda*:
"That which brings [the deity] face-to-face is intended as 'vāhana' (mounting/invocation)," and so it is stated. Furthermore, in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, p.
"One should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva, who has five faces and is present before one.
Thus it is said in that very same work, in another section:
"Invocation (āvāhana) is here defined as the state of being respectfully present face-to-face."
Then, having sat upon his own seat in the presence of Śambhu—thus it is stated. In the *Brahmaśambhu-paddhati*:
"Having meditated here upon Śiva, whose form consists of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), facing him..."
The faces of the quarters were whitened by the outflow of the supreme nectar.

"One should first present the *arghya* with the right hand, facing [the deity]. Thus, in the *Vṛttiviveka-prakaraṇa* of the *Raurava*, within the section on *mudrās*, it is stated that because the Supreme Lord is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*),
the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*saṃnidhāna*), and confinement (*saṃnirodhana*) are impossible.

To dispel this confusion, he explains [the term] as "distinctive presence" (*viśiṣṭa-sthiti*): that is, a distinctive proximity (*sāṃnidhya*) consisting in becoming manifest through the act of bestowing grace (*anugrāhakatva*).

In the Siddhāntaśekhara it is said: "That which is the manifestation of Śiva before the worshipper who meditates correctly with faith and a focused mind— that is declared to be the invocation (āvāhana)."
Therefore, for mobile lingas, it is precisely the orientation toward the practitioner that constitutes their grace toward the practitioner.

If you argue that such statements as "the pervasive Lord should be established facing the worshiper and the worshiper" and "Śambhu [should be installed] not facing the east," etc., would thus be understood, then regarding those statements—

In the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*, those who composed the commentary on the ritual and hymns have established—by means of many logical arguments—that worship and praise are directed toward a fixed (*sthira*) liṅga facing east, while setting aside the case of a mobile (*cala*) liṅga which faces the practitioner;

this [conclusion] alone should be accepted. Furthermore, in this very manual (*paddhati*), it is stated that a practitioner of a mantra for specific desires (*kāmyamantra*) should first inform the deity.

Having received permission, [he should place] the fire-mantras in female form at the tip of the southern petal of the auspicious lotus seat in the eastern part, and [the remaining mantras] in the western part. (p. 177)

Because of the injunction: "One should worship before the Lord the mantras such as Mṛtyuñjaya, which have male forms, and those such as Maheśvara, which have both male and female forms," by this also it is established that Śiva faces south. Likewise, in the Mṛgendra:
Then, having worshipped Maheśāna, one should worship the mantra for the sake of Śrī;
it must always be kept secret by practitioners in every way, as will be described hereafter.
"On the petals of the Yama-lotus, in the eastern and western portions, there are three forms;
the light of the Aghora-eye is in the center, and not anywhere else.

This is because the practice of mantra-sādhana for the sake of attaining the goal of the Vedic revelation is prescribed in the presence of Aghora, even for those who desire supernatural powers (siddhi).

The practice of mantra-sādhana is prescribed for the south; therefore, facing the south is established as necessary for those seeking liberation as well as those desiring supernatural powers (*siddhi*). This is the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*).
He states that this should first be performed with a handful of flowers while reciting the mantra:
"Pervading the interior of the *brahmaraṃdhra*," and so forth, refers to the *prāsāda* mantra, the mantra of Śiva.
Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) has been stated elsewhere by the author himself in the passage beginning, "the root mantra endowed with the *kalā*s such as *medhā*," and so on.

He will state: "The Śiva-tattva pervades up to the end of the Śiva-tattva; the Niṣkala-tattva pervades as far as that limit. [Objection: But has not the pervasion of the Śiva-seat been described by the passage beginning with "the seat starting from the Earth and ending with Kuṭilā, thus pervading, adorned with the seed-syllables of the pericarp initiated by the two Śivas," and so forth, as applying to the body of Vidyā as well?

If it is asked how [the Lord] is pervasive even within the Śiva-tattva, it is replied: in this scripture, the very form (mūrti) of the Supreme Lord is His power consisting of knowledge and action; and it has already been stated that, due to the distinction of its functions, that power consists of the five Brahmās. Therefore, regarding the distinctions based on the totality of the Lord’s [powers]...

Because it is based on the differentiation of functions, and because that [differentiation] is based on the differentiation of the objects to be presided over (*adhiṣṭheya*), and because the object to be presided over consists of the principles (*tattva*) above the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*).
That which is situated below the partless Śiva and is denoted by the term Sadāśiva is the basis for the state of "possessing all" (sākalya),
as it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The principle known as Sādāśiva is remembered as that which transcends Īśāna and extends to the end of Śānta."
Nor is there any Lord of the worlds, beginning with Nāda and the other kalās, other than Śiva.

"Having commenced—thus the principle of Sadāśiva has been explained to you in brief. Even Śakti is thus; this [state] is 'sakala' (with parts) due to its connection with the fivefold duties (kṛtya). The 'niṣkala' (without parts), however, always bestows the object of duty elsewhere. Therefore, because it denotes the collection of the three principles based on their totality (sākalya)...

It has been rightly stated that by the designation "Sadāśiva," the embodied form—another synonym for which is *vidyādeha*—is intended as the *sakala* (with parts) body. Likewise, it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*: The Sages asked: "In the initiation (*dīkṣā*), the Lord has declared that the reality (*tattva*) called Śiva is that which is to be purified (*śodhya*), pervaded by the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*). This [claim] contradicts what is here [stated]."
(180) O Īśvara, this which has been urged is indeed true; I shall speak it, so listen with concentrated minds.
This *bindu*, by virtue of its nature as *prakṛti*, is agitated by the Universal Self (*akhilātman*).
The agitated portion of this [energy] is Śāntyatīta-kalā;
its extent consists of the worlds beginning with Śānti, and it is of the nature of the Bindu.
The Śiva-tattva is said to be there, as well as the Sādākhya world;
that Sādākhya-tattva is indeed called Bendava in the Śivāgama.
"But these very [principles], as well as those previously mentioned, are to be purified in certain cases.
Thus it is said in that same [text]:
"This [individual] is not distinct from the Bindu, nor even from the worlds, for he is a devotee."
Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, Sthiti, and Nivṛtti—these are the great worlds; within these, Śiva assumes five designations.
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jāta follow in sequence;
these are the five faces of Sadāśiva’s state for the sake of enjoyment.
"The auspicious Nityā, consisting of five forms, both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), is to be known as the form of Sadāśiva, the initiator of all activities.

Therefore, the very power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord is the seat (*āsana*), consisting of knowledge (*vidyā*) itself—precisely for this reason. "Having understood the true nature of the seat and the one who sits upon it, one should begin the sacrifice," so it is stated in the *Kāmika*. Having thus described the nature of the body of knowledge, he explains the sequence for the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Śiva with the words beginning with "the root-mantra" (*mūlamantra*).
The root mantra is the *prāsāda* mantra. "Endowed with the *kalās* beginning with *medhā*" means: *medhā* is the vowel *au*;

those beginning with it are the *kalās*, which are thus called the *kalās* beginning with *medhā*. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the eleven [vowels] are indicated: *ū*, *m*, *bindu*, *ardhacandra*, *nāda*, *nādānta*, *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, *samana*, and *unmanā*.

The *kalās* are being described. Endowed with these, [the practitioner performs] the sequential abandonment of the causal deities beginning with Brahmā; by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva are indicated. The abandonment consists of the respective presiding lords of the causes stationed in their respective locations, together with the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m* which are the designators of those [deities], as well as the *bindu*, the crescent moon (*ardhacandra*), the *nāda*, and the *kalās*.

Uttering [the mantra] in sequence up to the end of dissolution (layānta), culminating in the partless Śiva (niṣkala-śiva), one becomes the creator of all; for he creates the entire world without exception, he is thus the "creator of all. He is partless (niṣkala), devoid of limbs, and all-pervasive (vibhu), encompassing everything.

The meaning is that its essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of knowledge and bliss; by means of knowledge, there is bliss—that is, unsurpassed happiness which is inexpressible and to be known through one's own experience, consisting of pure consciousness (*nanmaya*). Thus it has been said:
"Having thoroughly investigated with knowledge that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted."
Having understood that the Śaiva reality is to be accepted, one should abide within it, which is without support.
When all tantras have become partless, they know that bliss which is self-restrained,
free from conceptual construction, inconceivable, and devoid of cause or illustration.

"That bliss is declared supreme, which is to be experienced by oneself and is unsurpassed. Thus, it illuminates both itself and the other; "self and other" refers to *sva* and *para*, and that which illuminates these two is "self-and-other-illuminating" (*svaparaprakāśa*). Having contemplated that, one becomes absorbed in it—that is, in that Supreme Śiva.

The Śiva-mantra, which constitutes one's own essential nature, [is to be recited] from the limit of the ten directions (ādaśānta) up to the station of Paramaśiva by way of emanation, that is, in the forward order (anuloma).

Having emerged through the path of the flow of breath by means of *recaka* (exhalation), [the yogi perceives] that which is the realized *unmanī*, shining like the orb of the sun, resembling the solar disc, and issuing obliquely from the forehead between the eyebrows; likewise, the mass of nectar, having whitened— that is, made bright— the circle of the directions, the entire expanse of the quarters.

Having visualized [the deity] held within the hollow of one's joined palms, one should invoke [him] into the target image whose form consists of the mantra, using the *hṛdaya-mantra* together with the *prāsāda-mantra*, accompanied by the *āvāhinī-mudrā*. As it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
Having meditated upon the supreme Śiva— the omniscient, the creator of all, the pervasive Lord consisting of the bliss of awakening, partless, and self-luminous.
Having led the mantra to the abode of Śiva by abandoning its causal origin in Brahmā and the other deities,
one should then [visualize it] situated in the middle of the forehead, possessing the radiance of the shimmering moon.
Having meditated upon the supreme Śiva, who consists of the form of the *bindu*, is endowed with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*),
and is contained within the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should cause him to enter the target-form (*lakṣyamūrti*).
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Kāmika:

"Having placed his joined palms at the heart and holding a flower while reciting the Prāsāda mantra with devotion, the practitioner—whose range is the partless (niṣkala) and who has attained a state of aesthetic oneness (samarasa)—should meditate upon the upward progression during the ritual of power (śaktikaraṇa)."
"Thus, having emerged from the *nāda* and the *bindu* through the sequence of one's own powers and instruments, there shall be the invocation (*āvāhana*). Thus it is said.

Now, is it not the case that when the invocation (*āvāhana*) of another object is performed which was previously unmanifested (*aprāptasaṃnidhāna*), there would be a loss of Śiva’s omnipresence (*vyāpakatva*) if he were treated as a distinct manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*)? Furthermore, does this not contradict the established presence (*saṃnidhi*) of the self-manifested (*svayaṃbhū*) and Bāṇa-liṅgas? There is no contradiction; for those who have received the grace of their guru, the invocation here is of two kinds.

At the time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the invocation (*āvāhana*) performed upon the *liṅga* consists of the deposition of the living soul (*jīvanyāsa*); that [invocation] is of the nature of the manifestation of the [deity's] presence within the cavity [of the *liṅga*].
Thus, it is stated in the *Kāmika*: The sages said:
"O Lord, how can there be an invocation here of Śiva, who is omnipresent?"
p.
185) "If invocation were desired, its omnipresence would be contradicted.
The Lord said:
Just as fire situated from root to tip consumes both the wood and the fire itself, so too the manifestation of consciousness, though pervasive, is not obstructed in any single location.
Just as one's own coming and going here occurs through the medium of the body,
so too the desired coming and going of Śiva occurs through the medium of the consecrated body.
"He is endowed with inconceivable power, all-pervading, possessed of a body or devoid of a body; Śiva is the creator of all and omnipresent.
Because of the statement, "The rites here [begin] from the invocation up to the dismissal," [this should be performed] every day at the time of worship.
"Just as there is the mounting [of a vehicle], so too is there the act of making it face [the deity];
that which is the act of making it face is called *āvāhana* (invocation). Thus, in the *Suprabheda*, there is the facing toward that [deity] by means of the garment of Īśāna.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:

In that regard, the nature of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites performed by one stationed in the northeast, facing their respective directions with the head [of the deity] situated above, has been described in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*: (p. 186)
Facing [the deity] with reverence is here called invocation (āvāhana);
seating [the deity] there with devotion is described by the wise as installation (sthāpana).
O Jagannātha, the very perception that "I am yours" is like a seal;
even though the Lord is all-pervading, His presence [in the devotee] is not obstructed by that.
The non-exhaustion of [Śiva's] presence (saṃnidhi) up until the completion of ritual action (karmakāṇḍa),
even though Śambhu is all-pervading, is proclaimed as "obstruction" (nirodha).
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"Invoking (āvāhana), establishing (sthāpana), bringing near (sānnidhya), and confining (saṃnirodhana)—
these names are declared to be established according to their respective functions."
A certain [deity] is invoked by men, yet is not installed by anyone;
and by that [invocation], O Lord of Gods, proximity is neither obstructed nor brought about.
One should contemplate the supreme Śiva as all-pervading in the form of the mantra;
then it is called "mounting," and "forgive me" is the dismissal.
(As stated on p.

187) the definition of the *āvāhana-mudrā* (invocation gesture) has been explained in the *Sūryapūjā*; that should be understood here as well, because of the injunction: "One should invoke [the deity] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) or with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā]. The [gestures for] *sthāpana* (establishment), *saṃnidhāna* (proximity), and *saṃnirodha* (confinement) are also [to be performed].
One should perform [the rite] with the root mantra alone.
Likewise, in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*: "Having invoked Śaṅkara with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā] or with the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), and having established him with the *sthāpinī* [mudrā],"
Thus: when the body has been consecrated with the Lakṣmī-mantra, the installation [of the nose] is performed with the Hṛdaya-mantra.

Thus it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*. Then, having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the mantras, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*saṃnidhāna*), and confinement (*saṃnirodhana*) with their respective mudrās and the root mantra, while reciting up to the point of dissolution (*layāntam*) by abandoning the five causal deities, Brahmā and the others, who reside in the locations beginning with the heart.
Likewise, in the Vimalavatī and the Kālottara [Tantras],
the practitioner should invoke the deity with the Heart mantra; however,
he should perform the installation and the worship with the Heart mantra alone.
p.
188) "In the heart, none of that which is enjoined by ritual injunction exists. Thus, in that commentary, one should invoke Paramaśiva within the heart with devotion (*prāsāda*). And of these...

Because it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇatvāt*), the word "and" (*ca*) implies the collection [of rites] beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the offering of the recitation (*japa-nivedana*); one should perform all this ritual action within the heart alone.
This means that everything taught here in the *tantra*, which is rooted in the authoritative scripture (*vidhi-mūla-śāstra*), is included even if not explicitly mentioned.
For there is a statement in the *Samānatantropaniṣad*: "Whatever has been stated or unstated, all of that should indeed be performed with the heart. In this context:
