Aghoraśivācārya has explained that because the word "with the heart" (*hṛdayena*) is repeated again and again, even all rites accomplished by other mantras are accomplished by that very [heart-mantra] in their respective forms. Now, [it is said]:
"One should invoke with the *āhvāna* mantra, establish Śiva with the *vāma*, and [attain] his presence (*sāṃnidhya*) with the *aghora*."
"One should cause [the deity] to be restrained by means of the *puruṣa* mantra"—one should not suspect that this was stated in another scripture (*āgama*).

In this *paddhati*, after the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*saṃnidhāna*), and restraint (*saṃnirodhana*), one offers the guest-water (*svāgatārghya*); then, following the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) such as those of the heart (*hṛdaya*) and so forth, there is oneness [with the deity] by means of the root mantra (*mūla*).

Having performed the protection and veiling with the root mantra, having rendered [the deity] supreme by means of the *amṛtamudrā* and the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having bound the five-faced mudrā— thus, immediately after this concentration:

The procedure for the placement of mantras on the heart and other limbs (*nyāsa*), protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the display of mudrās has been described in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"Having invoked Śaṅkara into the heart with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā], one should establish him there with the *sthāpinī* [mudrā]."
Having brought him into close proximity, one should suppress him with harshness.
Having expelled the obstacles with the *hetimantra* "kālakaṇṭhyai phaṭ," which destroys misfortune,
and having performed the salutation with the *liṅgamudrā* using the *hṛdayamantra*, one should perform the *avakuṇṭhana*.
Thus [it is said]. Immediately thereafter, having performed the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of complete identification) with the six mantras, it is said: "Then, with one [mantra]...

After the saṃnirodha (the rite of confinement), the procedure for displaying the mudrās, the avakuṇṭhana (the rite of binding), and the nyāsas of the heart and other limbs has been stated. Furthermore, the various types of mudrās have also been explained.
Thus, just as there is a distinction in ritual action, so too is there a distinction in mantra; likewise in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Having placed [the water] in the *āvāhinī* [vessel], one should restrain it with the *aghora* [mantra]."
Then, having bound him cruelly, the limbs of the Lord should indeed be offered.

One should place the *netra* mantra at the region of the heart, or likewise install the *gāyatrī*; this is declared to be the *sāvitrī*. One should invoke [the deity] with the *jāta* mantra and establish Śiva on the left side.
One should effect the presence (*sānnidhya*) with the *aghora* mantra, and offer the *arghya* with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra.

Thus it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*. Here, the complete cessation [of the breath] has not been mentioned; having meditated upon the supreme Sadāśiva, one should perform the invocation with the *sadyojāta* mantra.
"Establishment is by the Vāma mantra, restraint by Aghora;
presence (saṃnidhāna) is by Nara, while worship is by Īśāna. Thus it is said in the *Makuṭa*. One should invoke with the Savidya mantra, and then establish with the Vāma mantra.
One should effect restraint through Aghora, but presence through Puruṣa.
"One should perform the consecration with the Īśāna mantra" (p.
thus, in the *Saṃtāna*, following the restraint of these two.
Regarding the presence [of the deity], what need is there for much? For it is said: "Even though the scriptures are many, one must act according to the succession of one's own guru.
Thus, one should practice exactly as taught by one's own guru. Now, he states the prayer to Śiva beginning with the word "O Lord": *svāgatārghyaṃ*, *saṃmukhārghyaṃ*, *nirodhārghyaṃ*.

*Parāṅmukhārghya* (the "turning-away" offering) is a synonym for these names. In this context, the *arghya* is of two kinds: the *viśeṣārghya* (special offering) and the *nirodhārghya* (obstructive offering). This distinction arises from the attainment of the *Śivatattva* and the *Vidyātattva*. Among these, during the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*), the *nirodhārghya*, which pervades up to the end of the *Vidyātattva*, should be offered. During the worship (*pūjā*), however—
However, the *śivārghya* (the offering of water for Śiva) has pervasion as far as the *śivatattva*. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"In the invocation (*āvāhana*) and in the dismissal (*visarga*), the obstructing *arghya* is employed;
the [arghya] named 'Śiva' is used in worship (*pūjā*), as well as in the foot-water (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*)."
192) Regarding this, some say that the *nirodhārghya*—the water of cessation—should be offered with five excellent tips [of the fingers].
However, it should be given facing upwards, facing forward, and facing away.
One should arrange [the offerings] in the presence of the arrived deity.
Regarding the dismissal (*visarjana*), the *Sarvajñānottara* states: "O son of Gaṅgā, the *arghya* should be offered with the face turned away.

According to this, the two *arghya* offerings for the face-to-face (*saṃmukha*) rite should be given only when the mouth is directed upward. Having established the non-difference between the limbs and the possessor of limbs by means of the root mantra at the locations starting from the heart and ending with the hands, and so forth, [one should perform the ritual]. One should effect the oneness of the limbs and the whole.
One should offer the Amṛtamudrā and Dhenumudrā with the root mantra ending in "namaḥ. Having gratified [the deity] with the Mahāmudrā and performed the visualization of the beautiful limbs,
it is stated in the Kāmika:
Just as Nala, Taraṇi, and others are capable by means of their respective splendors,
so too is Śiva capable of removing all distress through his limbs as described according to their inherent nature.
The realization of the non-difference between the parts and the whole, despite their being distinct,
is declared to be the "rendering immortal" (amṛtīkaraṇa) by means of the Lord’s Amṛtamudrā.
There should be an incitement for him, consisting of the conceptualization of beautiful limbs;
one should perform that by means of the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) known as "Liberation" and "Melting."
Thus, O Suprabhā, is the characteristic of the five-faced mudrā:
having placed the fingers of both hands joined back-to-back,
one should position the two little fingers and the two thumbs crosswise.
Having placed the two middle fingers upon the pair of ring fingers,
this mudrā known as Pañcamukhī is dear to Śaṅkara.
Thus [it is said]. The characteristics of the others have already been stated previously.
Regarding the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth to Śiva, he says "sahṛdā" and so on;
the procedures for the offering of *pādya* and the rest are specifically expounded in the *Śivatantrāṃhasyasāra*.
For the practitioner, the word known as *śatatva* has been extracted as the basis for the feet;
the water for the feet (*pādya*) is the syllable *yaṃ*, ending in a nasal drop (*bindu*), which is most auspicious, to be offered at the pair of lotus-feet.
Having uttered "namas" at the end of the name of the flowers, one should offer them to Śiva.
Having uttered the *śaṃbara* mantra ending at the *brahmarandhra*, followed by *svadhā*, [one offers] the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) as the cause for attaining the state of Sadāśiva.
The supreme preceptor, having lifted the vessel, should offer it to the deity amidst the five faces [of Śiva], which are the terrible and beautiful aspects within the Śākha scriptures.
Having uttered the root mantra ending in *svāhā* over the heads of Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, Jāta, and Mūrdhan, [one should proceed] as far as the station of the *dvādaśānta*.
He offered that flower as an arghya-offering, the cause for attaining the state of the Śiva-tattva.
Having extracted a single portion, the wise one should offer it to the deity,
reciting the Śiva-mantra ending with "Śivāya" and concluding with "Vauṣaṭ."
In these five limbs mentioned, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta,
the flower consisting of self-knowledge is the cause of union with Śiva.
"One should offer that which is endowed with a sweet fragrance for the sake of auspiciousness.
195) Having thus offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*) as before, one should perform the recitation of the mantra according to the previously stated method.
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) at the five faces, and one should present the water of honor (*arghya*) at the five heads.

Having thus consecrated [the deity] with the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) known as invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*saṃnidhāna*), total integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), water of honor (*arghya*), and the offering of flowers ending with *vauṣaṭ*; immediately thereafter—

Since the great ablution (*mahāsnāpana*) includes anointing (*abhyaṅga*) and other rites, it is improper for a mobile liṅga (*calaliṅga*) to move after the complete seated worship (*samagrāsana-pūjā*). Therefore, he states that even though the ablution was performed previously, it must be performed again through mental visualization (*manobhāvanā*), beginning with "anointing, rubbing," and so forth.

He describes the offering of perfumes and so forth with the words beginning "candana" (sandalwood). One should offer everything, including the girdle (*mekhalā*), the waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*), and sandalwood, at the root of the *sahṛdaya* [mantra]. The definition of the *manoratha-mudrā* is stated in the *Suprabheda* (p.

Having joined the palms together, the two little fingers are said to be bent inward; in the *vilīta* [mudrā], the left one of those two is known to be on the outside, and the middle fingers are also bent.
Having bent the tips of the index fingers and placed them upon the palms of one's own hands,
one should extend the two index fingers and join their tips together.
"The two thumbs are placed on the root-joints of those very [fingers] and are bent;
this is known as the *manorathā* [mudrā], which bestows union with Śiva.
Thus, when offering the mudrās, one should display it at the region of the heart of the deity.
As it has been said:
"One should not form the hand-gesture (karamudrā) below the two breasts;
even in the presence of the Liṅga, the Lord does not accept it if it is turned downwards."

The *mudrā* that bestows joy upon Śambhu should be placed near the region of the heart. Thus, in the offering of the *arghya*, one should not rotate the secondary vessel over the primary *liṅga*. Regarding "the hand"—it refers to the limbs of Brahmā being dissolved into their respective places of absorption (*layasthāna*).
The places of residence are the head, the face, and so forth—those respective locations.

Among them, "having approached" (adhyaṣya) means for the purpose of worshiping the enclosure; "having approached" (adhyaṣya) means having requested. This is because only one enclosure has been mentioned here.

In the daily rite (*nityavidhi*), only the worship of a single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*) should be performed; however, the worship of three or five enclosures (*tryāvaraṇa* / *pañcāvaraṇa*) should be performed on occasional occasions (*naimittika*) and the like. Thus, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"One should worship the Five Brahmans and the Six Limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the first enclosure."
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are in the second [circle], while the eight beginning with Nandin are in the third.
In the fourth [stage] there should be the Lokapālas, and in the fifth the Lokapāstras;
this path of five coverings (pañcāvaraṇamārga) is to be performed in rites for specific occasions and the like.
There is one covering for the obligatory rite, or else three coverings; for the occasional rite there are five, and for the optional rite nine is considered the number.

There too, as before, there would be the sixty-five [deities] in the fifth [house]; the Seven Mothers are said to be in the sixth, the Vasus are declared in the seventh, and the eleven Rudras are remembered [in the eighth].
"The Ādityas are declared [to be worshipped] in the eighth enclosure; they are considered [to be worshipped] in the ninth," thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara* (p.
"This is indeed the single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa) that accomplishes all desired aims.

Thus begins the method for the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*), starting from the five heads of Him [Śiva]. "Having taken" means having taken the mantras beginning with Īśāna from the locations of Śiva’s head and so forth, like one lamp from another lamp—as stated in the *Paddhati*.
In this manner, one should worship [the deities] upon the petals situated in their respective directions. Likewise, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"From the head, the faces, the heart, and the secret parts of the body of Śiva, [the powers] are to be grasped from these, just as lamps are taken from a lamp."
"By means of the yoga of meditation on one's own mantra, [one should perform] the *añjali* mudrā.
Thus, regarding "consisting of true being" (*sadbhāvātmakam*) and so forth: that which is both real (*sat*) and being (*bhāva*) is "true being" (*sadbhāva*).
The heart of Śiva is designated as consisting of true being—that is, having the nature of true being. True being...

"His heart" refers to the *pauṣkara* [lotus]. Regarding "the characteristic of all sovereignty": here, the manifold nature of the Lord (*īśvara*) is figurative (*aupacārika*), because it arises from the engagement with supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* and so forth.
But it is not by way of having that [limited] nature, because that is impossible for Śiva, who is devoid of such a body and sense organs, since they are attributes of the body and senses.
As it is said in the Mataṅga:
"Or rather, since the triad consisting of sovereignty, the power of atomization (aṇimā), and so forth, is established..."
The five qualities, beginning with attainment (prāpti), belong to the embodied soul and consist of instruments.
Thus it is said. For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra* that sovereignty consists of vision and action:
"He who possesses sovereignty consisting of vision and action, preceded by the granting of that [sovereignty], is the Lord.
And in the *Pauṣkaratantra*: "He is to be understood as the Lord through the *sūtra*."
"Sovereignty is His lordship over both the conscious and the unconscious manifestations.
Thus, "the crest-jewel of mastery not dependent on another" means that mastery is independence (*svātantrya*). "Not dependent on another" (*ananyādhīna*) means it does not depend on anything else;
it is *anyādhīna* (dependent on another), and what is not *anyādhīna* is *ananyādhīna*. And that is independent.
And "mastery" (vaśitvam) means that very form which possesses such a nature;
[the phrase] "a crest of such a form" is the intended meaning. Like one whose self is liberated, there is the removal of impurities through the activity of another Lord.

The meaning is that there is no independence manifested through a door. Regarding sovereignty (*vaśitva*), the *Pauṣkara* states: "Sovereignty is non-dependence; it is the crest-lock situated above Him. The *Śivatantrarahasyasāra* states: "The crest-lock of Śambhu’s sovereignty is supreme, consisting of non-dependence on another. As for the armor (*kavaca*) which is of the nature of light (*tejas*), that light is indeed those two: self-perception (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*).

That whose form is the power of knowledge and action—that very radiance is the armor. Furthermore, it is imperishable, consisting of the rays of one's own powers of vision and action; thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara. "The sphere of consciousness is the sphere of vision and action, having the form of the orb of the sun"; thus it is said in the Parākhya. It is the indivisible splendor of the Supreme Lord.

The armor is described as follows: in the *Mṛgendra*, it is said that "the splendor of Śarva was fashioned as armor, impenetrable"; and in the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra*, it is stated that "it is of the nature of majesty (pratāpa)," meaning that majesty is its blazing weapon.
p.

201) "That which is the overwhelming majesty (*pratāpa*) of Śambhu is called the weapon (*heti*). Thus [it is said]. In the *Pauṣkara*: "The majesty of the Lord shall be the renowned weapon that destroys the clouds of sin. In the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra*:

Having thus taken up the mantras of Īśāna and the others, as well as the mantras of the Heart and so forth, one should worship them after meditating upon them in their true form as described in the ritual manual (*paddhati*). According to the injunction, "One should worship the Weapon (*astra*) in the four directions," one should worship [Īśāna] by taking up the Śakti, Abhaya, Trident, and Varada mudrās while stationed on the right side of Śiva. For Tatpuruṣa and the others, [one should worship] from the left side.

In this context, since it has been stated that Śiva is established within the Tatpuruṣa and the other faces, one should understand that the southern direction is the left side of Tatpuruṣa; likewise, the western direction is the left side of Aghora, the northern direction is the left side of Sadyojāta, and the eastern direction is the left side of Vāmadeva. For these [faces], the rites of invocation and so forth are to be performed with their respective mantras.
The ritual procedures (saṃskāra) are to be performed. As it is stated in the Kāmika [Tantra] (p.
"One should worship these [rites], beginning with invocation (āvāhana), in their proper sequence with their respective mantras."
One should not conceal these, nor should one perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) upon them.
These eight ritual acts have each been prescribed individually by the wise;
bathing and the lighting of lamps are not separate [acts], because they constitute constituent parts.
"However, their meal is proclaimed to be by the side of the Lord.
Thus it is said. Regarding the inability to perform each of the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) individually, he states that they should be performed together as a collective;
or else, the characteristics of the *dhenu* and *padma* mudrās have already been explained previously in the section on the worship of the Sun (*sūryapūjā*).

The characteristics of the trident and other weapons are described in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*: "When the two index fingers are joined at the tips, the two middle fingers are joined behind them, and the remaining three fingers are joined together, while the rest [of the fingers] are extended, this is the trident (*śūla*)."
With the two index fingers facing forward and the two ring fingers slightly curved, the two thumbs crossed behind them— this is the *sugevamakara* mudrā.
The two little fingers are bent against each other with their palms joined; the two middle and ring fingers are extended with their tips joined together.
The two index fingers are bent at their tips and joined behind the middle fingers.
"The thumb and middle finger joined at their tips is called the *sruc* mudrā.

The characteristics of the *namaskāra* (salutation) mudrā have been stated previously. Now, with the words beginning with "paścāt" (afterwards), he describes what is to be performed after the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*).
"However, the rājasic worship would be [incomplete] without the act of *paramīkaraṇa* (the process of deification).
According to this statement from the *Mohaśūrottara*, *paramīkaraṇa* must be performed. The method for *paramīkaraṇa* is as follows:
with a handful of flowers in hand, one should recite the root mantra as before, extending it up to the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space above the head).

For the sake of enjoyment and for the purpose of fulfilling the power of the ritual extraction (*āhṛti*), one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva. With the thought that "all [deities] are identical with Śiva," there is a single internal inclusion of all the deities worshipped in the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*); this is the oneness (*ekatva*), the non-separateness of the part and the whole. As it has been said:

"One should not cause the various classes of all the Āvaraṇa deities to be separate. Regarding "various kinds of food offerings" (naivedya): these are pure rice (*śuddhānna*), milk-rice (*pāyasānna*), rice mixed with molasses (*gulānna*), and rice mixed with sesame and peas (*krasarānna*).

Whether by way of the various types of food such as *mudga*-rice and the like, or by way of the distinctions between what is chewed (*bhakṣya*), eaten (*bhojya*), licked (*lehya*), sucked (*coṣya*), and drunk (*peya*), as well as ghee, soup, vegetables, curd, milk, fruits, and so forth— being of many kinds and purified by the four consecrations (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*)—

everything including the food offering (*naivedya*) and the rest should be made pure through these four consecrations; this is indicated by the phrase "having offered with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*."
When the expectation arises as to "where," the practitioner should offer the food offering (*naivedya*) and other items into the right hand of Śiva.

He should contemplate that [Śiva] consumes it with his upward-facing mouth. In that case, the success of the hand-washing (*hastodvartana*) is achieved. Otherwise, if the practitioner were to offer the food offering into the upward-facing [mouth], then [there would be no success] regarding the hand-washing of Śiva.

There is no room [for it]. Because there is the contact with the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) on the hand of the practitioner, it is therefore considered correct that the food offering (*naivedya*) be placed in the hand.

(Likewise, in the *Kālottara-tantra* it is stated: "Now, since the offering of *naivedya* is prescribed in another scripture as being for the mouth of Tatpuruṣa, how is it that it should be given to the upper mouth?
To this it is replied: Because the upper mouth alone possesses *ābhimukhya*—that is, being oriented toward the practitioner or being oriented toward the door.

Because of the injunction: "The food offering (naivedya) and so forth should be given only to the upward-facing [mouth]. This is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "Whatever is prescribed by rule—whether it be food to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, or sucked in many varieties—it should be offered to the upward-facing [mouth]. Likewise, in the *Dviśatikālottara* as well:
O Six-faced One, the five kinds of food— namely, that which is to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked—
should be offered with the heart-mantra into the upward-facing mouth.
In the *Kāmika*: "The food offering (*naivedya*) is [placed] upon the five faces, or else upon the upper face.
In another scripture, it is stated that among the five faces, the face of Īśāna bestows fruits that surpass all others.
As it is said:
"The clarity of the Lord and the stillness of the person [are the source of this]."
The ferocity of the multiform one is the cause of liberation, maintenance, and destruction.
The nature of the Alluring One is seduction, and that of the Unborn is meditation;
for the purpose of concealment and manifestation, it is the collection of all objects.

And thus: For the sake of liberation, one should contemplate with a serene mind the form of a crystal; [one should contemplate him] as slightly smiling and cool, yet proud during acts such as paralyzing and so forth.
The matted hair is black and formidable, while the skull-ornament is yellow;
during the phases such as waning and disappearance, the forehead ornament is blood-red.
"One should remember the meditation on all states while intent upon the mind.

Thus, having offered [the oblations] to the limbs of Brahmā with their respective mantras, one should offer them individually here when vessels are available. For it has been stated: "Now, in which vessel? and because of the injunction given later. And it is said:
p.
207) "The offerings for the limbs of enjoyment should be given separately; in the absence [of these], they may be done as one.
Thus he states what is to be performed immediately after the offering (*nivedana*), beginning with "rubbing the hands" (*hastodvartana*): rubbing the hands...
The washing of the hands. Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "One should meditate upon Śiva, together with his limbs and his retinues, as having partaken [of the offering];
one should then offer the washing of the hands and the water for rinsing the mouth to Śiva."

"And then one should give betel," it is said. Regarding "mouth-perfume" (*mukhavāsa*): it is called *mukhavāsa* because it perfumes the mouth, that is, it makes it fragrant. A pill made from cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, jasmine fruit, *takola*, and musk, ground with cold water, is known by the name "mouth-perfume. [One should offer] a flower together with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains.

Having taken [the offerings] in the hollowed palms, thus is the offering of the *pavitra* described. Regarding the failure to perform this, it is stated in the *Mūlaśūrottara* that "worship without the *pavitra* is proclaimed to be *tāmasī*."

208) That offering of the *pavitra* is twofold: regular (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*). The first consists of leaves, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken rice grains; this *pavitra*, composed of all principles (*sarvatattvamaya*), is one thing, while the other is the *mithuna* [pair] according to the manner already stated and to be described hereafter.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight and on subsequent days, it takes the form of an offering. Since it protects from falling that which has been produced by the daily activities of speech, mind, and body, therefore the *pavitraka* should be given.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika.
And another method, which removes all defects, is declared as a supplement to the ritual—
that which was obtained by the gods through austerity from Hara for the nourishment of their own rites.
"Having obtained the purifier of Śambhu, one should fulfill the annual rite," so it is said in the *Mṛgendra*.
Regarding the *ārātrika*: it consists of lamps—nine, eight, or five—from a single vessel.
This is known by the name *saṃyuktārātrika*.
Then, having rotated it upwards three times, one first performs a rotation downwards three times.
Having performed this, one should then wave the *ārātrika*— provided with nine, five, or eight burning lamps— either upwards or three times;
it may be made of gold or silver, and honored with scents, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Then, gradually and step by step, he slowly brought her into his presence.
"One should cause the three *nāras* to revolve"—this is explained in the *Durbodhapadabodhinī*.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*, in the one hundred and thirty-third [chapter]:
"From the revolving of the *bindu* presided over by Śiva, [the distinction between] the pure and impure paths [arises]."
That by which the pervasive [deity] is meditated upon is intended as the lustration (nīrājana).

Thus, for the *bindu* presided over by Śiva, which consists of the *nivṛtti-kalā*, there is a fivefold [offering] beginning with the lamp. Due to its downward movement, it pertains to the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*); due to its upward movement, it pertains to the pure paths (*śuddhādhvan*). That which is meditated upon as pervading these pure paths is designated as *nīrājana*.
p.
210) One should cast [the ashes] onto that crest of ashes after circling it three times; this is said to be the warding off of obstacles.
Having taken the ashes with the hand and having circled them above the crest—
Immediately thereafter, one should cast [the offering] three times into the midst of the lamps.
O son, that which is perceived through the ashes perfected by the ritual manual (kalpa) serves as an offering for those who have fallen away and as a warding off of the rākṣasas.

Thus, because of the repeated mention of "having given the water for sipping and the offering (arghya)," the water for sipping and the offering that follow after the invocation (āvāhana) must be given only once at the mouth of Īśāna, distinct from the water for sipping and the offering that were obtained [previously]. Likewise, it is stated in the Kāmika:
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) once during the incense, the lamp, the food offering (naivedya), and even within the ritual strength (bala), the subsequent rite should be performed.
Thus, Nandikeśvara is the first of the Gaṇas, beginning with Nandin;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others are included.
Being praised by them, it is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
It was served by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and other gods who were attendants of Śiva,
through Vedic and Puranic hymns, mantras, and songs in manifold ways.
"The worshipper should contemplate Śiva as being pleased while being praised.
Likewise, in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"One should meditate upon Śiva as being satisfied while being praised by Viriñca and the other gods."

Regarding the phrase "endowed with sixteen digits" (*dviraṣṭakakalopetā*): the sixteen digits (*dviraṣṭakakalāḥ*) are the sixteen digits [of the moon]. Together with the temple (*prāsāda*) composed of those, along with the twelve digits mentioned previously in the procedure for invocation (*āvāhana*), there is the *samanā* [state] situated within the pervasive (*vyāpaka*).
It is known as the Endless (*ananta*) within the Void (*vyoma*). Thus it is said: "O Goddess, Śiva is to be known as having sixteen digits, residing in the Anātha and Anāśrita [tattvas]."
According to the scriptural statement, there are four kalās known as Vyomarūpā, Anantā, Nāthā, and Anāśritā belonging to the level of Samanā;
if these are joined above Vyāpinī, they constitute the sixteen kalās. Their arrangement and essential nature should be understood from such works as the Siddhāntasārāvalī.

212) Now he states the procedure for recitation (*japa*), beginning with "having taken the flower with the hands": "Through worship one obtains a vast kingdom; through the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), prosperity."
Through recitation, there is complete purification of sin; through meditation, wisdom is said to arise.

Since it has been stated thus, recitation (*japa*) should be performed for the purpose of destroying evil. That recitation is of three kinds, distinguished as mental (*mānasa*) and so forth. As it has been said:
"That recitation is to be known as threefold: [low] (*upāṃśu*), whispered (*bhāṣya*), and mental (*mānasa*)."
The mental [recitation] is to be performed with the mind by reflecting upon the meaning of the words of the mantra.

Whispered recitation (*upāṃśu-japa*) is that which is within the range of one's own mind and involves only the contact of the lips; loud recitation (*uccair-bhāṣya-japa*) is said to be that which is within the range of hearing by others.
The first is declared to be *sāttvika*, the second *rājasa*, and the third is clearly declared *tāmasa*; the *tāmasa* is found in cruel deeds.

The *rājasa* [mantra] is for nourishment, subjugation, and so forth; the *sāttvika* is for divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "having taken a flower in the hand," it means holding a flower in the left hand while using the rosary (*akṣamālā*) worshipped at the heart.
In this context, the rosary is of many varieties according to the *Āgamas*.

In that regard, the recitation (*japa*) should be performed with a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads, because the scripture declares it to be the bestower of extraordinary fruits. Therefore, the recitation with a *rudrākṣa* rosary should be performed; as it has been said:
The procedure for the rosary (japamālā) is now briefly declared,
along with its varieties and its fruits, for the benefit of practitioners of mantra.
Easy to accomplish with little effort and bestowing many accomplishments,
the garland of letters itself is first proclaimed for those who desire success.
With the letters of the Mātṛkā joined with the Bindu, arranged in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order,
together with the eight groups of consonants including Meru, a garland of syllables is formed.
Mantras endowed with each respective seed-syllable (bīja), when recited, bestow swift accomplishment.
In this regard, while performing the finger-counting of recitation, one should count using all the fingers including the thumb.
An action performed without the thumb becomes fruitless;
the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the fourth is considered the index finger.

The three fingers [other than the middle finger] should have three joints each, while the middle finger has only one joint. During the time of recitation (*japa*), one should avoid using two joints of the middle finger.
The wise one should begin from the middle of the ring finger and proceed clockwise.
One should recite [the mantra] ten times over the joints up to the base of the index finger;
or else, the middle joint of the middle finger consists of four parvans.
While circumambulating Mount Meru, the wise person should not recite the names at the base joint; rather, starting from the middle joint up to the base, he should perform the counting.
One should not separate the fingers nor slightly contract the palm;
for if the fingers are separated, the recitation flows away through the gaps between them.
Whatever is recited while the fingers are at the tips, whatever is recited while crossing over the *meru* bead,
and whatever is recited at the joints of the beads— all that becomes fruitless.
If one should recite out of negligence, transgressing the rules for counting, the Rākṣasas will seize it; therefore, a wise person should count with certainty.
One should perform the daily recitation (japa) with the hands, but not the optional (kāmya) recitation, because it is not understood [otherwise];
however, the practitioner should perform both the daily and the optional recitations using rosaries.

(214) Each single [mark] on the fingers is declared to be the count for *japa*; with the life-breaths (*prāṇas*) it is tenfold, with conch-shells it is a hundredfold, and with *śaṅkhas* it is a thousandfold.
A ten-thousand-fold [stūpa] is said to be made of coral and precious gems;
that same [structure], when made of crystal, is proclaimed [to be a hundred-thousand-fold], and with pearls, it is called a hundred-thousand-fold.
The merit from gold is said to be tenfold; from that, it is made a hundredfold by [the use of] *kuśa* tips; and the fruit from *rudrākṣa* beads is multiplied infinitely.
Because it is joined with the first syllable of the Kṣatriya [caste], it is celebrated as the "Garland of Dakṣa" (dakṣamālā);
one should fashion a rosary for recitation using beads equal in number to the syllables of that [mantra].
Alternatively, one may perform them slowly during a recitation common to all purposes;
through fifty-four repetitions, the accomplishment of desired rites shall be attained.
One hundred and eight recitations are said by the Creator to grant all accomplishments (*siddhi*);
twenty-seven for liberation and the like; and fifteen for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
This and so forth is stated as being common to all; however, regarding the rudrākṣa specifically: "By means of twenty-seven beads, and especially those with five faces...
"One should fashion the rosary in the shape of a cow's tail ring," as it has been stated;

therefore, one should join mouth to mouth with twenty-seven rudrākṣas, and join back to back. Having fashioned the rosary according to the described method, with the *meru* bead made facing upward—so it is said.
One should wash it with the *jāta* [mantra] and bind it with the *vāmadeva*;
one should fumigate it with the *aghora* and smear it with the *puruṣa*.
One should recite with the fifth [mantra] and likewise recite with the Ghora [mantra];
having displayed the eight mudrās, one should worship each one in sequence.
"O Śivā, it is knotted with five [threads] and should be worshipped as before with its shadow. Thus it is said;
one should perform the recitation (japa) while holding [the rosary] with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
This is stated in the Kāmika:
Success is said to be achieved by drawing [the breath] with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb;
success in the intermediate stage is desired through the union of the thumb and the forefinger.
(216) From the joining of the little finger and the thumb, the least accomplishment is said to result.
At the time of recitation, the rosary must be well concealed by the wise practitioner.
"Indeed, during the time of recitation, one should not show the rosary even to one's guru;
[the recitation should be] neither lazy, nor with a wandering mind, nor too fast, nor too slow. Thus it is said. Here, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.

Having raised the *nāda* from the *mūlādhāra* as described in the *āvahana* [rite], and having led it to the *dvādaśānta* by way of its departure from Brahmā situated in the heart and other locations,
one should draw in the right thread for the sake of enjoyment by means of the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*).
One should draw it up very slowly by way of the upper path for the sake of liberation.
"A practitioner of mantra must not overstep Mount Meru; by overstepping it, he becomes subject to fault.
Because it has been stated thus, Rudrākṣa—which possesses qualities such as worldly enjoyment and liberation—should be worn.
In this manner, one should perform the recitation (japa) one thousand and eight times, or even just one hundred.
Eight, twenty-eight, or eight [verses] should be recited by the Guru, as has been prescribed.
Having performed the recitation according to the number prescribed by one's own guru among the aforementioned options,
and having placed the rosary on the right thumb and held it in the palm;

Having resolved that the flower held in the left hand is the locus for the manifestation of the recitation (*japa*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *astra*, *kavaca*, and *hṛdaya* mantras upon the palm of the right hand; one should take with the right hand the flower situated in the left hand—
which has been protected by the *astra* and enveloped by the *kavaca*— and [place it] upon the palm of the left hand using the right thumb.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *astra*, *kavaca*, and *hṛdaya* mantras, and having placed the flower along with the *arghya* water held in the right hand upon the palm of the left hand, joining them together like a casket, one should recite the verse beginning with "O Guardian of the secret of secrets" (*guhyātiguhya goptra*). The meaning of this verse is as follows: "O secret of secrets" (*guhyātiguhya*) is a vocative address.
Since you are the protector of the most secret and most trustworthy among those who are secret and trustworthy— protecting them from obstacles— or rather,

because of the "secret" (*guhya*) and the "most secret" (*atiguhyam*), [the compound] *guhyātiguhye* is formed; here, by the word *guhya*, which is a synonym for "mystery," there is the Vedic revelation beginning with, "This twenty-fifth is the Puruṣa."

The established entities, such as *puruṣa*, *prakṛti*, and so forth, are being discussed. Having transcended these, there exist those established by the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), which are extremely secret; by the term "extremely secret" are meant the principles beginning with *bindu* and ending with *vaikharī*, starting from *nāda*.

All those who dwell in the respective principles (tattvas), beginning with Kalā and ending with Māyā—which consists of sound and form—are called "selves" (ātman), such as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) and others. You, whose domain these all are to be governed by, are Guhya-guhyasattva;
you alone, and no other, are the protector and guardian of all these selves. Therefore, O Protector, you remain [established] for that reason.

"Through mindfulness and through faith, by my recitation (japa), success shall come to me; accept this recitation performed by me"—this is the meaning of the verse. Just as wealth entrusted to a capable guardian among people who are not otherwise pervasive remains untouched by the wicked and leads once again to the success of those seeking prosperity, so too here, [success comes] when it is offered to Śiva.
The sense is that for practitioners who are not overcome by obstacles, *japa* leads to accomplishment (*siddhi*).
By the word "accomplishment," the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, which reside in various stages (*bhūmi*) within the context of the practitioner, are expressed. (p. 219)
Even for one desiring liberation, it is said that liberation is unimpeded by means of offering [the oblation] into that [fire].

Having recited this verse concerning the Lord of Enjoyment (Bhogīśloka), one should offer the water of the *arghya* with the root mantra into the hand of Śambhu using the left hand, while the right hand is held out as the "hand of grace" (*varahasta*).
Thus, according to the statement in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"One who is a seeker of enjoyment (*bhogin*), having been initiated by means of material initiation (*bhautikadīkṣā*), partakes in liberation after his own enjoyments. Likewise, in the *Rurusaṃhitā*:
O Gaṇapati, those who have been purified by initiation and born within the maṇḍala of the Guru, their bodies radiant with the splendor of the orb of the rising sun through the mantras of the Siddhas;
having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time accompanied by hosts of celestial nymphs, they cast off their longing for the world and [attain] Supreme Śiva.
They become possessors of the sovereignty of the quarters.
Thus, with the verse beginning "The most secret of secrets," one should offer oneself as the very essence of the act of recitation through many verses.

Some maintain that, according to the two verses beginning with "Whatever action [is performed] by Śiva," one who has been initiated through the *naiṣṭhika* initiation should perform the dedication of both his recitation (*japa*) and his actions.
As it has been said:

"Having studied even two verses, the sage who has dedicated his mind to Śiva should daily offer [the merit] through recitation and other means, if possible, as one seeking liberation. Regarding the verse beginning with "whatever": its meaning is that whatever [merit], whether good or evil, [has been done]— [The full passage continues: "Whatever [merit] has been performed by me, O Lord, whether intentionally or unintentionally, all that I offer to You; may it be for the attainment of Your state. This is the meaning of the verse beginning with "whatever. It refers to any good deed or evil deed whatsoever.

"O Lord, whatever karma is performed by us—both kinds of karma—please protect my merit (sukṛta) for the sake of securing my liberation until the end, for me who am established in the state of Śiva and initiated into the state of Śiva. [Note: Although the root *bhuj* is generally used in the parasmaipada, it takes the ātmanepada here because it means 'to protect' (*pālana*), due to its supreme sovereignty. This must be endured."

"Destroy the form of evil deeds; consume it"—this is an alternative reading. That, however, is another mantra consisting of two seed-syllables that destroys the two types of karma; by means of it, cause [the evil] to perish, just as for someone the destruction of sin occurs through the recitation of the Aghora-mantra and others as a rite of atonement (*prāyaścitta*).
p.

221) Likewise, here too, the sense is that the destruction of karma occurs through the utterance of two syllables. In the phrase "emanated by Śiva" (śivodāta) and so forth, by the word *śiva*, one who is endowed with the state of Śiva—which is stainless, unsurpassed, and consists of the knowledge and action of all objects—is meant.
The Supreme Lord is thus described: He alone is the giver; He is the purified Śiva, the enjoyer;

He is the sustainer and protector of all—this is the meaning. According to the root *bhuji*, which signifies both protecting and consuming, Śiva exists only in the sense of protecting, because for Him, who is eternally satisfied, the consumption of food is impossible. Śiva desires this entire world.

The remainder [of the verse] is as follows: Alternatively, that Śiva remains pervading this entire universe—which consists of the pure, the mixed, and the impure—as its protector and its purifier. Why? Because no other purifier or protector exists. One should abandon the ordinary state of mind expressed as "Śiva worships" and instead cultivate the realization: "I am Śiva."
"Until one has become equal to Him, one is not capable of worshipping [Him]; having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva"—
by such statements as these, he who has become Śiva through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and by means of the previously mentioned purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), etc., [is qualified].
Having become thus, he performs sacrifice in all the ritual sections (*adhikaraṇa*) enjoined by the scriptures for the sake of destroying his own impurity;
he worships Supreme Śiva, who is characterized by being the purifier and so forth. That worshipper [realizes]:
"I am indeed Śiva," and having worshipped with the thought "I am Śiva, the one to be worshipped," [he says] regarding both the object of worship and the worshipper: "O Lord of the World, I am yours."
The demonstration of acceptance is thus established as the presentation of the relationship between the self and its master, as stated in the scriptures.

For this very reason, it is called "the offering of one's own self. As Brahmaśambhu has said: "Having always offered one's own self with devotion, [one performs] recitation and worship. This refers to offering [everything] solely within the heart; this was stated regarding the dedication of recitation and other acts.
Or, O connoisseur of the heart, one may offer [the oblation] with the root mantra alone, omitting the three verses. Having thus explained the procedure for daily recitation (*japa*),

[the author] describes what must be practiced by the practitioner through the passage beginning with "the worshiper of the mantra to be accomplished" (*sādhyamantra*) and "the worshiper of the mantra for desired ends" (*kāmyamantra*).
Since the practitioner of mantra, having purified himself with mantras, should consecrate himself for infinite victory by means of the path prescribed for the *sādhya-mantra* and the Lord of Mantras.
Because it has been stated thus, the practitioner who worships with a *kāmya-mantra*, having received the *sādhaka-dīkṣā* prescribed in another *āgama*,

should pray to Śiva for the purpose of performing the worship of the *kāmya-mantra* and perform the recitation (*japa*) five hundred thousand times while stationed before the *dakṣiṇāmūrti* of the Lord. At the conclusion of the recitation, there should be ten thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta-homa*).
When the mantra has been propitiated in this manner, it becomes fit for ritual action;
consequently, whatever rites have been prescribed will undoubtedly be accomplished.

Thus it is stated in the *Kālottara* and its commentary: "Having worshipped the Supreme Lord in the *liṅga* and other [supports], one should worship Him on the right petal with the *sādhya-mantra* within the light of the Aghora-eye. According to this scriptural injunction, having performed the worship of the *sādhya-mantra* on the right petal of the lotus-throne of Śiva, one should perform the daily practice accompanied by the progressive increase of the *sāṃkhya*.

Having performed the recitation (japa) five hundred thousand times, and having performed worship of the maṇḍala at the conclusion, one should offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter into the sacrificial ladle (sruva) using the mantra of the object to be accomplished (sādhya). Thereafter, the rites prescribed for that [mantra] are to be performed.
They are accomplished. For it has been stated that a *homa* (fire sacrifice) should be performed every day at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), in accordance with its specific number.

One should worship the *kāmya-mantras* on the southern petal of the seat of Śiva. Having offered the seat and the form (*mūrti*) with the *praṇava* at the end of one's own path—where "one's own path" (*svādhvā*) refers to as many principles (*tattva*) as belong to whichever mantra it may be.

One should worship by reciting the *āsana-mantra* together with the *praṇava*, as well as the *mūrti-mantra*, extending as far as the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the root [mantras] up to that limit. Having stated what is to be done after performing the recitation (*japa*) in this manner, he says: "Thereafter, in the south-eastern quarter of the deity," and so forth—by means of a single application.
Oṃ hāṃ, [I offer] this lotus-seat for the Guru. Alternatively, having established the sixfold seat beginning with Ananta and ending with Padma, one should install the form (mūrti).

"Having worshipped the form of one's own guru with devotion, one should invoke Śiva into it"—thus, according to the words of Somaśambhu, one should worship after invoking Śiva into that image of the guru. This is because of the statement of Somaśambhu: "In one's own image, in the image of the guru, in a book, in water, in fire, in a painting and so forth, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila); among these, the last [the image of the guru] is the most excellent."
Although the worship of Śiva regarding all [entities] beginning with one's own form (nijamūrti) is characterized by the predominance of consciousness,

it nevertheless constitutes an ancillary part of the worship based on the five substrates— beginning with one's own form and ending with fire— and specifically of the worship based on the substrate of the *liṅga*.

Therefore, the worship of Śiva occurs both in one's own form during the section on the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and in water during the section on the offering of water (*arghya*).
This has been prescribed. Now, [the author] will speak of the worship in the form of the Guru, immediately followed by that in the Vidyāpīṭha and in the Fire.
"One should worship even in the Vidyāpīṭha in this same manner with a single utterance," it is said. One should worship the Vidyāpīṭha for ten million times (koṭi).
Having worshipped either a single *saṃhitā* inherited through tradition or the eleventh [chapter] therein, one should invoke Śiva there and worship him.

Since it is stated that "one should propitiate him with three handfuls of flowers, satisfy him with hymns, and pay obeisance," one should perform the hymn according to the method described in the ritual manual (*paddhati*), beginning with "O Lord of the Gods, having paid obeisance," and so forth.

Having offered praise—either briefly or extensively—in accordance with the extent of one’s own intelligence and in conformity with the expansion of that intelligence, and having performed three circumambulations by moving from left to right and right to left, one should prostrate with the eight limbs.
These are: the two feet, the two knees, the two hands, the chest, the navel, the two shoulders, and the head.
They say there are eight supreme limbs; with these, one should perform prostration to Śiva.
One should prostrate in the manner thus described; or else, one should perform a five-limbed or three-limbed prostration according to the requirements of place and time. As it has been said:

Having praised Śiva loudly with this brief hymn, one should prostrate. Prostration may be performed as a full-length prostration (daṇḍapraṇāma), or as a "wealth-prostration" (dhanapraṇāma) which consists of praise; it is considered to be threefold: eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga), five-limbed (pañcāṅga), or three-limbed (tryaṅga).
Having filled his joined palms with flowers and having uttered the Śambara mantra ending in "namaḥ," the knower of mantras, endowed with devotion, should meditate upon Śiva.
Having offered a flower before the deity,
one should prostrate to it with the head, the pair of hands, the two ears, and the chin.
One should prostrate to Śiva by touching the ground with the eight limbs;
one should prostrate to Śiva with five limbs—namely, the head, the two hands, and the two knees.
One should bow to Śiva with the head, the two hands, and the three parts of the body;
one may also bow as appropriate with these [limbs], depending on the place, time, and other circumstances.
Then, one should perform circumambulation according to the rule of right and left,
remaining silent while reciting the root mantra and not overstepping the boundaries set by the Guru and others.
Avoiding the shadow, the path of the moon, and conversation with people,
one should circumambulate Śiva from left to right, look upon the Lord, and prostrate before him.
He circumambulates clockwise, moving slowly by way of the left and the right.
"One should perform [the rite] as far as possible while meditating on Śiva as previously described.
Thus, having performed the desired recitation (svādhyāya) until the time of midday, [one should proceed].
One should worship the Supreme Lord after performing the bathing and other rites as previously described.
"Or, one should offer the eight flowers to the deity previously worshipped," according to the statement in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.
If the worship at a single time is omitted, one should mutter [the mantra] a thousand times as an expiation.
Once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or at midnight.
Whether one performs worship three times a day or even once a day, for all these [practitioners], the expiation shall be equal;
it shall not be greater for those of slender means.
Thus it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, in the section on expiation (*prāyaścitta*), according to its commentary, from page 229, beginning with "ekakālākāt."

For one who worships at two times, what difference is there if the ritual action is omitted? The meaning is: none at all. Since the twilight worship (*saṃdhyārcana*) must necessarily be performed four times a day, for those who perform it in brief form, it is seen that by offering the "eight flowers" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) at a single time, it serves as a representation of the other times as well.

The meaning is that because the performance of worship at that specific time is accomplished [in both cases], the expiation for the omission of worship at one time and the omission of worship at all three times is equal. Thus it has been said: "If worship at one time is omitted, one should recite the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra a thousand times."
In this way, for each omission of two times and so forth, one should increase the count by one hundred.
By omitting a single day's worship, one incurs a debt of one thousand three hundred [days];
if this is done intentionally while observing a fast, the penalty is double that amount.
Their worship may be performed four times a day or even once a day;
for all of them, the expiation must be exactly as prescribed, neither less nor more.

Because it has been stated: "The ritual for worship at two times is accomplished by including [the offerings] within the offering of eight flowers and so forth, even for those who worship at only one time. Thus, regarding worship at two times and so on:

If one is capable, one should bathe and worship even at the time of midday. If one is incapable, then at that very time [one should worship] with the eight flowers and so forth; he states that it may also be performed at other times for one who is unable to perform the twice-daily worship and so on, by saying "unable to perform the twice-daily worship" and so forth. Now, he describes the prayer to Śiva for the purpose of performing the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), beginning with "the one qualified for the fire-ritual" and so forth. Agni...
The official in charge of the ritual must be endowed with special initiation.
Thus, it is stated in the Kāmika:
"In this way, specifically in the case of the distinguished *samayadīkṣā*..."
"The child becomes fit for the knowledge of the fire, the oblation, and the scriptures.

By this, the *putraka* and others are also included. "With perfected implements" means endowed with the harmony of materials, time, and so forth. For this very reason, although one is qualified for each successive fire-rite (*agnikārya*), the implements...
"Because of such deficiency, being unable to perform that [homa], one should perform recitation (japa) as a substitute for the oblation.
As it is stated there, this refers to one who lacks the formal authorization (anadhikārī) and is merely endowed with the initiation of commitment (samayadīkṣā).
Indeed, for both the initiate (samayī) and the spiritual son (putraka), it is proclaimed that this must be performed constantly:
bathing, worship, recitation, fire-offering (homa), and meditation as the fifth.
Thus, regarding the phrase "always known as such" and so forth—it may be asked how it is heard that both types of *samayins* have the authority for the *homa*. A *samayin* is of two kinds:
the ordinary *samayin* and the specialized *samayin*. Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:

"But he who possesses the common convention (*sāmānyasamayī*) is remembered as a *śūdra* among the Māheśvaras; one who is devoid of the elevation of caste (*jātyuddhāra*) becomes a possessor of the common convention.
Likewise, in the *Varuṇapaddhati*:
Where there is yoga in the state of Rudra, and where there is yoga in the state of Īśvara,
yet no śikhā exists there— such initiation is of two kinds for the Samayin.
Thus, therefore, those who have taken the general initiation possess the authority for the worship of Śiva, as well as the authority for the fire-oblation (*homa*).
As it has been stated in the *Siddhārthasamuccaya*:

Furthermore, through the *samaya-saṃskāra* (the rite of initiation into the rules), preceded by the purification of the body composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika-deha*), one gains the qualification for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*). By that alone, the attainment of the world of Rudra (*rudraloka*) occurs.

However, through the specific *samaya-saṃskāra*, one gains the qualification for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites, as well as the fitness for the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*).

He attains [perfection]; he achieves the state of Lordship (īśvarapada). "Of these, the first initiation is proclaimed as that called 'the elemental' (bhūtākhyā). "The Hand of Śiva (śivahasta) should be bestowed, for it grants the station of Rudra. "Thus, one who is fit for the worship of Śiva shall undergo the Samaya-initiation."

He describes the going to the place for the sake of the fire-rite with the words beginning "having requested": "having requested" means having made a formal entreaty; "taking the *arghya* vessel and so forth"—the *arghya* vessel is the general *arghya* vessel; by the word "and so forth," *caru*, clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), fragrance, flowers, sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, and other such items are included.
They are grasped.
233) From the southern, southwestern, and northwestern [directions], in either case, in a direction other than those three mentioned directions. Likewise...
In the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"Except for the directions of the Wind (East), the Daityas (West), and Yama (South), [the altar] should be one cubit in measure,
with a height of four, three, or two finger-breadths, provided with a *mitrā* on the north."
It should be either circular or square, resembling the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree at its center,
twelve finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in width.
With his neck resting upon a support two finger-breadths high, facing westward with his navel positioned at the front, he should sit and perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus it is said. Here, because three directions have been prohibited, the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) must be performed in the remaining five directions. Accordingly, it has been stated:
"The beautiful hall of worship should be situated in the northeastern direction, measuring thirty-two cubits or even twenty cubits."
It may have sixteen sun-rays (or cubits), or eight cubits;
it should be square on all sides, or its length may be double [its width].
Having divided that length into three parts, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is formed by two of those parts.
It should be constructed with four doors, possessing all kinds of exquisite beauty;
by this [measure], the fire-hall (homa-śālā) shall be situated either to the east or to the west.
One should prepare a fire-sanctuary for the purpose of the daily burnt offering (homa) in the northern direction, in the northeast, or especially in the southeast.
One should perform the daily fire-rite in the perpetual fire within the sacrificial chamber,
following the prescribed ritual for the fire in the fivefold temple-pits in due order.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Kāmika*: "The daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) should be performed for the sake of others, or in the kitchen. Regarding the rule that one should face east or north, the *vacana* states: "Seated with the navel facing forward. If the sacrificial hearth (*yoni*) is in the western direction, one should sit facing east; if it is in the southern direction, one should sit facing north—this is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
Regarding the phrase "in a vessel or on a sacrificial mound," the detailed procedure and the concise one are the same.
235) Whether on a sacrificial mound or in its absence, one should establish the consecrated fire.
Indeed, in an unrefined sacrificial pit, the fire of Śiva is not perfected;
and when the fire of Śiva is not perfected, the oblation offered becomes fruitless.

According to this statement, having consecrated either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*)— consecrated with eighteen purifications, four purifications, or the two purifications mentioned in the *Apaddhati*,
as appropriate to the place, time, and other factors— one should generate the Śiva-fire therein and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). In the center...

With the Astra-mantra, [one draws] "eastward-pointing" in the center; that is, within the middle of the pit, pointing east, facing the east. Regarding the south and north, it says "within the middle of the pit [with the Astra-mantra, eastward-pointing]," and thus it is stated: "In the south, in the north, and in the middle of the pit, starting from the west up to the northeast, three lines should be drawn upon them. Thus, according to this statement, one should draw three lines starting from the west up to the northeast, both in the south and in the north, within the middle of the pit. Upon those [lines],...
In the center, starting from the south, a single line should be drawn.
236) This pertains to a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) facing east; if it faces north, the order is reversed, [the lines being drawn] from east to west.

In the center, starting from the southern direction, three lines should be drawn facing north; above them, in the middle, one line should be drawn starting from the west and facing east. After the drawing, one should sprinkle it with the *kavaca* mantra and then sprinkle it again with the water of the *arghya*. One should then visualize the entire sequence of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

One should contemplate the sacrificial vessel (*pavitra*) as being consecrated by the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that will be described in the section on the *pavitra*, through the two acts of scraping (*ullekhana*) and sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) alone. One should not think, however, that it is consecrated by only those two, because it has been stated that there is a division of Tantras based on differences in ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth; thus, in some cases, it is summarized in accordance with the capacity of the listener's intellect.
Because the scriptures proceed with detail in some places, it is likewise stated in the *Kālottara*:
"Henceforth I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual procedure for the fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*).
Scratching [the ground] is performed with the Weapon-mantra (*śastra*), while sprinkling is prescribed with the Armor-mantra (*varman*)."
p.
237) "The practitioner, having been consecrated by the *śakti*, should perform [the rite] with the heart-mantra. Thus it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"First, the wise one, having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (*astra*)."
Thereafter, one should subsequently encircle you with the armor (kavaca) in the proper sequence.
O Six-faced One, one should perform the re-scrubbing with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja) on the right and the north of the pit, and three [lines] in the middle and to its north.
Then, the knower of the ritual procedure should again sprinkle with the *kavaca* mantra;
he should then place a seat within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) while reciting the *praṇava*.

Thus, the fourfold set of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) has been described. In this way, regarding the production of the *śivāgni* (the fire of Śiva) and so forth, there are both concise and extensive versions. Therefore, since it is impossible to perform the daily rites (*nityakarman*) according to the extensive method, the Teachers have stated here [the procedure] in brief; or else, when the materials, time, and other factors are available, one may perform it extensively, as will be explained in the section on the *pavitra*.
It should be performed. (p.
238) Regarding the production of fire, he describes the worship of Vāgīśvarī:

In that regard, by the words "with the heart" and so forth: having offered a *viṣṭara*— that is, a seat— in that sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using the "heart," which is joined with the seed-syllable of the heart, one should [visualize] upon that seat the Form (*mūrti*), who is dark-complexioned, youthful in appearance, in her menses, and fit for conception, as described by the passage beginning with "arisen from the forest" and so forth.
One should fashion a firm fire-drill (*araṇī*) made from *śamī* wood or *pippala* wood,
measuring sixteen fingers in width and twenty fingers in length.
While recollecting the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should churn [the fire-drill] to the height of a finger-breadth;
the friction-wood should be consecrated with the Gāyatrī, and the churning itself should be worshipped with the Heart-mantra.
One should join the discus with the sword, likewise the stepping forward with the armor;
one should join the head-ornament with the tuft, and the binding of the hands with the turban.
"In this way, the fire is rendered beneficial"; by the phrase "beginning with the *karaṇī*," the twice-born (*dvija*), the planets (*graha*), and so forth are included.
As it is said in that very same place:
Whether it be light from the temple of the twice-born, or arising from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta), or common domestic light— thus,
that which originates from a pure dwelling, such as the house of a Brāhmaṇa or others endowed with virtuous conduct, is called the "portion of the flesh-eaters" (kravyādāṃśa).

It is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī* that one should abandon the "Rākṣasa portion" of that substance—such as corpses and so forth—which is corrupted by being fit for consumption; this abandonment of the "Kṛvyāda portion" should be performed in the southwest direction with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Having purified the remaining "Amarāṃśa" portion through the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*), [one should proceed] with this...
Because fire is elemental (*bhautika*), one must perform the conjunction with the navel-fire (*nābhyagni*) and the fire of knowledge (*vidyāgni*).
Having placed and settled the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), which is fiery, connected to fire, and shining like the flame of a lamp, into the fire situated at the navel— so it has been said:
Having brought [the substance] from the fire, which is always supported by [the deity], and placed it upon the pure vessel,
one should perform the purification through inspection and other means, setting aside the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyād).
Having unified the three channels—the expansive, the bindu-related, and the elemental—one [attains the goal].
"Having projected the consciousness of fire by means of the seed-syllable of fire, O Teacher," so it is said.

Having thus contemplated this fire as the supreme lord’s virility and the seed of Śiva, one should deposit it facing oneself— that is, in such a way that it faces one's own self— as it has been said: "The fire, consecrated with the Saṃhitā-mantras and rendered nectar-like by the Dhenu-mudrā..."
It is protected by the *heti* mantra and rendered unassailable by the *kavaca*.
Having worshipped it and circumambulated it three times above the fire-pit (kuṇḍa),
one should meditate on Śiva as the seed-syllable within the womb of Vāgīśī.
The practitioner, standing on the ground with knees bent, should visualize [the object] being cast away by the god Vāgīśvara; he should cast it from his own heart toward himself.

Thus, he states what is to be done immediately after the placement of the fire (*vahni-vinyāsa*), beginning with the words "having thoroughly merged" (*saṃmūhya*) and so forth: having thoroughly merged the fire in the region of the navel by means of the heart-mantra.

To the Goddess Vāgīśvarī, [offer] a garment (*vāsaḥ*, *vastram*); here, because a brief consecration (*laghu-saṃskāra*) is to be performed, one should worship the fire with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras for the sake of completing the rites beginning with the conception (*garbhādāna*), and offer five oblations (*āhutis*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Since no specific substance is mentioned here, [the oblations should be made] with sesame seeds (*tila*) and so forth.
One should perform [the rite]. Furthermore, one should recite the *sadyojāta* mantra over the heart; for it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:

"In the absence of materials for the fire-oblation (*homadravya*), one should instead perform recitation (*japa*). He describes the location for the worship of Brahmā and others, as well as Indra and others, for the purpose of protecting the fire, beginning with the words "eastern, western," etc. O, O!

"Brahmā and the other gods, as well as Indra and the other guardians of the world, having warded off the host [of obstructors], shall protect the child. Thus the fire-child should be requested for protection. Immediately thereafter, one should perform the naming of the fire with the mantra "Oṃ Hāṃ, you are the Śiva-fire" (oṃ hāṃ śivāgnirasi), which signifies its nature as the consumer of oblations. Then, one should dismiss the two parents; here, Vāgīśvarī is intended.
One should dismiss Vāgīśvarī.
When this has been done, it becomes the Śivāgni fire.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"The praise of Śiva as fire is now told by the concise path:
having taken pure fire, it is properly placed into the fire of the *bindu*."
Having directed those two into the digestive fire, one should sequentially cast them into the three fires as one,
and then offer them into the fire of the sacrificial pit with the Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*.
One should offer oblations of five kinds of sesame seeds and other materials with the root mantra.
With the heart-mantra, one should consecrate [the fire] with the name "O Fire, you are the fire of Śiva."

Thereafter, one should worship Brahmā and the others, as well as the four and the remaining ones. Thus has been described the concise consecration for the successful performance of oblations into the Śiva-fire.
Alternatively, one may offer clarified butter with the mantras of the Self-knowledge and Śiva;
three full oblations into the fire constitute the swift consecration of the Śiva-fire.
One should unite with the fire, by means of the root mantra, the supreme Bindu consisting of light, who is the Lord of Fire and Śiva; thus, the fire of Śiva is produced.
(243) Without having first accomplished [the fire-ritual], an oblation offered into the Śiva-fire becomes fruitless.
Now, he describes the procedure for the oblation (homa), preceded by the worship of the Śiva-fire.

Then, "in the heart-lotus of the fire," and so forth— thereafter, following the generation of the Śiva-fire, one should mentally construct the throne of Śiva, beginning with the Support-Power (Ādhāra-śakti) as before, within the heart-lotus of that fire; having worshipped Śiva upon that throne, from the invocation up to the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa-pūjā), using sesame seeds and so forth— the word "and so forth" (ādi) [referring to other ritual substances].
The materials for the fire-oblation (homa) are now described. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"In the absence of clarified butter (ājya), the oblation should be performed with black-seeded sesame (tila);
or else with rice, barley, or with unobjectionable sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh)."
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"One should perform the daily fire-oblation (homa) with sesame, rice, barley, clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, milk, and the like; with grains, honey, guggulu resin, and so forth."
One should meditate on the desired object while seated during the oblation of clarified butter, and during the oblation of cooked rice.
During the oblation of clarified butter (ghṛta-homa), [the practitioner] should remain lying down, and during the remaining rites, seated; furthermore,
the measurements of the oblation materials will be described in their proper order.
The clarified butter should be one karṣa in measure, and the honey and milk should be equal to that.
Curd is said to be the measure of a śukti; milk-rice (pāyasa) is equal to a prasṛti;
solid foods are the measure of a prastha; and parched grain (lāja) is by the measure of a muṣṭi.
One should take an equal amount of rice as a morsel, or a vegetable morsel-sized portion;
for roots it should be one-third [of a morsel], and for tubers one-eighth.
The gift of sugarcane should be one joint; for creepers, two finger-breadths;
fuel-sticks should be the measure of a span; and rice should be equal to a handful.
For sesame, parched grain, husks, and the like, the measure is that of the "deer-seal" (mṛgīmudrā);
for leaves, flowers, and fruits, however, an equal offering is prescribed.
One should apply these— camphor, sandalwood, musk, saffron, and agallochum— as a paste equal in size to a black ant, and guggulu resin as large as a jujube seed.
I shall now state this measure of the oblations (*āhuti*) and the specific fruits of each substance.
By the first-mentioned *tila* homa, all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) will certainly be attained.
With rice as the food there shall be an increase in nourishment; with curd, there is the strengthening of the senses.
Through the oblation of milk, one gains freedom from malice; through ghee, an increase in splendor;
through various kinds of grain, diverse accomplishments; and through sesame seeds mixed with milk, peace.
Indeed, by means of dūrvā grass, diseases are removed; with [the offering of] vaśyā, one becomes submissive;
by means of kumuda, one obtains a daughter; and with aśoka flowers, there is union with a beloved.
By the oblation of jasmine buds, the daughters of the Gandharvas are brought under control;
by Nagapushpa flowers, many women, and by Champaka flowers, the Apsarases are subdued.
Through the oblation of *vallī* leaves, prosperity shall be constant;
through white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), sovereignty shall be attained; and by means of *kadaṃba* flowers, a *yakṣiṇī* shall be brought under control.
Success is achieved with the best guggulu; fever is dispelled by mango blossoms;
red flowers, honey, and salts are for the purpose of subjugation (vaśya).
Yellow flowers are for paralyzing, black flowers for killing;
blue-colored flowers are for burning, and smoke-colored ones are considered for driving away.
"Rain [is indicated] by sesame seeds and reeds," and so forth; such is the fruit arising from substances.
Thus, the signs of the fire's color and other characteristics have been described in the *Suprabheda*.
The practitioner of mantra should now, according to this procedure, observe the color, the fragrance, the sound, the smoke, and likewise the crest of the flame.
Resembling diamond, gold, silver, sapphire, and vermilion;
like the rising sun, it possesses a luster equal to yellow orpiment.
Having the luster of beryl and blood, and naturally tawny,
it is said to have a single color resembling fire and molten copper.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and nutmeg fragrance;
the scent of jasmine and trumpet-flower, along with the sweet aroma of guggulu and clarified butter.
There were fragrant uśīra, nāga, and puṃnāga trees, along with auspicious campaka flowers; there was the sound of conchs and kettledrums, and the resonance of clouds and celestial drums.
The smoke of fire that brings about all prosperity—listen now to that as well;
smoke resembling the color of a kunda flower is supremely auspicious.
The *svastyāvaktra* is symmetrical in form; the *cakrākāra* moves upward;
the *śikhā* has the form of a crest or flame; the *kādaṃba* has the shape of a cock.
In that fire-offering where this crest-flame appears, success is certain; there is no doubt.
Thus it is stated in the Sarvajñānottara:
"When the fire has been purified by many offerings of fuel, well-kindled, smokeless, and flickering with tongues of flame, he who offers oblations therein attains success."
If an oblation is poured into the sacrificial fire when its smoke has not yet increased,
there will be a loss of ritual merit for him, and the priest himself shall perish.
Radiant, with a compact flame, fragrant, and swift in its movement;
smooth and curling to the right—such is the fire (Jātavedas) when it has attained success.

"A ground that emits sparks, licks with flames, is white and black, or turns counter-clockwise; and which is foul-smelling and rough—in such a place, there is no doubt that success does not exist. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, the expiation is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "In the case of such faults that must be remedied, the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra. Thus, there are twenty-five [oblations] for each individual fault.
It should be known.

"One should worship that ash" means after the dismissal (*visarjana*) of Śiva. One should apply the ash—which has been manifested as the form of Śiva by means of the *darbha* grass previously placed in the fire—as an ornament upon the head, forehead, and other parts. As it is stated in the *Sūkṣma*:
"The wearing of that ash increases the lifespan, prosperity, and fame of men."

Thus, having dismissed Śiva independently; one should dismiss him as will be described later. Here, when there is an abundance of materials, time, and so forth, the Caṇḍahoma should be performed.
