Having also made the offering of the oblation therein, and having completed the worship of the Śivaliṅga, one should perform the worship of Caṇḍa upon the mandala or other such place.
(p. 249) Afterwards, it should be performed in the fire. As it has been said:
"When the materials, the time, and other factors are complete, one should worship Caṇḍa and perform the fire-oblation (homa)."
Having dismissed him and worshipped the fire, one should offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis in due order.
"Having dismissed the fire and the gods, with Brahmā at their head, in reverse order"—
thus is the rule for the Caṇḍahoma, since its performance is prescribed upon the completion of the materials, the time, and other requirements.

It is established that [the rite] should not be performed when [the materials] are not available. He states the procedure for the inner and outer offerings (*antarbali-bahirbali*) with the words beginning "Then, in the southern direction... In his own southern direction—that is, to the south of himself—this refers to the case where he is facing east. One should offer the inner and outer oblations in the vicinity of the *āgneyī* pit.
Thus, according to the words of Somaśambhu: if facing north, one should draw two mandalas in the southeastern direction;

having offered the inner oblation (*antarbali*) to Rudra and others in the first mandala, and to Indra and others in the second mandala, in the manner prescribed in the *Paddhati*, immediately thereafter, from the mandala...

250) Outside, either outside the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) or within a mandala made of cow dung, one should offer the external oblation (*bali*) to the crows and others, according to the passage beginning with "to the crows and so forth. Alternatively, there is another view that it may be done concisely; likewise, [it is stated] in the *Mṛgendra*.
In the manual: One should offer oblations to the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions in due order;
in the center of that, one should present the oblation to the field-guardian (kṣetrapāla) and to the crows and other such beings.
Alternatively, one should offer or cast the bali-oblation briefly with this mantra.
Thus, having been explained, the method for the inner and outer offerings (*antarbali* and *bahirbali*) should be performed right near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) when intended for one's own sake.

If, however, it is for the sake of others, one should perform the offering for the gatekeepers and the deities of the external enclosures. Thus, in the *Kāmika*, in the chapter on fire-rituals (*agnikārya-paṭala*):
Right there, one should offer the internal oblation (antarbali) after preparing a small mandala on the ground,
or on a well-prepared wooden board, consecrated with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having stated from "one should offer [the oblation] to the Rudras in the east" up to "one should offer the *bali* to the *kṣetrapālas*," [it is said]:
"In this same manner, for one's own sake, the *bali* for the retinue beginning with Nandin is prescribed in houses and other such places, as well as in temples."
"One should offer [the offering] separately, separately"—this is stated in that very same *Naivedya-paṭala*.
However, when that is impossible, the food offering (*naivedya*) should be offered mentally;
for the deities of the outer enclosure, the food offering should be made separately, separately.
In the absence [of these], there should be an offering of bali, preceded by the presiding deity of the day;
this is done upon the external seats of the spirits (bhūtapīṭhas) established in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Regarding the subsequent rites to be performed, such as "one should offer [oblations] to the Rudras from the east," he says "tataḥ" and so forth:

"Then," meaning immediately after the offering of the bali, having performed the purification of the ears, mouth, and so on— by "and so on," it is meant that one has performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the sipping of water (ācamana), and the rest— he performs the dedication of the fire-oblation (homa-samarpaṇa), beginning with the words "yatkṛtam" and so forth.
The method: He states what is to be done immediately thereafter with the words "tataḥ" (then), etc.
After the offering of the oblation (*homa-samarpaṇa*), worship is performed in reverse order (*prātilomyena*), beginning first from Īśāna according to the sequence previously established.

The worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga-pūjā*) is performed in reverse order—that is, in the opposite sequence—beginning first with the weapons (*astra*), followed by the armor (*kavaca*), and so forth. Bhojadeva has described the characteristics of the *nārāca* and *divya* mudrās as follows: the *nārāca-mudrā* consists of throwing flowers from the tips of both index fingers and thumbs.

The joining together of the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers by rotating them rapidly around one another facing each other is the *divyamudrā*. One should say, "Forgive me" (*kṣamasva*); this is the method of dismissal with lingering attachment (*sāpekṣa-visarjana*).

However, the dismissal without lingering attachment (*nirapekṣa*) is as follows: at the conclusion of the worship of Caṇḍa, one should dismiss Śiva and the others who were worshipped upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) in this very same manner.
He will say: likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having raised the deities situated in the enclosure with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* by casting flowers, one should unite them with Śiva as is appropriate."
Upon the form of Śiva, which is free from the veil of the multitude of individual souls (*puṃja-līna*),
one should offer a flower with devotion using the *mūrti-mantra* and contemplate [the deity].
O Śivā, one should display the Dhenumudrā and the Mahāmudrā as before.
"From the common *liṅga*, one should take the deity— whether the stationary [image] or those such as the momentary—
and having withdrawn them by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should place them within the lotus of one's own heart.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
Having raised the deities stationed in the enclosure with the weapon-mantra and the withdrawal-gesture (saṃhāramudrā),
one should unite them with the form-mantra (mūrtimantra) so that they are joined with their respective forms.
Having uttered the root-mantra accompanied by the *hṛnmātrā* (the sound *hrīṃ*) as is appropriate for the ritual instrument,
it becomes free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and thus attains a partless state (*niṣkalatā*).

One should contemplate this emission (visarga), which is independent [of external objects], by means of the manifestation of the Śiva-principle situated within the heart; it is considered common to all [types of] lingas.
"In the case of a consecrated image (liṅga), it is dependent as previously shown;
in the case of a mobile image (calaliṅga) also, it is dependent; but on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), it is always independent."
Now, he describes the worship of Caṇḍa with the words beginning "tat" (p. 254): in the northeastern direction, on a pure ground—that is, on a portion of the earth purified with cow dung.
Or one may perform the worship of Caṇḍa upon the pedestal.
He describes his nature with the words beginning with "born from Rudrāgni" and so forth:
Caṇḍa is that fierce aspect (*raudrabhāva*) which has arisen from Rudrāgni, that is, from Kālāgnirudra. Or alternatively:
The fire of Rudra is his wrath; because his birth (*janma*) is derived from that, he is *Caṇḍa*.

As it has been said: "The portion of the Supreme Lord's wrath is celebrated as Caṇḍeśa. Thus, Caṇḍeśa is also the lord (*īśa*) of that which is fierce and terrible (*caṇḍaghora*) resulting from practitioners' transgressions of their commitments (*samaya*) and so forth; he is the one who effects its removal.

"Caṇḍeśa, all this section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) has been [composed] by me at your command, O Caṇḍa. By means of this declaration, the worship of Caṇḍa must be performed for all those who propitiate Śiva; otherwise, the completion of the worship is not appropriate—so say the Gurus. On this point, some [hold that] Caṇḍeśa is [attained] by the Siddha upon the rising of Bāṇa and during the *cala* [period].

255) Regarding the passage beginning with "svayaṃbhuvī," some claim that worshipers such as Bāṇa and others should not perform the worship of Caṇḍa due to the difficulty of understanding the intended meaning of the *Kāmika-vacana*. That is not correct.
[This applies] to the Śaivas, the Śāktas, those who know the Soma-siddhānta,
and to men who follow the path of devotion and possess five faces [or fivefold aspects] at the time of the half-pañcama.
And Caṇḍeśvara was their teacher; for those who had transgressed their respective codes of conduct, he took refuge in Caṇḍanātha, by which means [he brought about] the end of their worldly existence.
Therefore, Caṇḍeśa should be worshipped by all without hesitation.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Dīptāgama*.
Having placed the disciple before him, one should cause him to hear the rules (samayas).

This is because, in the section on initiation, it is prescribed that the hearing of the rules must be performed in the presence of Caṇḍeśvara. Therefore, there is no room for doubt regarding the worship of Caṇḍa. Furthermore, the worship of Caṇḍa applies to the case of Bāṇaliṅgas and the like.

However, regarding the prohibition [of worship] at a common *liṅga*: having abandoned consciousness (*caitanya*) and having dismissed one's own mantra (p. 256), one should therefore invoke Caṇḍeśvara and worship him. Thus it is said.

It should be understood that [this applies] either to the worship of Caṇḍa in the form of a *liṅga* as will be described in the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), or to the installation of Caṇḍa in the presence of those [deities].
Likewise, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Regarding certain liṅgas, some scholars do not desire the worship of Caṇḍa;
however, in the Siddhānta, the worship of Caṇḍa is enjoined for all liṅgas.
And wherever Caṇḍeśa is proclaimed not to have authority,
there the wise man should perform his installation.
"But one should worship Caṇḍa either on a pedestal or within a mandala;
one should offer him the *nirmālya* daily—of this there is no doubt.
[This means] "having given the previously established *nirmālya*"—referring to the vessel of molasses (*guḍapātra*) set aside for Caṇḍa at the time of the prior Śiva-pūjā.
The items such as perfumes and flowers that have been set out, excluding garments, ornaments, and the like. As it has been said:
257) "Earth, gold, cows, gems, copper, silver, molasses, and so forth..."
Other things such as betel-nut, water for drinking, betel-leaf, incense, and flowers.
"And one should give the remains of the offering (nirmālya) to Caṇḍa, just as it was consumed by Śiva.
Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.
For this very reason, it is also said in the *Paddhati*: "Liquids to be licked, things to be sucked, food, drink, and so forth."
One should not smell it, nor touch it, nor step over it, nor eat it;
nor should one ever neglect even minor duties when they are to be performed.
From giving [the gift] one is born as a flesh-eater; from eating it, one becomes an elephant.
By transgressing [the rule], there is loss of spiritual power; by smelling it, one becomes a wolf with fetters on its feet.
By selling this [offering], one becomes a Caṇḍāla;
by touching it, one becomes an Īśvara; and by [selling] the remains of an offering (nirmālya), one is born as a woman—of this there is no doubt.

Thus it is stated in the Kāmika [Tantra]. Furthermore, since the procedure for expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed there, how can [an offering] be given to Caṇḍeśvara? It is said that even regarding such giving, a fault is heard [in scripture].
Because Śiva was pleased by the asceticism of Caṇḍeśvara and gave his permission, there is no fault in the gift made by Śiva’s command. Therefore it has been said:
"By the command of Śiva, this offering of the remains (nirmālya) is presented to you.
Thus it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*.
Furthermore, in the ritual of worship, there is food, incense, and so forth, as well as fragrance and even the light of a lamp.
Contact with the canopy and the garlands does not defile it in any way whatsoever.
In cases of massage, leaping, or giving, there is no fault for one who has already performed the visualization of Caṇḍeśa,
provided it concerns substances intended for the food offering (naivedya) or the water-offering (arghya).

Thus, it has been stated that there is no fault in touching and so forth that which has been prohibited. Therefore, since the offering (nirmālya) is not mentioned even in the case of the Liṅgas made of jewels and other materials, the food and other items offered by their worshippers may be consumed.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika* [Tantra], in the section on fire-ritual (*agnikārya*):
In the case of lingas made of gems, gold, and so forth, as well as in mobile images,
paintings, statues, and even among teachers and during scriptural expositions, there is no such thing as *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings).
Whatever is offered to one's chosen deity (liṅga) is like the sacrificial pap (caru); of this there is no doubt.
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be given to servants, sons, and brothers.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: even in the worship of a *liṅga* made of gems and other materials, the worship of Caṇḍa is unavoidable; for it is heard in scripture that everything—food, drink, and so forth—that has been offered to the Supreme Lord must be given to Caṇḍeśvara:
"One should not intend the food of Caṇḍa, which is inviolable, for one's own enjoyment."
Since it has been stated in that very same section on the rites of fire (*agnikārya*) [that such food is forbidden], how can it be eaten? Do not say so;

for those who have undergone the *śiva-saṃskāra* and by virtue of their excellence in enjoyment, even the food of Caṇḍa may be eaten, but not by others. This is prescribed in that very same section on penance (*prāyaścitta*), as follows:

If a man, out of greed, should eat what has been eaten by me or what has been eaten by Caṇḍa, he is declared to be a sinner and one of evil intellect; he is not favored by the two aforementioned [deities].
If a man, praised as pure, should eat [this] with devotion,
his sin is quickly destroyed; he becomes a Brahmin of purified soul.
O twice-born ones, just as a person who is impure by nature cannot purify what he has eaten through greed,
so too a consumer of tastes brings about destruction by indulging in them.
In this world, those who possess a physical body, who are teachers, and who are solely devoted to me—they alone are worthy among all beings;
it is certainly not so for others.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Śiva Purāṇa:

"O twice-born ones, one should eat the pure *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of Śambhu from all sources; having eaten the *nirmālya* of another deity, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Thus [he is] possessed of fickleness of tongue.

"If one eats the remains of Śiva's offerings (śivanirmālya), he shall go to the Raurava hell"—thus it is stated in the Āditya Purāṇa. Regarding the phrase "with the root [mantra] accompanied by *pūraka*": having drawn [the element] with the *pūraka* breath, one should place it in one's own heart with the root mantra; for here, in the heart-lotus—

(261) There is the manifestation and dissolution of mantras. As the Śruti declares: "The power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), having dissolved into the Supreme, is established in the Self within the heart; from that the mantra is born, and into that very place it is dissolved."

Regarding the phrase "in the same way" (*evameva*) in the context of "Canda and the others worshipped on the sacrificial ground" (*sthaṇḍile pūjitāścaṇḍādayaḥ*): the meaning is that just as the Canda-mantra was applied previously to the heart-lotus, it should be done in that very same manner. Then, regarding the passage beginning with "having washed his feet" (*tato dhautapādaḥ*):
"then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after the removal of the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering); "having washed his feet" (*dhautapādaḥ*) means having cleansed his feet.
If he should be sprinkled with bathing water, milk, or similar substances,
then he should bathe or otherwise wash himself above the navel.

According to the statement in the *Kāmika*, "having sipped water (ācamya) and become pure," one should perform the washing of the feet and other rites necessitated by the removal of the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings). One should recite the *aghora* mantra twenty-one times;
having performed this recitation either immediately after the offering of the oblation (*homa*) or subsequently, one should dedicate it to Śiva.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"For the sake of liberation from defects such as omissions and the like, one should worship Ghorasambhara."
Or one should perform it one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times.
Recite the Aghora mantra as before, accompanied by the arghya water;
O Lord, whatever action there may be, whether always well-done or ill-done.
O Śaṅkara, for me who stands at your auspicious feet, consume and destroy whatever I have done out of delusion, whether it be deficient or excessive.
"O Supreme Lord, may all that be ever perfectly fulfilled for me. Having recited these two verses, he should offer them to that [deity]. Thus [it is said].
Now, he describes the worship of Kapila with the words beginning "Then," and so forth.
Five cows arrived from the world of Śiva upon the earth:
Sunandā, Subhadrā, Suśīlā, and likewise Surabhi.
Sumanas flowers, tawny cows, and likewise bulls are to be worshipped for the sake of benefiting all the worlds and for the propitiation of the gods.
The Cow-mothers (gomātaraḥ) are stationed on the earth for the purpose of bathing Śiva;
they consist of all the gods and are the mothers of all the worlds.
"Portions [of the offering] should be given to them and to those [deities]; that is the prescribed procedure," because it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* and other such texts:
"Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Sunandā; Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Subhadrā; Oṃ, salutation to Kapilā Suśīlā; Oṃ..."
Having worshipped them with the mantra, "Obeisance to Kapila and Sumanas," [one should say]: "For these are indeed the sustainers of all the worlds, yet they do not grant life;
may they, being pleased, accept this morsel of food, this most excellent offering.
One should daily offer this supreme oblation to others, for it is difficult to obtain without first having accepted it oneself."

"And they protect [the practitioner] from cruel fear; touching [it] destroys sin. Thus it is said. Alternatively, one should give a morsel: "Just as morsels should be given to cows, and indeed to a bull of the *saurabheya* breed, this fruit is seen to be equal; however, the mantras are distinct for each."

According to the statement [found on] p. 264, in the manner prescribed by the *Paddhati*: "O thou who art fragrant, arisen from the churning of the nectar of immortality, and who sustainest the world!
Accept this morsel; this is my supreme choice. Thus one should offer it. Immediately thereafter—
Because of her exhaustion; having touched her back:
"You have been saluted by Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Jahnu. O Kapilā, take away the sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me."
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Thus one should recite the mantra. The extraordinary fruit of reciting this mantra is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"A person who is pure and self-restrained should recite this daily at the three junctions of the day."
"Released from all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva. Thus it is said.
Following the worship of the tawny cow (kapilā), he says: "Until the time of midday...

The time of midday is the period of noon. After sunrise, the morning lasts for six *ghaṭikās*; the period following that until the next six *ghaṭikās* is the time for social gathering (*saṃgamakāla*). Thus, after twelve *ghaṭikās*, it is the time of midday; up until that point, one should engage in Vedic study and other such activities.

Having received [the instruction] from the mouth of the Guru, from the time one begins to serve the feet of one's own Guru, one must proceed everywhere and at all times solely according to the Guru’s word. Therefore, as before, in the morning and so forth, one should perform the worship of Śiva and other rites; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and others are included. Or rather, one should do it.

An alternative view: when Śiva has been previously worshipped—that is, worshipped in the morning—one who is unable to perform worship at two sessions or more should act according to the manner described above. Now, regarding the commencement of eating for the sake of maintaining the body, [it is said] "afterwards" and so forth;
this is because the procedures for the *cullī-homa* (fire-offering) and the *bali* (offering) have not been mentioned here, as those two are established by implication.
p.
266) That which is obtainable through the power of the word, or even through the power of the meaning,
or obtained through the force of the reality itself, should be accepted from another Saṃhitā.
Because of this statement, the *Saṃhitā* is extracted from elsewhere and written here. Likewise, in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"Having performed the midday ritual (*mādhyāhnika*), in a beautiful dining hall..."
In a secluded place smeared with cow dung, one should prepare pure cooked food.
Then, having recited the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra seven times ending with "vauṣaṭ," he should sprinkle him with drops of water contained in a conch shell together with Darbha grass.
Having set aside the finest portion of all cooked food, one should offer it for the sake of Śiva;
the remainder should be prepared on the hearth for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa) ritual.
Having purified the hearth according to the ritual, one should bring that fire, drawn in by the *pūraka* breath,
into unity with the fire at the navel, and then [unify it] with the *recaka* breath.
Having taken up the seed-syllable of fire (RA) in sequence from the first position of the KA-series onwards,
and having realized its nature as the fire of Śiva, one should place it into the fire of the hearth.
Hāṃ, obeisance to Agni; hāṃ, obeisance to Soma; hāṃ, obeisance to Sūrya; hāṃ, obeisance to Bṛhaspati;
hāṃ, obeisance to Prajāpati; hāṃ, obeisance to all the gods; hāṃ, obeisance to all...

Salutation to all. Salutation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having worshipped [the deities] starting from Vahni and ending with Pūrva in due order upon the *nala*, one should offer oblations ending with "svāhā," perform the *mārjana* (sprinkling), and then dismiss them. Then, [one should worship] Dharmāya namaḥ on the right arm at the level of the heart; Adharmāya namaḥ on the left arm; Oṃ Sarasvatyai... [and so forth].

Oṃ, salutation to Aindī; Oṃ, salutation to Kodṛgirikā—at the mortar (ulūkhala); Oṃ, salutation to Haraṇa, the beloved of Balabhadra—at the pestle (musala); Oṃ, salutation to Mṛtyu and Codi—thus [it is said]. (p. 268)
In the broom: *Oṃ, obeisance to Kāma, the wielder of the flower-weapon*. At the head of the bed: *Oṃ, obeisance to Skanda, the lord of the house*. [This is] beneath the central pillar of the house.
Having worshipped with an offering (*bali*) according to the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, one should then go outside the temple.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the crows and other creatures, and having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
he should perform the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) and enter the smeared dining hall.

Thus, it is adorned with four, three, two, or one line of ash— meaning, in a mandala formed by four lines for the Ācāryas; likewise, for the Sādhakas, Putrakas, and Samadhins, [it is adorned] with three, two, or one line, by those of the same caste (savarṇa), of equal lineage (samānajātīya), consecrated (saṃskṛta), endowed with the purificatory rites of initiation (dīkṣā-saṃskāra-yukta), and who sanctify the assembly (paṅktipāvana).
"With those worthy of eating in a row" means with those endowed with good conduct (*sadācāra*).
As it is stated in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"There, by those refined [brahmins] who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*), along with a line of the same caste."
In the *Somaśambhupaddhati* as well:
"By devotees of Śiva who follow right conduct, who are pure Śaivas, and whose wealth is their asceticism..."
"Mutually intermingled, entered into form, and unconfused.
Thus, when there is the availability of resources, vessels such as gold and so forth are prescribed for the sake of the Ācārya and others in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.
The preceptor and others [should sit] on seats made of gold, silver, copper, or iron.
Thus, in the absence [of these], that is, in the absence of gold and so forth, one should eat from bell-metal alone. This has been stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"In vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, when well-consecrated..."
The teacher, the practitioner, the son, and the fellow-student, respectively.
Facing the four directions and observing silence,
one should place the sevenfold purified ashes in an earthen, copper, common, or bell-metal vessel.
"One should eat one's meal from a vessel that has been consecrated by the Bahurūpa mantra.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* (p.
"In an auspicious vessel made of gold and the like, or commonly of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). Likewise, elsewhere:

"He who eats alone from a pure bell-metal vessel—his four qualities increase: longevity, wisdom, fame, and strength. Furthermore: "The ascetic (*yati*) and the student (*brahmacārī*) [should eat] from a bell-metal vessel, provided it is not smeared with betel or ointments."

Regarding the phrase "and a widow [should eat] from a vessel," for a householder, it refers to a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) among those not prohibited; furthermore, leaves such as those of the plantain tree (*kadalī*), mango (*cūta*), *mayūka*, *palāśa*, and lotus (*padma*) are said to be those not specifically prescribed.
As it has been stated:

(271) Even for a householder, [this applies] due to a specific consecration (*saṃskāra*). Regarding this, some maintain that there is a prohibition; however, the definition of *vīrāsana* is stated in the *Kiraṇatantra* in the passage beginning "or one bound in *vīrāsana*."
Standing with the right foot raised and the left foot placed beneath it,
doubled over and fallen forward— this is known as the vīrāsana posture.
Or, because of the alternative option "or in the heroic posture" (vīrāsana),
one should eat while remaining as comfortable as possible— either touching the ground with both feet, or with one foot only, as stated in other scriptures.

Garlic (*laśuna*), onion (*palāṇḍu*), *grañjana* (a type of garlic), varieties of garlic, and the well-known *alābu* (bottle gourd)—these, as well as those prohibited by general scriptures, should be avoided; that is, one should avoid even those vegetables prohibited in the general scriptures, such as the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and so forth. Thus [it is said]. *Śruti-smṛti*.

"The Purāṇas and other scriptures are the teachers of dharma; [they teach] both the general and the particular, namely the Śaiva and the Vaiśeṣika words. Regarding the phrase "having formed the *parigha* mudrā," the definition of the *parigha* is stated here.
Having raised [the hand], one should place it upon the left thumb of the left hand;
having extended both hands, one should place the right thumb in the mouth.
It is declared that this "to-be-worn" [garment] destroys unwholesome food.

Having thus explained the rules for the meal of a householder, he speaks regarding one who is dispassionate with the words beginning "But the dispassionate one," and so forth. "Established in samādhi" means being devoid of the appearance of meditation for the meditator.
Samādhi is the final limb of yoga among the eight limbs beginning with *yama* and *niyama*, characterized by the appearance of only that which is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*). As it has been said:
"First is *yama*, then *niyama*, followed by *āsana* and *prāṇasaṃyama*."
Withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and indeed meditative absorption;
It would be called *aniṣṭhaka* because it consists of twelve *mātrās*, ending with the *aniṣṭhā*.
With medium [counts], there is a medium exhalation; as has been stated by these [counts],
it is declared by the lords of sages that a single exhalation constitutes an equal *prāṇāyāma*.
The restraint of the vital breath for twelve [moments] is withdrawal (pratyāhāra);
one [unit] is concentration (dhāraṇā), and meditation (dhyāna) is traditionally held to be twelve [units].

"Dhyāna is proclaimed as twelve [units], and samādhi is from [that point] until the end of time. The nature of these [practices], such as yama and niyama, should be understood from the *Siddhāntaśekhara*; it is not written here for fear of excessive length. Having performed samādhi until midday...

Immediately thereafter, having performed the midday rites—such as the ritual bath, the transitional *saṃdhyā*, and the worship of Śiva—in accordance with the rules (*yathā-vidhi*), meaning without transgressing the prescribed injunctions; and having wandered about, meaning having carried out his subsequent movement;
being one whose food is restricted to alms (*bhikṣā-bhojana-niyataḥ*), that is, possessing the discipline of subsisting on alms; [he should avoid] the distress of begging and so forth.
The characteristics of *sāṃtānika* and other types of alms-gathering that obstruct [the practice of] prayer and so forth are described in the *Pauṣkara*:
"Alms for practitioners are said to be of four kinds: *mādhūkara*, *svayaṃdatta*," and so on. (p. 274)
Wandering from house to house for alms, she partakes of the *mādhūkara* (honey-gathering) style of begging;
she herself gives the alms-food to the practitioner, and she herself places the gifts into his bowl. Free from possessions, her only garment is the *brahma-śambhu-paddhati*.
When he has entered for alms and wanders about himself, that alms which is brought by his own giving—
free from a succession of disciples and the like— and whatever substance is offered to the Guru while he is consuming it, that indeed is the true nature of alms.

275) Because it is stated that there is a loss of merit (*dharma*) performed for the sake of the ancestors or the gods if it is abandoned without being requested; and regarding the determination of *dharma*, it is stated in that very same place: "One should not accept unasked alms from those who have fallen [from their caste] and so forth."

"One should abandon what is given by those who have fallen from their caste and those who are accused of crimes, even if it is unasked for. Regarding the phrase "grains as alms": here, "grains" refers to rice and the like.
Now, "the rule for that" refers to the manner of going for the purpose of begging.
The definition of that [garment] is stated as follows: "the loincloth and upper garment are exchanged;
it is twelve finger-breadths wide and thirty-six finger-breadths long."
The cord for the loincloth should be fifty threads long and hang down by one-third;
the thread made by a twice-born maiden should be tripled and then twisted.
This [cord] is indeed tripled, having three strands for the student;
it has a white upper garment with its flow turning clockwise around the navel.
Thus the characteristics of the vessel have been stated: the alms-bowl should be made twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in height;
it may be made of copper or fashioned from leaves.
"Thus, 'with shoes' means accompanied by foot-protectors;
'one who has adopted forbidden silence' means one by whom a prohibited vow of silence has been undertaken."
"Excluding the property of Brahmadevas and those who live off their own [means]"—by the word *brahma*, Brāhmaṇas are meant.

Their *sva* (property), such as fields, wealth, and so forth; and the *devasva* (property of the deity), such as cloth and so forth belonging to the Lord of the village—those who forcibly seize and enjoy such *brahmasva* or *devasva* are [the ones referred to]. These are the *brahmadevas*.

One should not collect alms from those who live off their own [wealth]. In pure households, one should avoid spitting, ejecting water from the mouth, touching anyone at all, taking by a path that is not the way, traveling by an improper route,
reviling, censuring, anger (which is well known), dispute, legal litigation, and the time of the annual flow of milk.
Through the union with the calf, the completion of the [cow's] milk occurs; having remained for that duration of time, she would depart.
277) He states what is to be done next, beginning with "Thus, it is sufficient," etc., by means of the three-syllable [mantra].

With the *mṛtyuñjaya-mudrā*, for the sake of self-protection—that is, for the protection of one's own body—one should perform the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) and other rites as previously described in the section on eating, and then eat. Thus, having set aside the practice of wandering for alms for one who is detached, he states the duty to be performed even by such a person when unable to perform the two daily worship services: "as before, [perform] *samādhi*."

Having performed [the rites] as before with the words "beginning with *kṛtvā*," and up to "as before, until the middle of the day" (*adhamādhyudinaṃ yāvat*) and so forth, [one proceeds] from the lotus-stalk situated at the *mūlādhāra*. As it has been stated:
"The location of the body-stalk for human beings is nine finger-breadths from the center of the body; by means of which the mantras [are established]."

Regarding the question of what kind of sound that *nāda*, the Śiva-mantra, presided over [by him], is like, he says: "Suprabhā" means one by whom the entire surface of the earth has been excellently illuminated—that is, made manifest—through its excellent radiance (*suprabhā*). For one whose mind has attained that state within that very Śiva-mantra consisting of *nāda*...

For one whose mind has entered into meditation (*bhāvanā*) on the sound of *bhāvanā* (p. 278), there arise [the states] born of the distinctions of Śānta, Rudra, and so forth, such as Śiva, Rudra, and so on.

Arising from that division, situated within Śiva—that is, situated at the *dvādaśānta* above that sky, which is the *brahmaraṃdhra*—in the manner thus described during the *saṃdhyās*; by the use of the plural, this applies to the evening as well as midday; for one who is unable to perform the worship of Śiva at midnight, [it should be done] immediately after the conclusion of each respective *saṃdhyā*.

One should perform meditative absorption (*samādhi*). And because of the injunction, "having performed the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) at night," one should also mentally contemplate the service of the twilight. Likewise, in the *Brahmaśambhu-paddhati*: "When midnight has arrived, one should perform the evening rite."
"Having sipped water (ācamya) or having performed the ritual purification with ashes (uddhūlya), one should sleep while meditating on the Lord as before.

Thus, he states that the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) as prescribed should be performed daily, beginning with the words "In the morning, one should meditate... He then states the purpose of the aforementioned worship of Śiva:
p.

279) Whoever worships in this manner, by means of the modes of worship beginning with Saura and ending with Caṇḍa, no sin arises for him. Through the worship of Śiva, [his sin] goes to destruction; at the end of his body, he does not return to the land of karma. By this—

The unsurpassed status of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga as a means to liberation has been declared in both general and specific scriptures, alongside [other practices] such as the yoga of knowledge, meditative absorption (samādhi), meditation (dhyāna), recitation (japa), and austerity (tapas). Likewise, it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Gods, Asuras, and others, Yakṣas, and sages free from envy..."
The worship of the Liṅga, its attainment, and eternal liberation from the cycle of existence.
Thus, by relying upon the *liṅga* endowed with these ritual actions, the practitioner attains the desired perfection; and one who is devoted to liberation attains liberation.
Just as water on a lotus leaf is exceedingly fickle when stirred by the wind,
even so is the life of all living beings.
O Śakra, youth is unstable, and wealth is likewise unstable;
sons, grandsons, and the like are unstable as well, because Raṃbhā consists of nothing but essence.
Therefore, [renounce] sons, wives, friends, companions, and wealth.
"Having abandoned the nets of delusion, one should undertake the acceptance of the *liṅga*.
Regarding this procedure of worship, he states its common applicability to all *liṅgas*, such as the fixed (*sthira*) ones and so forth, by saying: "the general sacrifice" (*sāmānyayajana*).

Now, one might object: "If this mode of worship is common to all liṅgas, it can be performed by those endowed with material wealth, but not by others. This should not be doubted. Here, no requirement for material substances has been stated; rather, it is in reference to mantras, tantras, and ritual actions. Therefore, worship should be performed by all people according to their own means.

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*, in the chapter on worship (*arcanā-paṭala*): "In the daily rite (*nitya-vidhi*), worship is performed with offerings according to one's means—whether very brief such as bathing and so forth, or extensive—with all [deities] beginning with the planets; however, in the optional rite (*kāmya-vidhi*), it must certainly be done."
Bathing, clothing, and unguents; flowers, incense, lamps, and oblations; betel-leaf with mouth-perfuming fragrance; as well as song and dance—(p. 281).
When Śambhu’s manifestation is present, all of this— the offering of oblations by men, the constant celebration, and the music— is said to be fulfilled.

In this context, as an incidental discussion, he describes the cessation of afflictions in one's own house and so forth by means of the milk-consecration (*kṣīrābhiṣeka*) and other rites during one's birth asterism (*ṛkṣa*) and so on. With the verse beginning "with a piece of [the plant] and milk," etc., he concludes by first presenting his own composed treatise, stating: "As it has been said in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures. Thus, every day...

Having explained the sequence of the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) to be performed, he now describes the rite called *pavitrārohaṇa*, which is an obligatory subsidiary (*nityāṅga*) to be performed every year. Regarding the word "atha" (now): after the exposition of the rules for the daily rites, the rule for the *pavitra* [rite] will be stated; this is the formal promise (*pratijñā*). As for the term *pavitra*: [it is...]
If there is an omission in the procedure for the daily worship of Śiva, the teachers and others suffer a loss of the accomplishments known as worldly enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (mokṣa).
That which consists of various and complete rites is described in the scriptures as "pavitra" (the sacred).

And that [rite] is performed by all the preceptors and others at the time of the Pavitrārohaṇa, following either the previously established procedure for worship— divided into the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) types, along with its primary and secondary limbs— or by whatever other means.
It does not become complete; therefore, for the sake of completing it, one must necessarily perform [the rite]. As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"Every day, there is a portion [of merit] produced by the activities of speech, mind, and body."
"Because it protects from falling, therefore this is called *pavitraka*.
Likewise, in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"The *pavitraka* is for the purpose of filling any gaps in the procedure of all worship."
Otherwise, the practitioner must act; otherwise, the mantra-practitioner will suffer the loss of accomplishment.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Another rite is proclaimed here which removes all defects. (p. 283)
May he who was attained by the gods through darkness take it away for the nourishment of his own ordinance.
Having obtained the sacred thread (pavitra) of Śambhu, one should fulfill the annual rite;
this secret pavitraka is the most excellent of all for those who have taken vows.
For the sole purpose of severing all worldly entanglements, by men who have taken up the *liṅga*—

whether they be householders, spiritual teachers, or others— who are intent upon the worship of Rudra, [this should be done] either in a sacred grove or in a cave, while being devoted to the worship of Rudra.
For householders, spiritual guides, and others who seek the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
there must be a pervasion by all the constituent parts when the ritual procedure is performed in its entirety.

If it is argued that this [state] is even more difficult to attain than that, and thus "this should not be done by anyone," and that because of the phrase "Hara is other than all consciousness," there is some distinction from ordinary expiation (*prāyaścitta*), [we reply]: for that [expiation] merely produces the non-sprouting of the seed of action consisting of the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited.

It is not a filler for what has already been done; rather, as it is said, "this [mantra] is a filler of such a nature, a filler for all ritual procedures of worship (*pūjāvidhi*), and a purifier (*pavitraka*) for the fulfillment of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Furthermore, this—
It does not deserve to be a *prāyaścitta* (expiatory rite), because an expiation is prescribed immediately upon the omission of a ritual act (*karmalopa*),

and because this [rite] has a fixed time (*kālanaiyatya*). If such is the case, then when the question arises as to which of the rites— known as *nitya*, *naimittika*, *kāmya*, or *prāyaścitta*— this *pavitra* is included within, [the answer is found] in certain [authorities].

The status of this as an occasional rite (*naimittikatva*) has been stated by the teachers in the *Āgamas* and in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*. It is said: "This is an obligatory limb (*nityāṅga*), yet it is defective [if performed otherwise]. Now, one should not suspect that because this *pavitra* is an obligatory limb, it must be performed every day like the *saṃdhyāvandana* and other such rites; for its performance is prescribed according to each specific occasion. This is established by the *sūtra*: [text fragment].

Because it is stated that one should always perform the daily worship with leaves, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and other pure materials during the *pavitra* [festival], and furthermore, even at times other than the *pavitra*, one should fashion [the thread] every day using one hundred and eight strands,
or twenty-seven, and so forth.
Since it has been stated that "it must be performed," if there is the accomplishment of the *sūtra*, then there would be no fault even if it were performed every day.
For one who is incapable of that, however, there is a fixed time. Thus, it is said in the *Kālottara*:
Since it is an integral part of the worship, this *pavitraka* rite should be performed regularly in this manner;
alternatively, one may perform it according to a fixed rule within three months.
On the fourteenth day at the end of Āṣāḍha, and likewise in Nabhasya;
when such a time has passed, one should perform the expiation.
Thus, worship performed without the *pavitra* is proclaimed to be *tāmasī*.
The worship of the rājasa type would be devoid of the act of supreme identification (paramīkaraṇa);
therefore, for that worship, purification as well as supreme identification are likewise required.
"This must always be performed by the virtuous who are fearful of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Thus it is said in the *Mohaśūlottara*:
"Furthermore, this must be performed precisely at the time prescribed by the scripture of the purifying rite (*pavitrakarma*)."
Thus he says, "the aforementioned time. Here, the nature of time is set forth by extracting it from another scripture (*āgama*).
According to the *Kāmika*: "The three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are [respectively] superior, middling, and inferior."
It should be performed on the eighth day of the month of Śukra (Jyeṣṭha), as well as in Āṣāḍha, and likewise in Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada—
on both the bright and dark fortnights— and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
"It should not be performed even in Āṣāḍha while Janārdana is not asleep," so it is said in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.
"Only during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, when Janārdana is indeed asleep..."
"One should perform the *pavitra* rite," so it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*.

In this regard, because of the restriction to only the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, it is implied by the statement "Janārdana remains asleep even beyond that" that the worship of the *pavitra* should not be performed even prior to Viṣṇu’s sleep. Now, in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
Whether out of delusion or ignorance, he who causes the *pavitra* to be made while Janārdana is not asleep is a sinner, deluded by passion.
Fasting for five days, one should recite [the mantra] fifty thousand times, O Hari.
In this way one attains accomplishment, but never otherwise;
one should not act out of delusion after having ascended, for one would then incur fault regarding the established doctrine.
By reciting the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times, one is purified even of that which was done during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha,
whether by fate or through ignorance.
"In that case also, O Purandara, the expiation is thus prescribed";
likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"One who is afflicted by the increase of diseases, or one oppressed by the king..."
He who does not perform the *sūtrarohaṇa* during the three months mentioned, having recited ten thousand repetitions with the *dakṣāṇu* mantra when the sun has entered Virgo, [attains the result].
"One should never perform the *pavitraka* rite for Śambhu during the month of Tulā.
In this context, Āṣāḍha is the last month of the solar months mentioned, corresponding to the zodiac sign of Gemini (*mithuna*). This is stated in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
Beginning from the month of Māgha and ending with Āṣāḍha, O beautiful one,
this should be known as the worldly time, the supreme Uttarāyaṇa.
Beginning from the full moon of Śrāvaṇa and ending with Puṣya, O beautiful one.
Worldly time is to be understood as the supreme southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana);
thus, the months beginning with Māgha are designated by the signs beginning with Capricorn (makara).
It is stated in that very [text]:
The Sun, situated in that Rāśi, initiates the month of Māgha;
likewise [he passes through] Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, and Taurus.
The Gemini sign has been described and questioned; six months are proclaimed within the zodiac signs:
Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, and Scorpio.
"And the Dhanus [constellation] is declared to be in the southern quarter, under the domain of Bhāskara (the Sun).
Likewise, it is stated by those who know the Āyurveda: "The six seasons are traditionally reckoned as consisting of two-month periods, beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa."
Likewise, according to the Nikhaṇḍukas: "Two months each constitute a season (*ṛtu*); three of those [seasons] make a year.
"The sun's two courses, northward and southward, constitute a year.

Regarding the lunar month, however, it begins with the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad), has its full moon (paurṇamāsī) conjoined with the asterism of Āṣāḍhā, and ends with the asterism of Māghā.
As it has been said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The month in which the full moon is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism is called Pauṣa;
Māgha and the other eleven months are defined in the same way.

Thus, those who follow the lunar system (*cāndra*) desire the month to end at the new moon (*darśa*), while the solar (*saura*) month is likewise determined by the Sun's transit through a zodiacal sign.
"When the sun is situated in Aries and so forth, whichever lunar month begins [at that time] is known as Caitra and the others, ending with that [lunar month].

Thus it is stated in the *Jyotiṣasaṃgraha*. Therefore, the lunar Āṣāḍha corresponds to Cancer (*karkaṭaka*), while the solar Āṣāḍha corresponds to the zodiac sign Gemini (*mithuna*). As it has been said:
The solar month and the lunar month are both to be specifically understood:
the lunar for the purpose of worldly transactions, and the solar for auspicious rites.

According to the injunctions of the astronomers (*jyotirvidaḥ*), among those [months] traditionally known as *saura*, the *pavitra* rite should be performed when the months beginning with Āṣāḍha have accumulated within the zodiac signs of Gemini, Cancer, and Leo. Prior to this, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed in the sign of Virgo. Furthermore, because of the rule "and in Libra, not even a drop," one should never perform it in the sign of Libra under any circumstances.

It must be performed. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement that it should be performed after Viṣṇu’s sleep and not before it, the time for that sleep is as follows: in a year devoid of an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), it is the twelfth day of the bright fortnight when the sun is in Gemini; however, in a year containing such an intercalary month, it is that same day when the sun is in Cancer. Thus, it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
Where two new moons occur devoid of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), that is to be known as an intercalary month (adhimāsa); Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
Thus it is said; and likewise in the Jyotiṣaśāstra:
"When the sun enters a new sign only after two new moons have passed, that is to be known as a *malamāsa* (intercalary month), excluded from all religious rites."
Having made a formal resolve for four months and having taken up residence in that place, [the food] was cooked.
However, their lack of restriction regarding actions consists in their acceptance of earth, ashes, and so forth.
"One should avoid this downward path; one should avoid [initiating] heavy [disciples] therein.
Even in times of distress, the five-night or three-night [observance] must be performed. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra* as well.
For four months, or three months, or two months, or even one month;
or for half a month, or seven nights, or five nights, or three days, or a single day.
"Or one should certainly cause the ritual action to reach its conclusion.
Thus it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati* that the *pavitra* (sacred thread) should be offered to Vahni, Brahmā, Ambikā, and the others on the lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*).
O Fire, Brahmā, Ambikā, Bhāsa, Vāk, Skanda, Arka, Irā, and Ilā;
O Durgā, Yama, Indra, Govinda, Smara, Śambhu, and likewise [the one] with eight arms.
The *pavitraka* rite must be performed for all these deities,
beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and proceeding in sequence until the fifteenth.
"In the bright fortnight for a householder, or in both fortnights during a vow.

Now, he states that the *pavitra* must be made according to the method prescribed in the scriptures, endowed with the specific number of threads, its width, and so forth: "Having prepared the *pavitra* as described."
Its specific nature is also recorded from another scripture: "The thread may be made of linen, cotton, or munja grass, or, if those are unavailable, [of other materials]."
Having gathered [grass] from *darbha* or from bark, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
Having tripled it and folded it three times, one should purify it with the *astra-mantra*.
Having dried it, the Guru should fashion the *pavitra* (purificatory ring) by means of the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Thus [it is said].
In the *Kāmika*: "Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* [it is said]:

'Silk, cotton, lotus-fiber, *darbha*, hemp, *mauñja* grass, and so forth—according to one's means; made by a virgin from among the twice-born and the like, or otherwise made with wealth and such, it is declared to be the most excellent and pure. [It may be] thick or thin..."
One should discard that which is knotted, broken, burnt, or defiled by impurities such as filth.
Having divided it threefold and tripled it, one should cast it as a single thread consisting of nine parts, [consecrating it] with the mantras beginning with Īśa.
One should know that the thread is prepared from a ball of wool dyed with lac, washed by a goat in milk, dried,

and then woven into a cord by a left-handed person using a blade. It is purified by the *ghora* mantra and colored red by a *puruṣa* mantra, and then [perfumed] at its knots with musk, sandalwood, saffron, and so forth, as well as with saffron from Kashmir, camphor, turmeric, and the like.
Or one should prepare the thread; it should be well-fumigated with the Īśāna mantra, kept concealed in its containers, and consecrated by the recitation of mantras.
Elsewhere, one should avoid from afar that which is impure or possessed of other defects.
It produces impure sin and, when consumed, brings fear of the king.
The gross [form] is said to cause disease; the subtle [form] causes the destruction of wealth;
the thread [of destiny] brings death; and when both are joined together, they destroy one's future state.
"The sacred thread (pavitraka) should consist of exactly one hundred and eight threads;
likewise, there may be three, half of that [sixty-four], twenty, or sevenfold.
The number of threads has not been stated for all liṅgas, beginning with the *svāyaṃbhuva*, in a general sense; however, in the *Somaśambhu-paddhati* and the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, it is said:
"The excellent [upper] purifier (*pavitra*) should consist of one hundred and eight threads; the middle one half of that, and the lowest one half of that."

Thus one should prepare the triad of purifiers (pavitra), as well as the Gaṅgāvatāra with one hundred and eight [threads]. On the hands and other limbs, the first purifier consists of twelve threads arranged in a twelve-threaded coil. In the Śivāgama, it is stated that for nine types of liṅgas, there are nine varieties ending with one hundred and eight [threads]. Likewise, in the Kāmika:
One hundred and eight of those threads is the most excellent of the excellent;
twelve more than that [one hundred and twenty] is for the twelve who are near him.
Then, or else, those who have attained perfection in other accomplishments (siddhis) and the like—
those of lesser age, those of the middle rank, and those characterized by their [specific] classes— are numbered in a sequence.

In the case of the Jyeṣṭha [liṅgas], the number of threads is considered to be that of the human [liṅgas] when they are found in self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅgas and the like, or in those made of stone, or even in those made of jewels.
Whether on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in a mandala, or on mobile or stationary images,
all the counts— whether even or odd— are to be gathered together.
O lords of sages, the householders’ attitude toward their family members and the gods is indeed equal; likewise, it is the same for those of meager means regarding the sectarian marks and such.
The threads increase one by one, starting from one, up to twelve;
the knots are equal in number to the threads, being smooth and containing a core.
"Or else, the knots may be of desired length, equal and situated everywhere.
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"The intervals between the knots of the purifiers (pavitra) should be made equal."
"Ten knots should be made, according to that same number.
Thus is stated the width and measurement of the purifiers (*pavitra*) in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"They should measure twelve finger-breadths in length, or eight finger-breadths in width."
The measurements for the width of the linga shall be four finger-breadths.
In the same way, the Piṇḍikā-sparśa [should be made]; the fourth is that presided over by the deity Sārpa;
the Gaṅgāvatāraka should be fashioned, which is most beautiful and supremely purifying.
Even in the *Bodhinī* commentary on that [text], it is stated:
"The circumference of the top of the *liṅga* is exactly like that of the *ātman*;
the circumference of the *vidyā-ātman* is likewise, minus two parts from that."
Therefore, that sacred thread called Śiva is deficient by two parts;
it is provided with ten or nine knots, equally spaced.

The space from the top of the head to the base of the pedestal should be made for all deities; or, in the case of Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Lokapālas, and others, it may be done according to what is available.
At every boundary of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), one should place a bull that follows behind the leader from its own limb;
it should be fashioned with all its joints intact, pervading all principles (tattvas).
A purifying thread (*pavitra*) consisting of nine strands should be prepared for the Guru and oneself;
and for the Śiva-pitcher and the *vardhānī* vessel, one consisting of twenty-seven strands.
The sacred thread for Heramba, the lord of the site, and the lineage of gurus;
[the offering] for Gṛhalokeśa and Lakṣmī, and for all the surrounding enclosures.
In the bell, the arghya vessel, the garlands, the vessels for the field-protectors (kṣetrapāla), and the images;
At the gatekeepers, the wealth [of the thread] should be made with eight finger-breadths;
likewise at the end of the twelve [fingers] for Bala, and eleven for the outer Bala.
"One should imagine all [the threads] as being fashioned from a single strand.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"In this manner, the purifier (pavitra) is prescribed for all the enclosures (āvṛtas)."
Only one [offering] each should be given to Caṇḍeśa and the Kṣetrapālas.
"One should encircle with three strands of thread the sacrificial hall, the place for the bull, the temples, the fire-shelters, and all the ritual implements.

Thus [it is said]. Now, having stated the procedure for the worship of the pavilion for the purpose of the preliminary consecration of the *pavitra*, he describes the rites to be performed prior to that.

By the words "on the seventh," and so forth: here, on the eighth day, one performs the worship of the *pavitra*; and on the seventh day, which is the day preceding that, one begins the consecration (*adhivāsana*). One should begin on the thirteenth day, [which precedes] the fourteenth.
Regarding the "occasional twilight rite" (*naimittikī saṃdhyā*): this refers to that which is performed on the occasion of the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the offering of the sacred thread).
As it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The twilight rite to be performed at the time of the *pavitrārohaṇa* is [so called] because of that specific occasion."
"Therefore, it is called occasional (*naimittikī*), not because it arises from an occasional act.

This means that one should perform the fivefold occasional *saṃdhyā* after having set aside the daily (*nitya*) *saṃdhyā*. For, according to the maxim "it is time that enjoins the ritual act, not the ritual act that enjoins the time," the daily *saṃdhyā* is indeed to be performed at the evening hour itself.

Immediately thereafter, for the purpose of donning the sacred thread (*pavitrādhivāsa*), the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) must be performed once again. By the very power of this procedure, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is also accomplished; however, the specific mention of "again" is for the sake of an extensive libation as prescribed in the venerable *Mṛgendra-tantra* and other scriptures, as follows:
Then, having sipped water again, the supreme guru [should worship] all those beginning with Brahmā— the five [faces], as well as the Vidyās and the Vidyēśvaras— with the tips of his fingers.
Meditating upon the lords of the principles within the maṇḍala of the end of time,
one should perform the libation with their names in the dative case, ending with *svāhā*.
Then, with the sacred thread hanging from their necks, they honored the sages.
He [established] Sanaka and the others, as well as Bhṛgu and the rest, along with the lords of their lineages and ancestral branches;
he established the kinsmen and others through the path of the youngest root and by means of the junctions of the lunar festivals.
Likewise, one should offer oblations to the fathers together with their wives, to the grandfathers, to the great-grandfathers, and indeed to the gurus, the water-givers, and the further ancestors.

"Brothers, friends, teachers, maternal grandfathers, and maternal uncles— [one should address] them by their personal names at the conclusion of the *svadhā* [offering], but not by their middle names. Thus, elsewhere, [are described] the nature of the sacrificial enclosure, the pavilion, and so forth, as well as the materials used as auxiliaries for the sacrifice.

We shall explain this more thoroughly in the sections on initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Regarding the specific nature of the substances, the author himself will state later in the passage beginning with "one should offer the limbs of the vow" (*vratacaryāṅgāni nivedayet*).
Because it was stated that [the deity] is between Indra and Agni, [the offering] is at that very spot belonging to the *vāstu* (site).

Having worshipped the Sun according to the method stated in such passages as, "Facing the east, one should worship the Sun during the daily obligatory rite" (Vanityoktavan-nityakarmani, p. 301), [one should perform] that [offering].

One should not perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) within the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), because it has been stated that the deities worshipped there remain until the conclusion of the rite. With the *praṇava* and *arghya* in hand—that is, with the general *arghya* in hand—one [addresses] the "doors" using the plural number because the pavilion has four doors; thus, the phrase "of those two branches" refers to the two door-posts.

Regarding the two jars situated at the sides of the [main] jar: at the western gate, one should worship Gaṇapati and the others upon the *ūrdhvodumbara* and other [limbs], as in the daily rite (*nityavat*).
In the verse "having offered a flower in the southwest" (*nai-ṛte puṣpaṃ datvā*), one should contemplate the *Vāstudeva* in the southwestern direction (*nai-ṛtyāṃ diśi*) as in the daily rite.

One should worship Brahmā. One should worship Vāstunātha in the southwest (Nairṛti), because it will be stated later in the section on the worship of the water-jars (kalaśa). Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi)—that is, having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) and so forth according to the method described in the section on daily worship (nityapūjā) ending with *vauṣaṭ*—...

Having performed the ritual actions ending with "one should consecrate by uttering the *śakti*-mantra" (p. 302), one should immediately thereafter perform the *aṅganyāsa*. According to Śaśinī, this is the *kālanyāsa* as previously described.
One should also perform for oneself the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*), beginning with Āditya, upon the upward-pointing head.

Internal worship (*antaryajana*) is internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*); offering (*havana*) is oblation (*homa*). One should also perform meditation (*dhyāna*) and absorption (*samādhi*) in the locations of the heart, the navel, and the *bindu*. Having protected the sacred space (*adhāma*) by means of the three claps of the hands (*tāla*) and so forth, this is the purification of the place (*sthānaśuddhi*).

Having performed the three *tāla* gestures as described in the *Prakaraṇa*, beginning with "having performed [the protection]" and ending with "one should contemplate the performed protection," one should also prepare the special *arghya*. He describes the making of the *Śivahasta* with the words "first the application of sandalwood paste"; its nature is explained in the *Dīkṣāprakaraṇa*: "Then, the right..."
He will explain this clearly with the words beginning "the palm of the hand" (*hastatala*). Now, he describes his own contemplation of Śiva:

"Śiva"—that is, the primordial omniscient one. He is both "primordial" (*ādi*) and the "omniscient one" (*sarvajña*) among all the gurus, such as Ananta and others; thus, he is the "primordial omniscient one. As they say: "The teacher even of the ancients."
Regarding the phrase "because it is not limited by time" (p.
303), he states what is to be performed immediately after the contemplation of Śiva: "the five products of the cow" (*pañcagavya*) is scattered.

The scattering of parched grains (*lāja*) and other items, as well as the placement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), should be understood from the section on initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*), even though they constitute the nature of the scattering (*vikira*). Now, regarding the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-saṃskāra*): "in the southwest" and so forth refers to those consecrations of which inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) is the first; thus, they are "inspection and the rest. Those [consecrations] which end with the four-footed [rite] are "inspection and the rest."

One should consecrate the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) to be described later, using the concluding verses of the four-line [mantras], and one should likewise consecrate the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Now, he describes the worship of the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*) and the prosperity-pitcher (*vardhanī*), together with the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Then, beginning with "In the northeast," etc., [he describes] the sesame seeds situated among all kinds of grains.

[The deity] is situated upon the seven grains known as mustard, mung bean, kuluttha, chickpea, and rice; [the deity is] facing west, that is, with his face directed toward the west. As it has been said: "The face [of the deity] in the jar and other vessels is indeed turned westward. This refers to the essential form of Śiva as the manifested image (*mūrti-bhūta*). Regarding the phrase "movable and immovable seat": the name "movable and immovable" (*calācala*) refers to the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāna-āsana*).

As it is stated further on: "The moving and unmoving seat [is worshipped] by means of the bull-seat; having fully worshipped with the lotuses of infinite dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, [the deity] is concealed. Thus, following the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), there is the *śivakumbha* (Śiva-vessel).

The Śiva-kumbha and the vardhanī should not be obstructed for the purpose of circumambulation. Subsequently, after the worship while seated in a steady posture (sthirāsana), the obstruction should be performed. This refers to when [the vardhanī] is situated in the south-southern direction of the Śiva-kumbha placed upon its southern base, remaining there in the same manner as the Śiva-kumbha, in seven ways.
The meaning is: [the vessel] filled with flowing water and adorned with mango sprouts and so forth.

"Going before the jar" (kumbhāgragāminīm) means that which goes in front of, or before, the jar—the Śiva-jar. "With an unbroken stream of milk" (avicchinnapayodharām) means an uninterrupted flow of water. "Firm seat" (sthirāsanam) refers to the Ādhāra-śakti and the rest.
Having conceptualized [the pedestal] ending with the seat of Śiva (śivāsana), one should place the forms of Śiva, the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), and the eyes upon it; then,
having worshipped from the invocation of Śiva (śivāvāhana) up to the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa), one should worship the Pāśupata weapon in the *vardhanī* vessel as before.
The ritual concluding with the *avabhṛtha* bath, up to its final completion, is called the "seat of the *vardhanī*"; this refers to the seat of the *astra-kumbha* (the weapon-vessel),
prior to which [offerings] are made to the elements (*bhūtas*) using a bundle of *kuśa* grass (*kuśa-kūrca*).

That from which all obstacles—without exception or remainder—have been driven away and dispelled by means of the mantras arising as missiles and weapons; that which is called the *brahmasthāna*, meaning the four-pada space situated in the center of the pavilion divided into eighty-one sections; in that [space], the altar (*vedikā*).

Having prepared the mandala there, one should worship Śiva within that mandala as well; for it is said that [Śiva] is the witness of all rites in the mandala and the protector of the sacrifice in the pitcher (*kalaśa*). "With divine vision" (*divyadṛṣṭyā*) refers to the gaze performed by the placement of the root mantra (*mūlamantra-nyāsa*). Regarding the phrase "having come to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit" (*kuṇḍa-sakāśam etya*), the word *kuṇḍa* [refers to the fire-pit].

We shall describe the nature of the *homakuṇḍa* (fire-pit) as well in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). "Puraskurvan" means making it the foremost part. Now follows the procedure for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the pit, beginning with the words "Therein," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "with the root [mantra] placed":

"Nirīkṣaṇa" (inspection) is said to be the gazing with an eye upon which the root mantra has been placed, for the purpose of warding off obstacles situated on the ground. One should perform that rite with the Śiva-mantra; "prokṣaṇa" and "tāḍana" refer to sprinkling and striking. Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is performed with the *patākā* mudrā using water; striking (*tāḍana*)—
One should perform the purification of the ground with the *sa-kuśa* (grass-tipped) *āmaya-aṅguli* (the "disease-finger") using the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,

in order to prevent the re-entry of the obstructing spirits (*vighnas*) who have been driven away. The sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*), which consists of throwing water upwards with the *sa-kuśa* raised palm (*uttāna-patākā*), should be performed with the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should perform it. "Digging" refers to the ritual act performed upon that ground to remove defects such as thorns and the like;
its gentle extraction is called "scattering. This is done so that the ground is free from worms, insects, snakes, and so forth.

Filling with pure clay is called "filling the work" (*karmapūraṇa*). Making the filled area free from depressions and elevations is "leveling" (*samīkaraṇa*). After that, [it is] by filling with water...
The softening of the earth, its sprinkling, its stabilization by means of a mallet or similar tools, and its pounding;
after stabilization, the scattering of dust upon that dried spot, which is sweeping;
and thereafter, the smearing with cow dung, which is plastering—these are the eight purificatory rites beginning with digging.

One should perform [the marking] with a sword, a weapon-mantra, or *kuśa* grass. Regarding the phrase "extending eastward": if the *hotṛ* priest stands facing the east, one should draw three lines within the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), beginning from the west and extending to the eastern direction; then, if a single line is drawn upon them starting from the south, together with that [line].

There are four lines. If it is situated facing north, one should draw three lines starting from the south and extending to the northern direction; then, if one line is drawn above them from the west to the eastern direction, together with that, there are four lines. This is the nature of the *nityahoma*.
It is written in the *Prakaraṇa* that it should be noted there; "on both sides" means on both flanks in the form of a trident (p.
In the center of the *kuṇḍa*, one should perform the destruction of the three *kuśa* blades and their transformation into a vajra. One should contemplate them as being firm like a vajra.

Within the center of the *kuṇḍa*, one should arrange one *darbha* blade each with its tip pointing east and its tip pointing north, thereby creating a crossroads—a fourfold path consisting of four routes in the four directions. This drawing of lines constitutes the "vajrification."
One should perform all three—the laying down of the crossroads and so forth—using only the *astra* mantra. As it has been said:

"Having gazed at the pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *śambhu* [mantra], having sprinkled it and struck it with the *astra*, having sprinkled it again with the *varma* and the *astra*, and having dug, cleared, and filled it..."
Then, having leveled it, sprinkled it, smoothed it, and wiped it clean;
having smeared it with plaster, fashioned the form of the digit (kalā), and clothed it;
One should draw three lines facing east with threads of triple-strand, or three lines facing north;
or else, one may do so in reverse order for the purpose of forming the vajra.
"Having performed the placement (nyāsa) at the crossroads, one should place the 'eye' (akṣa) upon the armor (varman). Thus it is said.
In the *Mṛgendrapaddhati* and likewise in the *Kāmika*:
"The gazing [at the site] is performed with the Śiva-mantra, and the sprinkling with the Astra-mantra.

Having said this and so forth: "The wise one should fashion the four lines, the arrangement of the vajras, and the arrangement of the *śṛṅgāṭaka* (triangular figure), all of this with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
Regarding "within the fire-pit" (*kuṇḍasyābhyantareti*): "within" (*abhyantara*) refers to the inner region, extending equally on all sides.

One should arrange a screen (*akṣapāṭa*) made of upright-pointed *kuśa* grass with the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*). Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the fourfold path (*catuṣpatha*),
[one should then worship] Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara.

In certain texts, for the sake of systematic arrangement (*saṃyoga*), the act of splitting the dice (*akṣapāṭana*) has been mentioned; having treated the form of the *kalā* and the worship of the *kalās* as one, it is stated that there are eighteen [categories] including the splitting of the dice.
If that were the case, the worship of the *kalās* should have been mentioned immediately after the conceptualization of the form of the *kalā*, rather than in the middle of the three sūtras.
Since the wearing [of the garment] is prescribed, both [the upper and lower garments] are indeed each [to be worn] individually; furthermore, since it has been stated that the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*),
like the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), undergoes eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and because the axle-board (*akṣapāṭa*) serves no purpose therein,
it is established that the axle-board is separate.

310) He states what is to be done immediately thereafter—namely, "in the middle": one should place in the middle, that is, in the center of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), a seat (*viṣṭara*) consisting of three blades of *kuśa* grass, fashioned with a *brahmagranthi* knot and measuring one span (*vitasti*).

Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara are the two aspects of Śiva and Śakti. As it has been said: "She is Vāgīśī, who is Gaurī; he is Maheśvara, the Lord of Speech. Therefore, one should meditate upon and worship that Vāgīśvara. Just as the dark form, fine garments, and other attributes of Vāgīśvarī have been described, so too one should meditate upon and worship Vāgīśvara. Thus it is said:

"Having placed the *viṣṭhara* (seat) made of the tip of *rudrākṣa* wood, one should place Vāgīśvarī; and likewise Vāgīśvara—that very body which is the form of Śivā. Thus [it is said]. Regarding "the instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth—the nature of the instrument has been explained in the section on the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
The method for producing fire from a sun-gem (*sūryakānta*) is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having spread out a black antelope skin upon a clean ground with a protective armor (*varman*),
one [produces] fire from a sun-gem when the rays of the sun are joined with the sun."

The fire sustained by a jewel-born [substance] arises; that too is praised. From a "twice-born" planet—that is, from a planet such as a Brāhmaṇa, or from a "good" planet (*sugraha*) endowed with virtuous conduct—from the "flesh-eating" portion (*kravyādāṃśa*). "Flesh-eating portion" means...
Regarding the portion for the *rakṣas*, it is said:

"One should divide that which is awakened, placed in a pure vessel, and blazing, into three parts according to the division of gods and asuras; one should cast the *rakṣa* portion into the southwest (*nirṛti*)."
"Having gathered [the fire] at the navel region"—gathering (*saṃmūhana*) is the concentrating in one place of the scattered fire by means of the *Śiva-mantra*.
"The covering of the garment"—the complete shrouding of the lower garment with the *Kavaca-mantra*.
With fuel produced from sacrificial trees. As it has been said:

Having kindled the fire there with dry wood from sacrificial trees, [and] having ensured it is free from hair, insects, and the like, one should thus establish the *garbhāgni*— the fire situated within the womb— and then perform the fanning of that fire located within the navel region of the embryo whose seed is situated therein.
Now, the purification of the lower garment consists of sipping water while reciting the *Hṛdaya* mantra.

Having performed the worship of the fire within the womb, one should bind a protection made of darbha grass for its preservation with the *śara* mantra; one should bind it upon the lotus-hand of the Goddess.
Thus, for the sake of the *garbhādhāna* rite, on account of the *garbhādhāna*,
one should offer five oblations with the *Hṛdaya-mantra* immediately after birth.

O God, the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) should be performed as a divine act; likewise, in the *puṃsavana* (rite for a male child) and others, worship must be performed preceded by the remembrance of Śiva in the form of Vāmadeva and so forth. However, it is stated in the *Mṛgendra-tantra* that at the offering of a drop of water, the reconnection with the individual soul (*jīva*) should be performed; yet, during the *puṃsavana*, one should deposit a drop of water upon a blade of *darbha* grass.

Intending it to be "living" (jīva), the person should offer [the oblation] through meditative visualization (bhāvanā). One should offer the visualization as the person; that is, by means of the crest (śikhā) alone—that is, by the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra) itself. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having offered three oblations with the crest alone, the arrangement of the faces and limbs is performed with a blade of darbha grass and the crest."
Some maintain that *niṣkramaṇa* (emergence), *niśśeṣakaraṇa* (rendering exhaustive), and *tacchodhana* (its purification) [are synonymous]. This has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Having performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the opening of the mouth, and the purification," so it is said. And in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The arrangement of the faces and limbs should be fashioned, as well as the extraction of the faces and the expiation."
