With a blade of *darbha* grass and a lock of hair, one should offer three oblations into the fire with the *jananārya*, *jātakarmanimitta*,
and *puruṣeṇa tatpuruṣeṇa* mantras. Once born, following the birth, the *jātakarman* rite is performed as before in the tenth month with the *nṛ* and *varma* mantras.
Having performed the ritual bath for the newborn fire to eliminate the impurities of the womb.
Having bathed with the *arghya* water, one should release the bracelet from the hand of the Goddess;
on the hand, however, one should mentally place a golden thread with the *varma* mantra.
Thus, "with tips pointing north-east"—this means that for the eastern and western girdles, the threads have their tips pointing north.
Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon the southern and northern girdles, one should likewise place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*).
In the case of a single girdle, one should wrap it around the waist;
in the case of two girdles, the second [should be wrapped] around the middle; and in the case of three girdles, [the same applies].

According to the statement "the outer [space] is sprinkled," one should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the grass seats (*viṣṭara*) upon the single girdle of a pit with one girdle, specifically below that girdle.
In a pit with two girdles, one should place the enclosing sticks on one girdle and the grass seats in the region below it.
In a pit with three girdles, however, one should place the enclosing sticks on the middle girdle and the grass seats on the girdle below that.
One should arrange the seats (*viṣṭharān*). Regarding the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, [the text] says "then" (*tataḥ*) and so forth:

having rotated them together with the *kuśa* grass—that is, having performed a circular movement all around—one should [touch] the tip of the *sruk* with the middle of the *kuśa*, the middle of the *sruva* with the middle of the *kuśa*, and the base [of both] with the root [of the *kuśa*].
The base of those two, the *sruk* and *sruva*, refers to the parts touched by the *kuśa* grass—the tips, middles, and roots.
Their necks are encircled by three threads; that is, their throats are wrapped with a triple-stranded thread. He now describes the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*).
(p. 315) Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth: "gavyam ājyam" means that which is produced from a cow is "gavya. Cow's ghee is said to be the best;
that produced from a buffalo is middling; and that ending with [the ghee of] goats is inferior. Therefore, [one should use] that which is derived from a cow.
"It is praised. Thus, "having purified by means of gazing and so forth. As it has been said:
"Having first taken the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī), one should sprinkle it with water from the weapon-mantra (astra)."
Having poured clarified butter into it, it is consecrated by means of the rites of inspection and so forth.
Thus it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), and pouring over (*abhyukṣaṇa*) are meant.

Since whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and heating (*tāpana*) and so forth are mentioned later on, the clarified butter (*ājya*) also undergoes eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). As it was said by the Teachers: "The four [rites] beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*), and that whirling in the fire three times."
The heating, the removal from the support, the leaping up, as well as the immersion,
the Pūtanā-rite, the lustration, the illumination, the mantra-illumination, and the consultation.
"Protection, veiling, the palace, and ghee—the tenfold consecration.
316) Thus, following the four consecrations beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*), there is one threefold circumambulation above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Immediately thereafter, the offering of drops of clarified butter (ājyabindudāna) for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra consists of three purificatory rites known as heating (tāpana), placing on the fire (adhiśraya), and removing from the fire (udvāsa). As it has been said:
"Having meditated upon one's own form as consisting of Brahman and having taken [the vessel] from the tips of the kuśa grass..."
One should offer a drop to Brahmā with the heart-mantra, ending with "svāhā."
That is declared to be the *tāpana* [oblation]; then, having placed clarified butter in the northeast corner, one should likewise offer it to Viṣṇu, who is composed of his own [essence].
Thus has the placing upon the fire been described; having likewise placed clarified butter at the navel, Rudra should offer that to Rudra—this is declared to be the rite of dismissal (udvāsana).
In some traditions, this triad is taught by means of the *hṛdaya*, *śiras*, *śikhā*, and so forth.

Thus, one should cause [the fire] to overflow three times while facing the fire; this is called *utplavana* (overflowing). Likewise, [causing it to overflow] while facing oneself is called *saṃplavana* (converging overflow). [This is done] with clarified butter over which a flaming blade of *darbha* grass, consecrated with the *hṛdaya* mantra, has been cast by means of the *astra* mantra.

By casting [the grass] away, there is one rite called *pavitrīkaraṇa* (purification). By means of another blazing blade of *darbha*, two rites are stated: that which is called *nīrājanā* (lustration) by "another blazing [blade]," and that which is called *saṃdīpanā* (ignition) by "by the subsequent blazing [blade]. [The word] *dagdha*...
The flames emerging from the *darbha* grass are called "the firebrand" (*ulmuka*) or by the name "meteor" (*ulkā*). As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:

"Then, having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) with clarified butter, the wise one should cast the firebrand into the fire. This is the ritual known as "Illumination of the Mantra" (*mantradyotana*), and so forth.
Thereafter, in due order from right to left, [he should place] Piṅgalā on his own right side.

One should contemplate the bright fortnight as being on the left side and the dark fortnight likewise as *iḍā*. Having taken clarified butter from the left side, one should offer it into the left eye of the Fire with the mantra "svāhā to Soma. For the sake of the clarified butter, having offered a little into the black-pathed fire with "svāhā," one should [offer] the remainder of the clarified butter with "ha" and "ājya"; here, in this context concerning the *caru*, [the procedure is as follows].

The method for the *saṃpātāhuti* offerings to be described hereafter should be performed. Regarding the phrase "in the dark fortnight" (on page 318), the sequence beginning with "to Soma, svāhā" and so forth, which was previously performed starting from the left side, should now be done in reverse order. This has been stated:
In the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"The white and black fortnights are the two wings in the right and left portions [of the body];
one should meditate upon the iḍā and piṅgalā there, with the suṣumnā between them."
Four oblations should be offered as the *saṃpāta*; the deities for them are Agni, Soma, Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt, and the fourth is Sviṣṭakṛt.
The Śambaras, beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), containing their respective seed-syllables, and ending with Svāhā,
should be offered in sequence into the three eyes and the mouth of Agni for the purpose of awakening him.
Taking clarified butter from the southern portion,
one should offer it into the right eye of the Fire with the mantra "agnaye svāhā," for the purpose of the clarified butter, into the one whose path is black.
Having offered the remainder of the clarified butter with the *hetu* mantra, one should cast it into the left (or right) portion.
Then, taking clarified butter from the middle of the vessel, one should offer it into the middle eye of the Fire-god (*Kṛśānu*).
One should offer oblations into the fire for the sake of clarified butter with the mantra "To Agni and Soma, Svāhā," while reciting the *uṣabudhi*.
One should pour the clarified butter from the middle [of the ladle] with the sound "Ha," and the remainder of what has been offered remains in the *sruva* spoon.
Taking from the south, the north, and the middle of the clarified butter, that ghee is drawn out.

One should offer half of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into the fire with the mantra "vahnivaktregnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā," and the remaining third portion of the ghee with the mantra "heti. This rule applies during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*); in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the order is reversed.

One should offer four oblations in this manner with the residual ghee (*saṃpātājya*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*): to Soma, to Agni, and to both of them, [offering] to the left of the fire and above it. Having consecrated [the offering] with the *saṃhitā* [mantras], this consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), protection (*rakṣā*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) [are performed].

The eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) are said to be together with the instruments (*karaṇas*). Having thus described the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*), [the author] speaks of the oblations to the faces (*vaktrāghāra*), the connection between the faces (*vaktrānusandhāna*), and the unification of the faces (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*) and so forth, starting with the words "then" (*tataḥ*) and so on.
The term "support" (*ādhāra*) refers to the five faces of the fire, seated upon a white lotus throne.

He will state this with the words beginning "five-faced" (*pañcavaktra*) and so forth. For those faces, in the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta, each one serves as the support for the kindling of the oblation. This has been stated in the *Ṣaḍgrahasrikā* (p.
"From the western direction up to the lord of the [northeastern] quarter, by means of the application of oblations with one's own mantra, there is the sprinkling of the faces;
this is the excellent illumination of the faces of Kṛśānu.
Thus it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
One should offer clarified butter with the *sadyojāta* mantra into the western mouth of the Fire;
having offered it into the eastern mouth with the *vāmadeva* mantra, one should then offer it into the southern mouth with the *bahurūpa* mantra.

With the mantra of Īśāna, one should perform the sprinkling with ghee— either with each individual oblation or with three combined— into the mouth of the male [deity] as before, and upwards into his face.

Thus, for the purpose of unifying the faces, there is the offering of a single oblation into the *catuḥghora* fire, which constitutes the joining of the faces (*vaktrasandhāna*). As it is stated in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"The rite of unifying the faces is accompanied by the three supports."
With these two [lines], one should perform [the drawing] situated between the two, namely the eastern and northern [sides].
And one [face] is situated in the southeast and northwest;
the other two are located in the southwest and northeast corners, respectively, by means of the Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Aghora faces.
Regarding the phrase "by the *Śivanaiśāna* mantra" (p.
in its commentary it is explained as "endowed with the three supports" (*ādhāratrayānvita*), which refers to the oblation of the supports (*ādhārāhuti*) consisting of those three.

By the passage beginning with "endowed with that, brought about by two by two," it is meant that those faces situated in the four directions must have one union performed by the two, Sadyojāta and Aghora;
a second by Vāmadeva and Tatpuruṣa; and subsequently, [a third] by the two in the northeast.
The junction between the two faces consists of three lines in the middle, situated between the east and north;
and there is one [line] extending toward the southeast and northwest, according to the sūtra. Thus, the eastern face is Tatpuruṣa and the northern is Vāmadeva;
by means of that Tatpuruṣa and Vāmadeva, one junction is to be made. Another is with Aghora and Sadyojāta at the top.

"With Śiva" means with the Īśāna mantra; "with two" is understood to follow. Thus, by this [mantra], one should join [the lines] in this very sequence and order. What is meant by this? Having joined the sets of four lines at the four faces in the four directions.
It has been explained that one should subsequently effect the unification of the faces by means of two lines in the western direction;
this refers to the establishment of non-duality for the purpose of realizing the intended identity within a single face among the five faces.
The unification with that [deity’s] face occurs because a difference in results is heard to arise from a difference in faces;
thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"In the daily rite (*nityakarman*), in the consecration of disciples, and in that which is called the observance (*samaya*)."
One should meditate upon all beings as being within the mouth of Sadyojāta.
Likewise, for attraction, pacification, subjugation, nourishment, the purification of bonds,
and for the sake of good fortune, prosperity, wealth, and so forth, one should likewise employ the face of Vāmadeva.
The wise practitioner should fashion other faces within [the central one] for the purposes of killing,
paralyzing, inciting hatred, expelling, and the purification of sins.
One should contemplate other beings within the face of Aghora;
[one should contemplate] the medicinal pill, the collyrium, [and so forth], in the netherworld and in the birth of the disciple.
One should contemplate various accomplishments (*siddhi*) and so forth within the face of Puruṣa;
one should contemplate that liberation is included within the face of Īśāna.
Having thus performed the conjunction of the sprinkling of the faces either in the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta or in the sequence beginning with Īśāna,

one should perform the unification of the faces specifically in the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta. Even there, having placed the face designated by oneself in the position of Īśāna and visualizing the face of Īśāna in its place, [one should contemplate] that which is designated by oneself...

One should fashion the mouth [of the fire-pit] according to the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*; or else, having remembered the mouth as the measurement of the *kuṇḍa* according to one's own preference, one should contemplate that all other faces are contained within it. And so it is said in the *Kālottara*:
One should perform the sprinkling and joining of the mouth with the *Sadyojāta* and other *Śambhava-mantras*;
thereafter, one who knows the ritual should effect their non-duality through the *Vaiśvānara* and other mantras.
Having meditated upon the five faces according to the fire-ritual by which any rite was performed,
one should place that face at the top, with its mouth directed upward in that position.
The other faces are included within it, and that [mandala] is equal in measure to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
or else, one should visualize that which has the desired number of faces as being the measure of the pit.
The other faces are included within it; the unification with that [central face] is what is intended.

Thus it is said. And in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "One should pour a stream of ghee from the five faces, beginning with Sadyojāta; starting from the southeast corner, that [stream] should extend as far as the northwest corner."
Starting from the corner of Nirṛti and extending to the corner of Rudra,
one should effect the unification of the faces with an uninterrupted stream of clarified butter.
One should recollect the other [dimensions] according to the measurement of the desired sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus, as it is said:

"Though she is one, she possesses many forms and bestows the fruits of all desires. Since it has been stated that her tongues are manifold, one should remember that the other faces are included within the face of Īśāna; [therefore, she] bestows the fruits spoken of by each respective face.

Even when performing [the entire rite], one should contemplate it as belonging specifically to the face of Īśāna. In this context, as an incidental matter, one should perform the kindling of the tongues [of fire] by offering oblations one by one.

"Having joined them two by two, one should lead [the fire] into dissolution in the middle"— thus say some who delight in elaboration. Others say that by means of the unification of the faces, one should perform the joining and unification of the upward-facing mouth and the seven tongues, such as Hiraṇyā and the rest, with their respective mantras and the sprinkling of the tongues.
That mantra is as follows: "The final two groups [of consonants] without the letter *ra*, joined with the sixth vowel and endowed with *bindu* and *nāda*;
these are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the tongue in sequence.
The meaning of this is: "without *ra*" means devoid of the letter *ra*; "the final two groups" refers to the *ya*-group and the *śa*-group; thus, [the syllables are] *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *śa*.

The *ṣa-sahs* are thus described: the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *ha*, when accompanied by the sixth vowel—the sixth vowel being *ū*—and joined with the *repha* (the letter *r*) as the sixth and the *svara* (vowel) followed by the *bindu* (anusvāra), result in the application:
*dhrūṃ*, *lrūṃ*, *hiraṇyāyai svāhā*.

326) Now, with the words beginning with "tataḥ" (then), he describes the rites to be performed immediately after the consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*). For the purpose of the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), that is, as the occasion for the naming, [one should worship] Īśāna with the Īśāna mantra, or Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara with the Heart mantra.

In this context, with the heart [mantra] joined with the heart-mantra, namely *oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ* and so forth, one should contemplate the measurement of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), that is, the dimensions of the pit, as it has been specified. Whichever face of the pit the practitioner desires for the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should visualize that face as the width of the pit. Regarding the phrase "in the middle tongue," here [the tongue] is Kanakā.
Then follows Bahurūpā and Atiraktā;
Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, and another Raktā who is golden—
these three are situated at the upper face, while the remaining ones are positioned starting from the east in sequence.
"Abiding," according to the statement in the *Kāmika*,

means abiding in the upward-facing [face], specifically in the middle of the three tongues, on the tongue called Bahurūpā. "Beginning with the topknot (*cūḍā*)" refers to the topknot— the rite of tonsure (*caulakarma*)— and those other purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*).
"In order to bring about satisfaction and for the perfection of the remaining consecrations, one should subsequently cause the *pūrṇāhuti* to be offered"— thus it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Having given him the name Śivāgni and offered oblations,
one should perform the dismissal of the parents, as well as the tonsure, initiation, and other rites.

"Then, having performed the sacrament at the conclusion of the marriage," so it is stated in the *Vāyavī-saṃhitā*. "For the sake of accomplishing the sacraments such as the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) and the tonsure (*cūḍā*), one should then perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) upon the tongue situated in the center," so it is stated in the *Kāmika*. Therefore, [the rites] beginning with the tonsure...

The *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) is established for the sake of completing the rites concluding the marriage ceremony. Wherever the *pūrṇāhuti* is performed with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should perform it specifically with the *vauṣaṭ* ending. Thus, it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
"In the *homa*, there should be the utterance of *svāhā*; however, for the *pūrṇāhuti*, it should end in *vauṣaṭ*."
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"The wise one [should perform the rite] with the mantra preceded by Oṃ and ending with Svāhā. (p. 328)
At the conclusion of each *svāhā*, one should offer oblations to the mantras and their deities while reciting them.
"The full oblation, however, is performed with the word 'vauṣaṭ' at its end. Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should perform the offering of the complete oblation accompanied by dhāraṇā;
O child, one should mentally visualize the supreme nectar flowing [downward]."

The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra repeatedly for each full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); he should then remember [the formula] ending with *vauṣaṭ*: "This is nectar; may it be yours again. This was stated in that very same place by means of the root-mantra of Śiva: "At the time of the fire sacrifice, the Śiva-mantra of Śiva is prescribed."

Regarding the phrase "by the offering of the final oblation" (*saṃpūrṇāhutidānena*): it has been stated in that very [text] that the accomplishment of the fruit for the practitioner occurs at the time of the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) through specific meditative visualizations (*bhāvanā*) directed toward each respective mantra.
Having offered one's mind to the mantra, one whose body is adorned by the mantra...
With a single-pointed mind and having attained identity with the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should perform the fire-oblation;
indeed, he who thus offers oblations should recite the mantra with full concentration.
One who is merged into the supreme reality of sound shall become a partaker of the fruit of perfection.

Thus, [the meaning is that] they utter the mantra preceded by the contemplation of its dissolution into its own cause, according to the principle that "the essence of sound is dissolved in the Supreme. He states what must be done immediately after the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the words beginning "for the sake of the sacrificial pap" (caru), etc.

For the sake of the *caru* and so forth—that is, for the sake of cooking the *caru* and the like; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is stated that if there is another sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the dismissal (*visarjana*) should be performed for its sake as well as for the sake of incense and lamps.
Thus, it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
For the purpose of chewing [betel], for incense and lamps, and for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa) in the collection of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
one should extract the fire from the pit and perform each respective rite.
Thus, having performed the collection of fire from the other pit in the sequence starting from the east, and having cast it into the respective pits situated in those directions—

One should perform the oblation (*homayet*). He describes the meditation on the Śiva-fire with the words beginning "seated upon a white lotus-throne" and so forth. Now, [it is said]: "It has two faces and one heart, four ears, two nostrils, six eyes, is tawny, adorned with seven hands, and possesses three girdles."
Having three legs and a beautiful forehead, endowed with seven tongues,
possessing four horns, mounted upon a bull, and equal in radiance to the various suns.
He was endowed with the sacred thread and adorned with a crown of matted hair.
On the right side he has four hands and on the left side three hands;
with his right hands he holds the sacrificial ladle (sruk), the spoon (sruva), a rosary (akṣamālā), and a spear (śakti).
A spear and a fan with his right hands, and a vessel of clarified butter with his left hands.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, and Kṛṣṇā are on the right face;
Suprabhā and Atiraktā are on the left face, O you of many forms.
One should meditate upon that Śivāgni, facing west, situated in the midst of the fire;
thus is the Śivāgni renowned in the Śiva Āgama.
(Thus, on p. 331) the nature of the Śiva-fire is declared in another Āgama.
Here, how is it that the form with five faces and four arms is true, while the form with two faces and so forth is optional?

This has been established as the object [of meditation] in the *Suprabheda*. Thus, a skilled instructor should visualize the form of Agni in this manner for rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*); however, for obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, he should specifically visualize the five-faced form.
Thus it is said. However, in the *Kāmika*, the nature of the Vedic fire is described as follows:
"Henceforth I shall explain the sequence of the ritual procedures for the fire-offering (*agnikārya*). The fire-offering is traditionally held to be threefold: Vedic, mixed, and [Tantric]."
That which is prescribed solely by Vedic mantras is called Vedic;
that which is prescribed by auspicious Vedic mantras along with others is called mixed.
In the Śiva scripture, this sequence for the production [of the fire] is thus prescribed:
that which is joined with three enclosures above and with two fuel-sticks.
The Vedic fire is thus designated, while the mixed fire possesses the nature of both.
The *praṇītā* vessel, when joined with the *brahmakūrca*, is declared by the Vedic tradition;
likewise, the mixed fire (*miśravahni*) is the Śaiva fire, and when joined with that, it is new.
O learned ones, hear the true nature of the two fires, Miśra and Vaidika:
he is endowed with a single body, yet possesses two faces and two nostrils.

Having described the nature of the Vaidika and Miśra fires from the beginning up to the end of the passage "thus the location of the tongue is proclaimed," the Śaiva fire is subsequently described: "O Brahmins, listen with concentrated minds;
[it is] endowed with five faces, red in color, and resplendent with seven tongues. By these words, the nature of the Śiva-fire is stated.

Therefore, meditation on the essential nature (*svarūpa-dhyāna*) according to the method described in the *Paddhati* is superior for the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and other rites.
Now, he describes the manner of worshipping Śiva in the fire with the words beginning "O Fire, you... and so forth; it is "pertaining to Īśvara" (*aiśvaram*), meaning related to Īśvara.
Because it has been stated [in the passage] beginning with "having meditated on the seed-syllable of Śiva" (p. 333) that Vāgīśī is produced through effort,
[the phrase] "having entered the middle of the body" (*vigrahamadhyam*)— that is, the middle of the physical frame— refers here to her entry via the *iḍā* channel.

The act of entry [is performed] into his heart-lotus; there, in the heart-lotus connected with his fire, one should worship the Lord (Bhāskara), the Supreme Lord, the radiant one, together with his seat— the seat beginning with Ādhāra-śakti and ending with Śiva— as previously described in the section on worship, according to the influence of the limiting adjuncts of the substratum.

Since it is stated that "He is red-colored, his body is red, he has three eyes, and his arms are endowed with the weapons of Śiva," one should worship him together with his enclosures (sāvaraṇam), accompanied by the surrounding deities. This is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Then, having entered that form through the channel and worshipped Śaṅkara in the heart, one should unite [the self] with Him"—and likewise:
In the Kāmika:
Having thus petitioned [the deity], one should then place his seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) within the lotus of the heart and fashion the radiant form, which is both supreme and non-supreme.
Having brought about the presence [of the deity] within that [image] by means of invocation and other rites, one should worship the cause;
then, having worshipped it externally, one should worship the limbs of its enjoyment.
Having meditated upon the luminous [deities] individually, according to their respective bases and attributes.

Having inspired [the disciple] and rendered him supreme, and having effected the union of the fire of Śiva’s mouth with his own mouth— having thus issued forth from the form of the fire and come outside— he explains the sequence of the union of the channels (*nāḍī*).
By the passage beginning with "uttering the root mantra" (*mūlamantramuccaran*) and so forth:

"Vahni-stha" means he who dwells in the fire; that [fire] is Śiva, thus he is Vahni-stha-Śiva. His nose has emerged from the nose; she whose form is precisely that which has emerged from the nose is "Jyotirūpā," and she is also the Crest (*śikhā*).

The crest of light has emerged from the nose, and thus it is called the "crest of light. Here, by the word *śikhā*, the *suṣumṇā* is meant. [She] is merged with the crest of Śiva who resides in the sacrifice; that is, she has become one with the crest of that Śiva who resides in the sacrifice and stands within the mandala.
(On page 335:

By the term *raśmi*, "ray," luster (*kānti*) is meant. To that extent, by the non-separation (*aviyoga*)—that is, by the inseparable union (*saṃyoga*)—of the mantras, [the luster is] uninterrupted (*avichinnā*) and undivided (*abhinnā*).
One should meditate upon her as having taken up residence—that is, having made her dwelling—in both places: in the fire and in the mandala.
As it has been said:
"The deity worshipped in the fire [is one with] Śiva worshipped in the mandala."
"Then one should join [the breath] by means of the procedure consisting of the union of the channels.

Thus, according to the manner described, [one joins it] with the jar, sacrifice, fire, and Śiva; here, by the word "jar" (kumbha), both the jar of Śiva and the weapon-jar are meant. By the word "sacrifice" (yāga), the mandala is meant. [This applies] to the jar, the sacrificial ground, and the fire.
One should perform the union of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna) together with one's own self and the worshipped Śivas. As it is stated in the Parākhyatantra:
"When the sacrifice to Śiva has begun, Śiva resides as the fifty-fold [deity]."
He is situated in the knife, in the water-pot, in the fire, and established upon the sacrificial ground.
And this entire [deity] residing in the five states, situated within the Guide (Deśika), is the liberator from bonds.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
One should meditate on the auspicious Suṣumnā, which has emerged from one's own body, appearing as a trembling, radiant light, united with Śiva, and then returning once more into oneself.

In the same way, let it be joined again with the Lord residing in the fire by means of the mantras beginning with "ātmasthām" for the purpose of libation; such is the case regarding these general mantras.
For the purpose of general libation (*tarpaṇa*), for the purpose of specific libation, for the purpose of special libation, and for the purpose of the satisfaction of the mantras—
the word "and" (*ca*) here indicates that one hundred and eight oblations (*homa*) should also be performed.
Having prescribed one hundred oblations with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) for each of the general and specific libations, [this concludes] the initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Because it will be explained in the relevant section (*prakaraṇa*). Regarding "the place and the time": this is for the purpose of accomplishing the prescribed place and time for the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) as stated in the scriptures, even if there is some slight deficiency or excess therein.

337) In that regard, should an ill omen occur, one should perform one hundred oblations for each [deity] for the purpose of averting it and for the purpose of bringing about a good omen. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of making [the rite] pure," this includes the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth, up to this point.

Since the *dīkṣā* is common to all rites up to their conclusion, including the *pratiṣṭhā*, from this point forward it must be performed with each respective rite as its objective; for here, the *pavitra* being the subject at hand, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) for the purpose of performing those various acts. Immediately thereafter, [one offers] the *saṃhitā-mantras*. Its...
One should perform the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) by offering individual oblations ending in *svāhā* at the beginning of that ritual action;
one should also perform the kindling (*dīpana*) with three oblations ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. The procedure for this is exactly as described in the *Paddhati*.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "One should perform the satiation of the Śabaras, beginning with the crest-lock (śikhā) and ending with the weapon (śastra),
once with clarified butter, preceded by the Praṇava and followed by 'svāhā'."

One should perform the "kindling" (dīpana) with mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), containing the seed-syllable of the *śikhā* between two [other] seed-syllables, ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and being in the dative case.

Now he describes the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking) with the words beginning with "tataḥ" and so forth. "Sthālīm" means a vessel for the *caru* offering; it should be free from defects such as cracks in the rim or loose joints, and it must not have been previously used—meaning it should be devoid of that which has been used or is old. These two qualifying attributes refer specifically to earthen vessels, extending up to those made of copper.
Because that has already been stated. Likewise, in the *Kāmika-tantra*, in the chapter on the procedure for the food offering (*naivedya*):
"One should prepare a pure vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or the like, which lasts until the end of the dissolution (*layāntika*), or even a new earthenware pot, at each junction of the day."
"Thus, the *caru* should be well-cooked, neither too slow nor lacking in heat. It should be cooked in such a manner as is possible;
for a penance is prescribed for being too slow or too intense, and a fault is heard of [in the scriptures] in such cases. By the word *caru*, food containing rice grains inside is meant.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"That which remains inside like the kernel of rice is called the *caru*; for its successful preparation, [the mantra] ending in *svāhā* is used."

In the phrase *saṃhitatha*, there are mantras such as *oṃ hāṃ susvinno bhava svāhā* and *oṃ hiṃ susvinno bhava svāhā*, etc., which are like the *saṃpātāhuti* (dropping-off oblations) to be mentioned later. Regarding the drop of clarified butter (*ājya-bindu*) thrown into the fire—where *svā* is in the fire and *ha* is in the clarified butter—the name for this heated pouring is *taptābhighāra*. [The mantra is: *oṃ hāṃ suśītalo bhava auṣaṭ*.
Thus, that which has been prepared is designated as "cold sprinkling" (*śītābhidhāra*). Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:
"One should cook it as before so that it becomes medium-cooked;
when it is hot, there should be 'hot sprinkling' (*taptābhidhāra*), and when it is cold, 'cold sprinkling' (*śītābhidhāraṇa*)."
"O carrier of the oblation to Śiva, by your own will and through the power of the mantra,
become well-sweated at the conclusion of the offering, for you are the cause [of this]."
In this manner, [the rite] named Taptābhidhāra should take place in the second mandala; then,
once it has been joined with the sprinkling and other rites and duly worshipped, let [the disciple] be initiated.
"Be very cool," thus [one says] with the word *vauṣaṭ* accompanied by a sprout.

"In this way, one should [perform] the rite called *śītā* upon the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the collection of mantras. Thus, having placed whatever substance is to be consecrated—such as the *pavitra* and so forth, which will be described later—upon the fire with the mantra "svāhā," one should cast it down by shaking and moving the *sruva* spoon over it; that is, one should throw it in.
Thus it has been said:
"One should perform the *saṃpāta-homa* with clarified butter over the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) using the *saṃhitā* formula ending in *svāhā*,
pouring it into the fire with the *sruva* ladle for the sake of the clarified butter, saying *svāhā*."
The remaining clarified butter (*ājya*) and the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) should be poured into the *heti* [ladle]; this is the sequence.

Having resolved upon three portions—one for the offering to Śiva, one for the fire-oblation (*homa*), and one for oneself—having thus divided it into three parts, one should offer the portion for oneself with clarified butter alone, while the two portions for Śiva and the fire are [to be offered] with ghee.
One should mix it with honey.
Then, one should divide the cooked rice (*caru*) placed in the vessel into three parts using a *darbha* blade.
Taking one part of that, which has been worshipped with the heart-mantra in the vessel, [one should proceed].

One should offer a portion to Śambhu, to the one stationed on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and to the one situated in the water-pot (kumbha); likewise, one should give a supreme share to the Weapon (astra) stationed in the scissors (kartarī), and to Citrā in the northeast (vasu).
The wise one should offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle into the fire established for Śiva;
having placed the remains of the offering back into the vessel, he should stir it.
Because it is to be offered to Śiva, the Kumbha, and others;

having divided the portion intended for Śiva into five parts: three parts are for Śiva—who is worshipped in the sacrificial hall together with the Sun, the door-keepers, and others, and who holds the water-pot (kalaśa), the razor (kartarī), the mandala, and so forth in his hands—and [one part each] for one's own chosen liṅga and other deities.
Having given one part to the one stationed at the *karaṇa*, the remainder should be offered at the time of the *vṛtāṅga* offering.
Likewise, having divided the portion for Agni into four parts, one part [should be offered] after the offering of the *caru* to the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśvara*).

Having taken [the portion] for the purpose of offering to Śiva residing in the fire, one should give the second *anna* as the internal *bali*. Having given that third [portion] into the fire at the time of the *pavitrāropaṇa*, the *bali* should be offered with the fourth [portion]. Likewise, one's own portion [should be offered] to one's own self.
Having divided [the offering] according to the number of disciples, one should partake of it together with them at the conclusion of the ritual—this is the meaning of the statement:

"The *caru*, clarified butter, fragrance, and so forth, in the eastern [direction]. Then, regarding the two statements to be mentioned later—"having taken a third portion of the *caru* for the Blessed One established in the fire"—the teachers maintain that these serve as indicators (*sūcaka*).

He states what is to be done immediately thereafter with the words beginning "then" (*tataḥ*). "Then," meaning after the *sthālīpāka* offering, [the phrase] "in the nine-threaded [strands]" (*tantu-navakeṣu*) means "in the nine threads contained within the cord" (*sūtra*), because of the rule that a "thread" (*tan-tu*) is a single cord made by tripling three [threads]. In the knots—namely, the nine knots of the *pavitra*—one should likewise [perform the rite] according to their respective names as before.
Regarding the instruction "one should place [the mantra]," one should place it with [the name] in the dative case, preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and a salutation (*namaskāra*).
This refers to the knots located on the three bracelets, because the descent of the Gaṅgā has already been described and will be described again later.
One should perform the *nyāsa* of the sacred thread named *Gaṅgāvatāraka*, which is the very nature of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*).

Upon the eighteen knots situated on that sacred thread, one should place the sixteen digits (*kalā*) belonging to the *Prāsāda-mantra* (the sixteenth) and the two-fold union of Śiva and Śakti (the thirty-second). In the case of the alternative method where the knots are made according to the number of strands (*tantu*), these same [digits] are to be placed.
The *kalās* should be placed by rotating them again and again, either partially or in their entirety, as appropriate.

Regarding "the fourfold mandala": this refers to the fourfold mandala of Sūrya, Soma, Agni, and Śakti, together with their respective presiding deities (*sādhipati*), just as in the case of the purifiers known as the principles (*tattvas*) of Vidya, Śiva, and the three mandalas.
One should worship [the deity] in the sacred *Gaṅgāvatāra* [festival], which consists of the year—that is, that whose essence is the year. To explain: from the ancient Āṣāḍha until the second Āṣāḍha.

The witness of the propitiations and those who perform them, such as the twilight rituals; the imperishable, perfect protector; the guardian of the fruits of all actions; the refuge, that which serves as the support.

Recalling Śiva—the cause for attaining the fruits of one's actions and the basis for the attainment of those fruits—within the heart, in the *śivaliṅga*, and in the fire; and [recalling] that which is joined with fragrances such as musk in the verse beginning "gandhapavitra" (*Gandhapavitram*), as well as in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Musk, sandalwood, jasmine, camphor, *takkola*, cloves, and *koṣṭha*..."

"Uśīra, cardamom, nutmeg, iron filings, three palas of saffron, and red sandalwood—having ground these into a powder and mixed with fragrant substances, one should smear it over the *liṅgas* with the *Śivasaṃvara* [mantra].
A thread smeared with that very same fragrance is called the 'Fragrant Purifier' (*gandhapavitraka*). Thus it is said.

(345) The name "Sūrya" is distinguished; the invocation accompanied by the name "Sūrya"— consisting of the words of invocation to be mentioned later, beginning with *oṃ samastavidhi vicchidra pūraṇe ca* and so forth— is [to be applied] here in place of the word *śambho*.

Recite "Sūrya" and proceed. With the root mantra of Sūrya (*tanmūla-sūryamūlamantra*), one should offer the purifier (*pavitra*) to his limbs and to the planets (*graha*)—to the planets such as Soma and others—with their respective mantras (*svasvamantrais-tattanmantraiḥ*). These limbs, beginning with the heart (*hṛdayādi*), have been purified in the directions starting from the southeast (*āgneyādiṣu*). [Offer it] near the deity, the Śiva-liṅga.
Nearby. Now, the method for presenting the materials that are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the vow (*vrata*): "One should present the constituent parts of the vow-observance," and so forth.

This collection of materials useful for the vow—such as the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), earth, ash, water, the products of the cow (*gavya*), substances for the fire-oblation (*homa*), the staff, the rosary (*akṣasūtra*), and so on—which constitutes a part of the vow, should be offered for the sake of increasing the efficacy of the vow. *Rocanā*.
"Saffron, betel, and other such articles of enjoyment should be given for the increase of enjoyment"— this is stated in the *Durbodhapadabodhinī* (p.

In the *Mṛgendra-ṭīkā*, however, it is stated that while these aforementioned materials are for the benefit of the practitioner, all other substances should be offered for the satisfaction of the respective directional deities (*digdevatā*). Next, he describes the method for the invocation of the deity and the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitra*) with the verse beginning "scented with perfumes and so forth" (*gandhādyadhivāsitaṃ*), referring to what was previously mentioned.

Having taken in his joined palms (añjali) a cloth made of *kalpa*-fibers, scented with musk and other perfumes, possessing threads of appropriate purity for each specific rite, provided with a lesser number of threads [than prescribed], and accompanied by flowers— having placed it within his joined palms—
he [recites] the mantra consisting of words; here, the word "word" (*pada*) indicates that which expresses [the meaning].
Here, Amara-datta [states]:
"The word *pada* denotes resolve (*vyavasita*), protection (*trāṇa*), place (*sthāna*), characteristic (*lakṣma*), foot (*aṅghri*), and object (*vastu*).
This means it consists of a collection of words intended to illuminate the address. *Oṃ* is for the purpose of illuminating the mantra.
O Lord of the fulfillment of all flawless rites, you who are capable of perfecting every deviation in ritual action, toward me at each sacrifice...
O Lord, O Master, I— acting to fulfill Your will and having obtained the necessary requisites through Your will and Your command— invoke You to accept a special worship; I seek Your permission.

Therefore, O Lord of the conscious and the unconscious—the Lord of both the conscious souls (*cidātman*) and the unconscious powers such as *māyā*—grant permission for the success of my endeavor; that is, command the accomplishment of the fruit of the rite known as *pavitra*. In every way, by all means, at all times, and forever, let there be salutation unto me!

"Be gracious; be pleased"—this is another form of address, as in "you have been addressed," etc. Regarding the rule for the duration of the observance (*niyama*) until the end of the vow: in the case of immediate consecration (*adhivāsa*), having first performed the preliminary consecration on a single day, immediately thereafter, in the case of the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitra-samarpaṇa*), it is at dawn.

Regarding the term *pavitraka*, one should say "the *pavitraka* at the time of immediate [purification] (*sadyaḥkāla*)," because it has been stated that when the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is properly restrained by means of exhalation (*recaka*), it proceeds correctly upwards.

Together with the yoga of exhalation (*recaka*), one should [contemplate] the root *Śiva-mantra* until its dissolution, reaching as far as the *dvādaśānta*. Thus it is said in the *Kāmika*: "In this way, [the mantra] is joined with the knots, fashioned from the threads of *kalpa*."
Having taken up incense fumigated with flowers, the Guru [places it] in his joined palms.
"That [offering] is consecrated by the invocation; it is rendered delicious by the nectar-mudrā.
Having placed it upon the head of Śivā with the exhaling breath (recaka) and the Śiva-mantra," so it is said. And in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:

Having thus addressed Śiva and meditated upon Him, one should utter His root mantra along with the *recaka* breath, and after pronouncing the name ending in "Śiva," one should offer auspicious scented thread (*sūtra*) upon the head of the excellent Liṅga for the sake of Śiva. After the offering of the scented purifier (*gandhapavitra*), he states what is to be performed next with the words beginning "with incense, lamps, and so forth": [The text continues: "With incense, lamps, and other offerings, [one should worship] the Lord of the World, who is the embodiment of all deities, who is the supreme Brahman, and who is the essence of all mantras. Having offered these, one should perform the *japa* of the mantra as prescribed, and then offer the *arghya* water. [The text continues: "Then, having worshipped the Lord with flowers, perfumes, and unguents, one should offer the *naivedya* (food offering). One should offer various kinds of food, including milk-rice, sweetmeats, and fruits, as well as betel leaves and other delicacies. Having offered this, one should perform the *pradakṣiṇā* and prostrations. [The text continues: "Then, having offered the *tāmbūla* (betel nut) and other items, one should recite hymns of praise. Having thus completed the ritual, one should take leave of the Lord and depart. [The text concludes: "Thus, by performing this worship with devotion, one attains the state of Śiva; there is no doubt about this."

By the phrase "with lamps and so forth," items such as the parasol and fly-whisk are included. Regarding the fire-ritual, he describes that action with the words beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*); [he takes] the third portion of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) which has been divided for the sake of the fire.

Having offered the third portion that has been obtained and having given it to the limbs of Brahmā, one should present the *pavitra* to the limbs of Brahmā— who have been worshipped as subordinate to Śiva, who is the locus of the fire—
along with the root mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of expiation and for liberation from defects such as omissions, according to the scriptural injunction.

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of pacifying defects of deficiency or excess in the rite of *adhivāsana*. One should restrain the auspicious [deity] abiding in the fire by means of the *niṣṭhura* (harsh) *mudrā*. Regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblations:
there are four oblations beginning with the fire. In the phrase "having sipped water" (*samācamya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) follows immediately after the offering of the *bali*.
Because it is prescribed, one should perform the salutation of the ear or breath-control (prāṇāyāma). [One should offer] Śiva, who resides within the maṇḍala, to the surrendered [soul].

One should also worship with the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* offering that which remains of the rite (*kriyā*) or the action yet to be performed, and then bring it to rest. Now, he describes the protection of the purified *pavitra* following its consecration (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the words "purified" (*pūte*): in a vessel that is pure (*pūte*), clean (*śuddhe*), and made from bamboo or similar materials (*vaṃśādisambhave*), such as one fashioned from reeds (*veṇvādinirmite*).

Having placed [the vessel] in a casket and wound it with threads—since this procedure is prescribed here—it means that one remains in that which has the *kalaśa* as its very arrangement (*āyatana*) and configuration (*saṃsthāna*). Thus it is said in the *Dīkṣā*: "Having established it near [the altar] for the sake of protection, he stands by the *kalaśa* as the protector of the sacrifice."

Because it will be explained later that one must be protected from obstacles and the like, one should inform [the teacher] accordingly. According to the statement of Somaśambhu: "One should go near the feet of one's guru—whether he possesses the book of the Siddhānta or the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha)—and with devotion offer the pavitraka."
351) He states what must be done immediately thereafter with the words "vahnir" and so forth. "Outside" means outside the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
According to the previously stated procedure, following the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), there is the eating of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

Having performed that, one should thereafter perform the cleansing of the teeth. Even one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) should act in this same way; thus, one should partake of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth.

According to the *sadyojāta* seat tradition, one may perform the subsequent rites without having first consumed the *pañcagavya* and so on. This is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the sacred thread (*pavitra*).

Having thus described the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the *pavitra* and other items, he states with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*) what must be performed for the rite of offering the *pavitra*: the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the sacrificial ground of the pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapabhūmi*), and the deity— the Śiva residing within the *liṅga*.

Since it was not stated that the dismissal (*visarjana*) should take place on the preceding day, one should perform the dismissal only after taking the fragrant *pavitra* and setting it aside elsewhere; otherwise, there would be a need for its re-offering once again.
Because it is unfit [for the mouth], and because the teachers have stated that even a *gandhapavitra* (scented purifier) should be given at the time of bestowing the *pavitra*,

one should set aside the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), water, flowers, and so forth; then, taking up the materials required as limbs of the vow, one performs the two daily rites— namely, the morning and midday duties— as indicated by the phrase "the two daily [rites]" and so on.

Having recited the verse beginning with "The one named Sūrya, the distinguished self of time," and so forth— where "having recited" means having performed the recitation of the two verses to be spoken hereafter, starting from "Because he is the self of time"— and having recited "O Śambhu" as "O Bhānu," one should offer the *pavitra* to Śiva-Sūrya. Now, prior to the offering of the *pavitra* to the Deity:

Regarding what is to be done, he says "having fully worshipped Śiva," and so forth; that is, having fully worshipped Śiva residing in the chosen *liṅga*, one should perform a special worship according to one's capacity following the daily worship (*nityapūjā*). Thus it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"One should perform worship according to one's means immediately after the daily [worship]."

"Having cleansed the teeth, one should place [the substances]— true ashes and clay— along with the fruits of the dhātrī tree into vessels in the directions beginning with Indra and ending with Śaṅkara. Thus it is said.

After the offering of the materials for the observance (*vrata-bhoga-aṅga-dravya*), one should present the sacred threads (*pavitrāṇi*). In this offering of materials, only fresh water, saffron, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), betel leaves (*tāmbūla*), and incense sticks (*cakra*) should be given; all other items are those already offered on the previous day.

Now, preceded by the prayer for his own desired object, he describes the installation of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) for the Lord himself with the verse beginning "O Soul of Time" (*kālātmanā*): "O Soul of Time, consisting of the moments of *truṭi*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*,
*muhūrta*, *yāma*, day and night, fortnight, month, season, year, *yuga*, and infinite *kalpas*..."

He is the "Soul of Time" (Kālātman), because time— consisting of sixteen states, excluding the two states known as *vāyā* and *māyāminī* within the eighteen states called the *mahākalpa*— is that which is eternally presided over by his own body.
Thus it has been said:
"The God who consists of the non-existence of all things exists within the universe of the moving and the unmoving;
Maheśvara, whose form is the universe, is conceived in the form of Time. (p. 354)
O God, whatever afflicted action has been performed by you in my rite—that is, in my ritual procedure—how was it afflicted?

For indeed, when the Blessed Lord Maheśvara is worshipped with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), an action lacking those offerings is called "afflicted. It is not merely afflicted; [it is something more].

Even regarding that which is indeed set aside (*samutsṛṣṭa*)— namely, the procedure for the worship of the Blessed One taught in the scriptures through the ten consecrations (*saṃskāra*) such as invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth— if, due to ignorance,
one omits some of those consecrations and the worship is nevertheless performed, that is called "set aside. The same applies to the heart [mantra] as well.

Even from the perspective of conditioned cognition, when an action is performed without prior awareness— having been diverted by distraction due to the exigencies of a task— that karma is said to be "stolen" (*hṛta*). Thus, even this fourfold karma is considered "done by me."
"O Śambhu, whatever has been done by me that was afflicted, let it become unafflicted; whatever was poorly performed,
let it be made excellent, complete, and fulfilled— just as it should be."

By this, there is a simultaneous designation (*tantra*) of those who have abandoned, those who have taken [the vow], and those who are protected, because all of them have been rendered non-existent [in their worldly state].

However, specifically by your will— that is, by your command— through that which has been performed with the whole self (*sarvātmanā*) as a fulfiller in every fourfold action, [he is one] whose own nature is such, or else, by the whole self.

By means of this purifier—which, by being of the nature of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) and so forth, is all-pervasive, meaning it fills everything—fill, fill the gaps in all actions characterized by affliction and the like. Here, the repetition [of the verb] is intended to demonstrate the excellence of complete fulfillment. *Magha* is the sacrifice; *vrata* is the vow.
The observances such as the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, non-anger and so forth, the Maghā constellation, the vow (vrata), and the restraint (niyama)—these are the "Maghā-vrata-niyamas.

He is their lord and master; regarding the phrase "to him svāhā," the word *sva* here denotes the Self (*ātman*), according to the rule that one should state synonyms for the sake of metrical symmetry. The prefix *ā-* signifies bringing or taking; thus, the meaning is: "I offer myself"—that is, I announce my own self. As it has been said by the learned: "The Self is to be called 'Brahman,' and nothing other than the Self."

"Obeisance! You have [the power] within Your hand. Then, he states that the *pavitra*—which consists of the triad of principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*) and is known as the "Descent of the Gaṅgā"—must also be offered by means of the specific recitation of the root mantra, using the words "pervading up to the principle of *prakṛti*" and so forth; here, by the word *prakṛti*, that which is beyond the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) is meant.

*Prakṛti* is called *māyā*. According to many scriptural passages, such as "The *ātman-tattva* ends with *māyā*," because of the pervasion by the mantra, and because of the statement that *māyā* is a *tattva*, the *ātman-tattva*—as described in the Śrutis and other texts—is the pervader of the portion of the path ending with *māyā*. In all these instances, the locative case (*saptamī*) has the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).

Some, however, maintain that the locative case here has the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); they explain this by supplying the word "Śiva" as the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), meaning "therein [is] Śiva. Regarding the phrase "protected by Brahmā," this Brahmā is as described in the venerable *Kiraṇa-tantra* and other scriptures.
One who abides on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) is indeed pure. Now, some say he is "prākṛta" (belonging to primordial nature),
because here— as with the *mantras* and *mantreśvaras* through the division of *aṇu*, *śakti*, and *śambhu*— the Lords of Causes (*kāraṇeśas*) are likewise threefold.

The Gurus maintain that it is specifically the powers of Śiva, conjoined with the presiding deities such as Brahmā and the rest, that are designated there by the terms "Brahmā" and so forth. This has been stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"Though he is one, he exists in five ways through the distinctions of his names. This is the nature of the *saṃdhyā*.

This has been explained in detail in that very section; it should be noted there. Regarding the phrase "having uttered up to Māyā" (*māyāntamuccārya*), by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication), the term "up to Māyā" here refers to the principle of Śuddhavidyā.

Having meditated upon the *vidyā-tattva*, which pervades the portions of the path ending with *māyā*, and upon Śiva as its presiding deity, one should recite the mantra beginning with the letter *a*— which denotes Rudra and illuminates everything up to the end of *māyā*— and place the *pavitra* upon the top of the *liṅga*. In this same manner, at the time of offering the second *pavitra*, [one should do so] up to the end of the *śuddhavidyā-tattva*.

Regarding the term "pervasive" (*vyāpaka*), the intention is that the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) pervades the portion of the path up to the end of the principles; having meditated upon Śiva as its presiding deity,
one should "utter the principle of Īśvara," which means uttering the mantra signifying Īśvara— which illuminates the path ending with Īśvara— and terminating in the *bindu*.
One should place [the thread] upon the top of the *liṅga*.
Regarding the utterance "ending with Śiva" during the offering of the third purifier (*pavitra*): here, the limit is "ending with Śiva-Śakti.

That which has that as its boundary is such; it means that the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) pervades everything up to the end of the path of the principle of Śakti (*śaktitattvādhvan*). [One should offer it] to the presiding lord of that.

Having meditated upon Śiva, one should utter for him the mantra ending with Sadāśiva and culminating in the *nāda-kalā*, and then present the sacred thread (*pavitra*). In this manner, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) [performs] the lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhikī*).

One who has been initiated by initiation (dīkṣā) should offer the three purifiers (pavitra). However, one who is desirous of enjoyment (bubhukṣu) and has been initiated by the two specific initiations pertaining to the material world—namely, that of the worldly path (lokadharminī) and that of the Śiva-path (śivadharminī)—should first utter up to the level of the Śiva-principle (śivatattva) and then offer the purifier of the Śiva-principle; after that, the purifier of the Vidyā-principle; and immediately following, the purifier of the Ātman-principle.

Having thus described the worship of Śiva— who is joined with the triad of foundations and who is designated as the portion of the path of principles (tattvādhvan) presided over by the individual instruments— [the author] now states the worship [of Him] who resides as the triad of foundations collectively within all the principles, beginning with the words "afterwards" (*paścāt*), etc., [referring to Him] who is protected by all causes, starting from Brahmā.

When protected by the five causes, the limit is the end of dissolution (*layānta*), which is the boundary of the twelve [fingers]. In this regard, concerning those who desire enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), some [say] that even the upper [state]—p.

The *pavitraka* of the Śiva-tattva, which was first superimposed by virtue of its abiding in the state of the *vidyā*-tattva and so forth, is extracted after the *pavitraka* of the *vidyā*-tattva has been superimposed; having been extracted, it is placed above that. They say that the same applies to that which consists of the *ātman* and the *vidyā*.

That is incorrect, because such a scriptural authority is observed, and because it is possible through the three rings existing in an upward and downward position according to different measurements. As it is said in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"The circumference at the top of the *liṅga* is exactly like that of the self."
The extent of the Vidyātattva is then [the same], excluding two parts.
"Therefore, that sacred thread (*pavitraka*) called Śiva, which is deficient by two parts.
Regarding what is to be done immediately thereafter, he says,
beginning with "having joined the palms in a handful of flowers," up to the point where the state characterized by liberation (*mukti*) is described.
In the Śrīmat-Svāyambhuva (p.
"That which is the final state of a person whose seed of transmigratory existence has been burnt..."
That should be understood as his destination; there is no remaining in another body.

Thus [it is said]. In the *Parākhya*, it is stated: "That attainment is its state of equality. Since movement is impossible for the Supreme Lord, it should be understood that He is denoted by that [attainment] because it is the cause thereof. He is established in all living beings, both moving and unmoving, stationary and animate, existing as their presiding controller. Likewise, through His internal movement, He is the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*).

The observer of auspicious and inauspicious karma; the witness of action through physical activity, by means of the mind such as meditation and so forth, or by speech in the form of praise and the like; "the destination" (*agati*)—meaning that You alone are the object of the actions of my body, mind, and speech, such as meditative concentration (*saṃdhyāna*); "the uncreated," fallen away.
Whatever [rites] such as the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsanā*) may be, they are devoid of speech; likewise, greetings, inquiries after one's welfare, and so forth, are devoid of speech.
[He who performs them thus] is thoroughly purified—meaning he is exceedingly pure.

"Pure" means beginningless and stainless; by that very nature it is "sacred," because it protects one from falling. Therefore, it is the supreme destroyer of sin; having destroyed sin, lead living beings to the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*). Since such is Your character, the entire world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, has indeed been purified by You alone. [Pavitrī...]

That which has been performed becomes stainless and will remain so; therefore, through true devotion to the vow and the mantra, one should always perform proper worship and service to the Blessed One. Furthermore, fasting accompanied by the mantra, the ritual substances, and the constituent parts of the action is required; that which lacks even one of these parts is deficient, and the state of being thus deficient pertains to the self.

Therefore, whatever has been fragmented or rendered incomplete, may all that become unified and complete; since it is woven and strung together by the thread of Your command, may all that become complete—this is the meaning of "if You remember it, then it becomes so. Thus.
Regarding what must be done immediately after the request for instruction,
he says [in the verse] beginning with "incense and lamps" (dhūpadīpa): "the preceptor of all the gods"— here, "of all the gods" refers to...

By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that the practitioner should give the *pavitra* to all the deities stationed in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), including even those for whom the mantra is being accomplished (*sādhya*).
Some say this is because he has been initiated into the authority over them. Others, however, [hold that it applies] only to the deities worshipped during the daily rites (*nityakarman*).

The intended meaning is that one should perform the *pavitrāropaṇa* (the rite of offering the sacred thread). By the phrase "from the four months" (*caturmāsāt*) and so forth, it is meant that— having undertaken a vow and observance (*vrataniyama*) for either four months or three months, or for any other desired period among the previously mentioned options as instructed by the Guru— the term "vow" (*vrata*) refers here to practices such as eating only once a day (*ekabhukta*), up to the ultimate limit, prior to the aforementioned time.
Alternatively, that time limit which was personally indicated by the Guru himself, distinct from the aforementioned times, should also be observed.
Thus, one must not travel at a time other than the one thus regulated.
As it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
O Thousand-eyed One, one must not depart while the pavitra has not been dismissed;
but once it has been dismissed, one may indeed go wherever one pleases.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of filling and stabilizing the gaps in the ritual injunctions" (*vidhicchidra-pūrti-sthairyāya*), one should perform a *homa* for the purpose of stabilizing the purificatory rite (*pavitrakarma*) whose nature is the filling of gaps in the injunctions performed by oneself. Regarding what is to be done on the second day in the case of the one-day (*ekāha*) rite, he says, beginning with "on the following day" (*aparedyus*), etc., [referring to] one who desires liberation (*muktikāmaḥ*)—that is, one who desires enjoyment (*bhogecchuḥ*)—and one who desires liberation (*muktikāmaḥ*).
One desiring liberation should announce the vow as described in the *Kāmika* [Tantra], saying: "May this be the means for me to achieve the fruit.
One desiring worldly enjoyment, however, should say: "May this vow be an obstacle to that [liberation] through its action."

Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the method for the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the sacrifice. By means of the verse beginning with "O you who abide in the fire" (*vahnisthāya*), one [unites] the Lord Śiva, who resides in the fire, with the deity worshipped in the fire-pit through the conjunction of the path of the channels (*nāḍīmārga*).
Since it is stated that "Śiva is worshipped in the maṇḍala," one should perform the union [of the deity] with Śiva residing in the maṇḍala.
Immediately thereafter, one should recite the mantras— namely, the mantras denoting Śiva and his limbs, as well as the mantras for the enclosing fence and the sacrificial grass—
or alternatively, according to the rule "until the end of the worship of Caṇḍa," this should be done after the dismissal (visarjana) of Śiva from the fire.
Since it is prescribed later on that one should worship Caṇḍanātha and offer a hundred oblations without having performed the dismissal of the fire (*vahni-visarjana*),

one should worship even that Caṇḍanātha in the fire immediately after the worship of Caṇḍa, and having offered oblations, dismiss the fire at the conclusion of the ritual service (*upakarma*). Regarding the mandala, one should consider the specific requirements according to the appropriate substratum, such as one's own desired [deity], a *liṅga*, or other bases.
Regarding the phrase "or independent" (*nirapekṣaṃ vā*), one should dismiss that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*) while remaining in the desired *liṅga*.

The nature of dismissing the dependent and the independent has been explained in the context of the worship of Śiva. Thereafter, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the guardians of the directions, etc.," there is the inclusion of all deities worshipped in the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*).

The meaning is that one should dismiss, without dependence on others, the sequence of worship beginning with Guru Gaṇeśa and ending with the Pāduka (p. 366) in reverse order, just as the pure *pavitra* [threads] are [dismissed].
Having brought forth the logic here, these pure and sanctifying sets of four pavitras are prepared for Caṇḍa;
according to the rule, they are [applied] to Sūrya, Agni, Caṇḍeśa, Maheśa, and the Kumbha, with an abundance of threads as spoken by Śambhu.

Or, according to the procedure stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* and other texts, "in the case of an abundance of threads" (*sūtrasamṛddhau*), it is prescribed that in the event of a scarcity of threads, one should give only a single thread each to Caṇḍeśa and Kṣetrapāla; thus he says. Or, having first offered a single purifier (*pavitra*) as mentioned in another [text] to Caṇḍeśvara, the purifiers consisting of the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) from Ananta should also be given.

In the phrase *andhakupādikā*, one should burn in the fire the flower-garlands and other remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), as well as the pure and stainless purifiers (*pavitra*). Regarding the method for purifying the ground, [the author] states what is to be done immediately after the purification of the ground with the words beginning with *tataḥ* and continuing with *ācamed* and so forth.
p.

367) Having bathed as usual and worshipped even the deity previously worshipped—namely one's own chosen *liṅga*—because it was worshipped after having been set aside for the *pavitrāropaṇa*, in order to purify the *nirmālya*, one should worship it. Now,
He describes the sequence for the consecration (*adhivāsana*) and the offering of the purifier (*pavitra*) on a single day with the verse beginning "sadādhivāsa," and so forth:

even for one who observes the rules of the four-month period (*caturmāsya*) and other such observances, at the conclusion of the vow, having again performed the sacrifice as before and having dismissed [the deities] according to the stated procedure, he should perform the *iṣṭi*. He now describes the worship of one's own guru.

By the passage beginning with "The Guru should be worshipped like Śiva," he states that this rite of purification (*pavitraka*) must be performed only in the presence of the Guru; then, by the passage beginning with "Even though staying five *yojanas* away," he provides the conclusion of this section with the words "O Supreme Lord," thus [describing] the *pavitra*.

Having explained the procedure for worship, [the author] next states, beginning with the words "In Caitra," etc., that the procedure for the worship of *damana* must necessarily be performed, due to the fear of non-attainment— that is, the fear of failure.

If it is argued that there is fear of not obtaining the fruit of the merit of one's own performed Śiva-worship, an ancient legend (itihāsa) is written here: Formerly, there was a war between the gods and asuras, who were intoxicated by mutual pride and envy, which caused the sudden destruction of the world. A great anger arose in Hara, from which Bhairava was born. By that Bhairava—

Their pride was thus humbled. Consequently, because he subdued the gods and asuras, that Bhairava became known by the name Damana. Thereafter, thinking that it was not yet the time for the world to be destroyed by the mere sight of his unbearable splendor, [Śiva], though pleased by his prowess, acted for the welfare of the world.

Because Śiva had declared that he would become a tree on the surface of the earth named Bhairava, he manifested as such. Furthermore, a boon was granted to him, stating: "The merit resulting from the worship performed in the month of Caitra by those who shall perform the worship of this [tree] with sprouts and other offerings shall belong to you. Thus it is said in the *Svacchanda-bhairava*.

The ancient account as taught in the Tantra has been written in brief by Somaśambhu, as follows: "In former times, Bhairava named Damana was born from the wrath of Hara; by him, all the gods and the Dānavas were subdued."
Then Śiva, being pleased, said to those of great strength: "Become a plant on the surface of the earth; having assumed that body, you shall exist for my enjoyment.
Those mortals who worship you with sprouts and other parts, O Damana, shall go to the supreme abode through your power. But those who do not perform the *dāmana* [worship],"
To them, I have granted the fruit of merit arising from the month of Caitra;
although this has been proclaimed as a sacred seat (pīṭha) in the Svacchanda-bhairava Tantra.

Likewise, because it is similar here as well, this has been established even in our own Siddhānta. Therefore, since it was granted as a boon by the Supreme Lord himself, it is stated here in the *Paddhati* of Bhairava as well: "The practitioners (sādhakas) have adopted the ritual procedure for the Damanotsava festival, even though it was prescribed therein [in the Siddhānta] as an internal [practice]."
(370) But surely, O Guha, for those who are always disciples of the Śaiva Siddhāntas arising from the upward-facing [face],
neither the Tantric practice (tantrācāra) nor the Left-hand practice (vāmācāra) would be suitable.
"One should not practice mixed conduct; if one does so through negligence, there will be a downward fall"—according to this statement from the *Kālottara*.

If it is asked, "How then can that which is prescribed in a tantra other than the Siddhānta be performed?", do not say so. Although this was stated in the Bhairava Tantra, nevertheless, because of the granting of a boon by Īśvara to Bhairava, it must indeed be performed.

It is not logical to conclude that an *itihāsa* (ancient narrative) mentioned in one place is false merely because it is not recounted elsewhere; for if that were the case, it would follow that all historical events are untrue simply because they are not recorded in every source, which would result in the cessation of the practice of the fundamental dharma. [The method of worshiping Damana is described] by the words "that," and so forth, for one who has faith therein.
In that worship with *damanaka* flowers, one who possesses faith should perform the sacrifice as if it were a purificatory rite (*pavitra*).
By this [method], on the seventh or the thirteenth day, for the purpose of consecration (*adhivāsana*)— (p.

Having completed the sacrifice, one should perform the ritual actions up to the end of the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooked offering), preceded by the worship of the Sun and the Gatekeepers. Regarding the method of consecrating the *damanaka* plant: reciting "I am born of grace," one should go to a nearby garden—if it is situated close by—taking with one five parts of the plant along with its root, stalk, leaves, flowers, and fruit.
One should consecrate the *damanaka* plant. If it is located at a distance, one should bring it home, keep it protected, and then consecrate it.

As it is said: "Having gone near the *damanaka* on the seventh or thirteenth lunar day, and having consecrated it while it is still standing in its place, one should protect it and return to one's residence."
If one brings it from afar, together with its roots and the surrounding earth;
Having placed it back into a vessel filled with clay and having purified it with water,
the wise one should perform the consecration at home according to the previously stated procedure.
Thus it is said. For this very reason, it is stated here in the *Paddhati* (p.
"Having brought [the fire] to the vicinity of the house, or having performed [the rite] there, one should make it purified by the *saptāhutis* of the *pavitra*. Now, [the procedure continues]:
The manner of offering the *damanaka* along with the substances that are limbs of the vow is stated in the passage beginning with "one should offer," and so forth.

By the words "I am offered" (*arpito'smi*) and so on, he describes the subsequent rites. In the phrase "at the time of *sadyas*," this is stated concisely by resorting to the option of immediate consecration (*adhivāsana*), because of the injunction: "One should perform the sacrifice like the *pavitra* rite."

When the second [rite] occurs, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the previous day in the afternoon, everything should be carried out on the following day according to the prescribed procedure for the *pavitra* rite; such is the method for the offering of the *damanaka*. Then, with the words beginning "tataḥ" (thereafter), the manner of prayer after the offering of the *damanaka* is described, starting with "O Blessed One," and so forth, regarding the *dāmanaka*.
This is the flower-offering for the Damanaka festival on the auspicious day (parva).

Regarding the subsequent duties, [the text] says "to Agni and others" (agnyādibhyaḥ); by the word "others" (ādi), it is indicated that the Damanaka plant should also be offered to the gods of the inner hall and so forth.

By the statement "one should dismiss the sacrifice," it is indicated that after performing the dismissal of the deity residing in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), one should also perform the worship of Caṇḍa and then dismiss him. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of Damana.
I have written this commentary on the *Paddhati* composed by Ācārya Eka, by means of a twice-born man named Ākaṇḍa who worships his feet.
With his back, waist, and neck broken, his arms stiffened, and his face cast downward, he has written this book with great hardship; let it be preserved with care.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, which was brought to completion by the illustrious Śivācārya Kacchapeśvara.
Salutations to the illustrious Śiva and Śivā.
